insight.step: This week, take one conversation you've been putting off and have it on a walk.

options.label: A proper dinner

insight.reveal: Dating, to you, is worth dressing up for. You're the type to book ahead and pick the place with care. A long meal shows you a lot, too: how they treat the staff, and how they handle a quiet moment at the table.
insight.step: This week, notice how the people you meet treat staff and strangers. It says a lot.

options.label: Whatever they suggest

insight.reveal: Their comfort matters more to you than your own preferences. That makes you easy, generous company. It can also leave a date knowing less about you than they'd like, so sharing even one thing you love helps them see who they're actually with.
insight.research: Strangers who spent 45 minutes taking turns answering slowly deeper personal questions felt closer than pairs who made small talk.
insight.step: Next time someone asks what you'd like, name one real preference.

questions.prompt: Do you ever look at an ex's social media?

options.label: Never

insight.reveal: Once something ends, you close the door and keep walking. You move on fast and keep your eyes on what's ahead. Every so often, though, an old feeling may catch up with you all at once, set off by a song or a place you didn't see coming.
insight.step: Tonight, think of one good thing a past relationship taught you, and let it be just that.

options.label: Now and then, out of curiosity

insight.reveal: Exes are like old chapters you reread once in a while. For you it's usually about seeing how far you've come, not wishing you could go back. That same reflective streak may have you scrolling old photos and messages now and then, too.
insight.step: Next time you look, notice how you feel after. Then decide if it's worth it.

options.label: Mostly after a bad day

insight.reveal: On your hard days, the past can feel like a warm blanket. You're a sentimental, loyal person, and the ex is rarely the real point. The tough day is, which is why a call to a friend tends to comfort you more than the scroll ever does.
insight.step: Next bad day, message a friend before you open any profile.

options.label: More often than I'd admit

insight.reveal: That story may have ended before you were ready to let it go. You attach deeply and loyally, and checking keeps the door open a crack. That's very human, and closing it a little at a time, rather than all at once, is usually how the pull finally fades.
insight.research: In a month-long diary study after breakups, love and sadness faded over time, but faded more slowly for people who stayed in contact with their ex.
insight.step: This week, mute one account for seven days, just as a trial, and see how it feels.

questions.prompt: Early on, what makes you lose interest the fastest?

options.label: They're rude to a waiter

insight.reveal: How someone treats the person serving them tells you a lot. Decency beats charm for you every time. At work, too, you're likely to watch how a new manager speaks to the cleaner before deciding what you think of them.
insight.step: This week, notice someone who is kind to strangers and tell them you noticed.

options.label: They stay on their phone

insight.reveal: Full attention is the clearest sign of interest you know. You give it too, phone face down when you're with someone. And you notice fast, at work and with friends, when that attention isn't coming back.
insight.research: Couples were observed in everyday time together. When one partner tended to ignore the other's small bids for attention, their arguments more often turned into attack and defend.
insight.step: Next time you're with someone you care about, put your phone in a bag for the whole meal.

options.label: They seem too keen, too soon

insight.reveal: Slow and steady is how you like closeness to grow. Relationships built your way often rest on solid ground. The catch is that strong early interest can feel like pressure to you, even when it's really just warmth.
insight.step: Next time someone is very warm early, give it one more date before deciding.

options.label: They like me more than I like myself

insight.reveal: Easy affection feels odd when your inner voice is harsher. You probably hold yourself to high standards at work and everywhere else. When someone likes you more than you like yourself, the gap usually says more about how hard you are on yourself than about their taste.
insight.research: After chatting with someone new, people tend to underestimate how much the other person liked them, a gap that lasted for months between new roommates.
insight.step: Tonight, write down one thing a friend or past partner loved about you, and read it twice.

questions.prompt: Think of your past crushes. Do they have something in common?

options.label: Not really

insight.reveal: Your heart follows the person, not a pattern. You may have been surprised by who you fell for, and enjoyed it. That same open mind shows in your friends, the food you'll try and the places you want to see.
insight.research: Friends often judge traits like intelligence and creativity more accurately than we judge ourselves, while we know our own anxiety better than they do.
insight.step: This week, ask a close friend if they see a pattern you don't. Friends often notice more.

options.label: A similar look

insight.reveal: You know exactly what catches your eye first. You may have just as clear a sense of your own taste in clothes and design. The more telling part, though, is what kept you interested, which often has little to do with looks at all.
insight.step: Tonight, think of the person you liked the longest and name one thing you loved that wasn't their looks.

options.label: They were a little out of reach

insight.reveal: The chase makes you feel alive. You're probably ambitious and driven in other parts of life too. Calm, available people can seem a little dull at first, yet they sometimes turn out to be the deepest connections you'll ever have.
insight.research: In one small study, women who were unsure whether a man liked them thought about him more and felt more attracted than women told he liked them a lot.
insight.step: Next time someone kind and available shows interest, give it a second chance.

options.label: They remind me of someone in my family

insight.reveal: You're drawn to what feels like home, whatever home was like. Spotting that takes real self-awareness, and it changes things. Once you can see the pull, you get to choose which parts of home you want more of, and which you'd rather leave behind.
insight.step: This week, name one family trait you'd love in a partner, and one you'd rather not repeat.

questions.prompt: Someone you like is replying more slowly than usual. What do you do?

options.label: Assume they're busy

insight.reveal: You don't build stories out of small silences. That makes you easy company, since you don't need constant reassurance. You likely bring the same calm to a late email from your boss or a friend who cancels plans.
insight.step: Next time a friend worries about a slow reply, share your calm reading with them.

options.label: Check when they were last online

insight.reveal: You can turn a tiny clue into a very big meaning. You're quick to spot patterns, which is useful in lots of places. Here, though, checking usually hands you a fresh question instead of calming the first one.
insight.research: Adults differ in attachment anxiety (worry about rejection) and attachment avoidance (discomfort with closeness), and both shape how relationships feel.
insight.step: Next time you want to check, set your phone face down for twenty minutes first.

options.label: Slow my replies to match

insight.reveal: Keeping things even is how you keep yourself safe. Fairness and self-respect matter to you, and that's healthy. Matching silence with silence, though, can turn two interested people into two careful strangers before either one says what they want.
insight.step: Next time, reply at your natural pace and see what happens.

options.label: Quietly start losing interest

insight.reveal: You switch off early, before anything has a chance to hurt. You're good at protecting your energy, and that has its uses. It can also end something that only needed one honest question, like a simple 'is everything all right?'
insight.step: Next time you feel interest fading, ask once: "Still keen to meet?"

questions.prompt: Someone great wants to make it official. What do you feel first?

options.label: Happy, let's do it

insight.reveal: Commitment feels like a door opening for you, not closing. You likely bring the same easy yes to new jobs, new cities and new friends. Your enthusiasm makes people feel chosen and safe with you, which is a lovely thing to give someone.
insight.research: Across 43 studies of over 11,000 couples, feeling that a partner was committed was among the strongest predictors of happiness together, far more than either partner's personality.
insight.step: This week, tell someone close to you about something that's making you happy.

options.label: Nervous, in a good way

insight.reveal: Big moments give you butterflies, and that's a good sign. You may feel the same flutter before a new job or a long trip. Those nerves usually mean something matters to you, not that something's wrong.
insight.step: Next time you're nervous about something good, tell yourself it's excitement.

options.label: A little trapped

insight.reveal: Your freedom matters to you, maybe more than you say. You do best in a relationship where you keep your own friends, plans and space. That trapped feeling is often less about this person and more about the fear of losing yourself.
insight.research: Adults differ in attachment anxiety (worry about rejection) and attachment avoidance (discomfort with closeness), and both shape how relationships feel.
insight.step: This week, name one thing you'd keep for yourself in any relationship, and plan to say it early.

options.label: Doubt they really mean it

insight.reveal: Even good news makes you wait for the catch. Once you commit, you're probably loyal and careful. That doubt usually comes from older stories, not from anything this person has done, and it can soften one kept promise at a time.
insight.step: Next time someone says something kind, try answering with just "thank you" and let it land.

questions.prompt: The bill arrives on a first date. What do you do?

options.label: Offer to split

insight.reveal: To you, fair is fair, even on a first date. Owing or being owed sits badly with you, in love and in friendship. After a group dinner you're happy to work out who paid what, and people trust you with it.
insight.step: This week, when someone owes you something small, let it go on purpose and see how it feels.

options.label: Pay, I invited them

insight.reveal: Generosity is one of the ways you show you care. You pick up the coffees or cover a friend's ticket without making a fuss. Giving lifts your own mood too, which may be part of why it feels so natural to you.
insight.research: Spending money on other people lifted people's happiness more than spending the same money on themselves.
insight.step: This week, treat someone to something small, for no reason at all.

options.label: Let them pay if they offer

insight.reveal: You're good at receiving, and that's harder than it sounds. You accept compliments and kind gestures without much awkwardness. Letting someone be generous is a kindness too, because it gives them a way to show they care.
insight.research: Across 27 studies with over 4,000 people, doing acts of kindness gave the kind person a small-to-medium boost in well-being.
insight.step: Next time someone offers you something, just say thank you instead of refusing first.

options.label: Freeze and wait to see what they do

insight.reveal: You're so careful about the rules that the bill can feel like a test. That care makes you tactful and considerate almost everywhere else. And here's a secret: the person across the table is very likely feeling the same small panic.
insight.research: In a survey of over 17,000 single adults, most said men still pay more, yet 64% of men felt women should chip in, and 76% of men felt guilty accepting a woman's money.
insight.step: Before your next shared meal, decide what you'll offer, so the moment is easy.

questions.prompt: On early dates, how much of the real you shows up?

options.label: All of it, take it or leave it

insight.reveal: You'd rather be turned down as you than liked as someone else. You might get fewer matches that way, but better ones. The same frankness shows up in job interviews and new friendships, and the people who stay really know you.
insight.step: This week, share one honest opinion in a setting where you'd usually stay neutral.

options.label: A polished version

insight.reveal: You treat a first date a bit like a job interview. You read what a moment calls for and rise to it, which is a real social skill. Still, the unpolished you, odd habits and all, is probably more interesting than you give yourself credit for.
insight.step: On your next new meeting, share one small odd thing you love.

options.label: It comes out over weeks

insight.reveal: You open slowly, but when you open, you open all the way. New coworkers and dates may underestimate you at first. Then, a few weeks in, they're surprised by how funny and deep you were all along.
insight.research: Strangers who took turns answering slowly deeper personal questions for 45 minutes felt closer than pairs who made small talk.
insight.step: This week, tell someone new one personal story a little earlier than you normally would.

options.label: There's one part I hide until I'm sure

insight.reveal: There's one part of you that you're scared might be too much. You're careful about who you trust, and that's wise. That hidden part, though, is usually far less strange to other people than it feels from the inside.
insight.research: People asked to share something hard and honest with someone close found it more pleasant and connecting than they expected, and listeners reacted better than feared.
insight.step: This week, share a small piece of that hidden part with a friend you trust.

questions.prompt: After a few dates, you're not feeling it. How do you end it?

options.label: A short, clear message

insight.reveal: Being clear is how you're kind. You don't hide behind vague words, at work or in love, so people tend to trust you even when the news isn't what they hoped. A short, honest no is a gift, even when it doesn't feel like one at the time.
insight.research: People tend to expect honest talks to hurt their relationships more than they do. In tests, being honest felt better and more connecting than people predicted.
insight.step: This week, say one clear no you've been putting off, kindly and briefly.

options.label: Tell them face to face

insight.reveal: You think people deserve to hear bad news from your own mouth. That takes courage, and it's often remembered with respect long after the sting fades. You'd probably be the kind of manager who delivers hard news in person, too.
insight.step: Next time you must give hard news, think of one kind true sentence to start with.

options.label: Reply less and less until it fades

insight.reveal: Drifting away feels kinder to you than saying something that hurts. You're gentle and you hate conflict, which is understandable. The fade, though, often leaves the other person guessing far longer than one short, kind message from you would.
insight.step: Next time, send one short honest line: "I enjoyed meeting you, but I don't feel a match."

options.label: Keep going a bit longer so they're not hurt

insight.reveal: You carry other people's feelings like they're your own. That kindness is real. The same habit can keep you in jobs, plans and friendships long after you already know they're over, and staying out of guilt isn't really a gift to anyone.
insight.research: Across four studies, helping because you chose to boosted the well-being of both helper and helped, while helping under pressure did not bring the same benefits.
insight.step: This week, notice one thing you're doing only to avoid disappointing someone, and plan a kind way out.

questions.prompt: A stranger on the street looks lost. What do you do?

options.label: Walk over and ask if they need help

insight.reveal: You act first and wonder later. You speak up when a meeting stalls, or ask the driver which stop it is instead of squinting at the signs. Now and then you rescue someone who was only checking their map, and you both end up laughing about it.
insight.step: This week, offer help to one stranger before they ask.

options.label: Help if they ask me

insight.reveal: You'd hate to barge into a stranger's day uninvited. Once someone asks, though, you go all in and might walk them the whole way there. Most lost people feel relief, not intrusion, when a kind face offers first, so your politeness can afford a step forward.
insight.step: Next time you see someone confused, make eye contact and smile. That alone invites them to ask.

options.label: Assume someone else will help

insight.reveal: You admitted something that usually stays unspoken. In a crowd, it's easy to assume someone else will step in. In real life, though, someone usually does step in, and noticing your own pause is how you become the person who goes first.
insight.research: In 219 real street conflicts caught on camera in three countries, someone stepped in to help in 9 out of 10, and more bystanders meant help was more likely, not less.
insight.step: Next time you think "someone else will", be that someone, once.

options.label: I want to help but feel too shy

insight.reveal: Your heart is already halfway across the street. You spot someone's trouble from a distance, then the words get stuck, and later you replay it and wish you'd said something. One ready line, like 'Are you looking for somewhere?', can carry you the rest of the way.
insight.research: Across 94 studies, making a specific when-then plan ("When X happens, I will do Y") had a medium-to-large effect on reaching goals.
insight.step: This week, make a when-then plan: "When I see someone looking lost, I'll ask: can I help you find something?"

questions.prompt: A neighbour you barely know asks you to water their plants for a week.

options.label: Say yes, happily

insight.reveal: To you, a spare key is the start of a friendship. You take in deliveries, feed the cat next door and somehow get invited whenever there's food. Your key ring may well hold more keys than you have doors.
insight.research: On days when people had more chats with casual acquaintances, not just close friends, they tended to feel happier and a stronger sense of belonging.
insight.step: This week, introduce yourself to someone who lives near you but whose name you don't know yet.

options.label: Say yes, then worry I'll forget

insight.reveal: You say yes, then set three reminders for one watering can. A promise sits heavy with you, even a small one, and the plants will probably do better with you than with their owner. The only cost is your own calm, which deserves the same care you give those plants.
insight.research: Habits tend to grow when one simple action is repeated after the same daily cue.
insight.step: Next time you say yes to something small, tie the reminder to a daily habit, like brushing your teeth.

options.label: Find an excuse

insight.reveal: Your home is your quiet place, and you guard the door. You know the people next door by face more than by name, which suits you fine. The catch is that small swaps of help are how strangers turn into people you can call when your own pipe bursts.
insight.step: This week, do one tiny good turn for someone nearby that fits your own schedule.

options.label: Say yes, then wish I'd said no

insight.reveal: Your yes often comes out before you've checked how you feel. A week of someone else's chores seems easier than five awkward seconds of no, so your calendar fills with other people's plans. The kindness is real. It just deserves a quick pause first.
insight.research: Helping because you chose to tended to boost the well-being of both the helper and the person helped, while helping under pressure did not bring the same benefits.
insight.step: Next request you get, say "Let me check and get back to you" before answering.

questions.prompt: Some unexpected extra money arrives. What would you enjoy most?

options.label: Saving it

insight.reveal: You'd rather have breathing room than a new thing. You can happily wait for the things you want, and that patience adds up over the years. The tricky part for you is the spending: even a treat you've fully earned can feel like it needs a good excuse.
insight.step: Next time extra money turns up, spend a tiny part on something purely fun and notice how it feels.

options.label: A treat for myself

insight.reveal: You celebrate good luck while it's still warm. You're fun to be around when things go right, and you don't wait for a perfect moment to enjoy life. One small twist: looking back, a good evening out will probably make you happier than a new thing.
insight.research: A review of happiness research suggested money brings more joy when spent on experiences, on others, on many small treats rather than one big one, and on things to look forward to.
insight.step: Next treat, choose an experience instead of an object and compare how long the happy feeling lasts.

options.label: A day out or trip

insight.reveal: You'd trade a new gadget for a good story any day. What you keep from a year is moments: a walk, a meal, a trip with someone you like. Ask you about your best day this year, and you'll describe a place, never a purchase.
insight.research: People often report that experiences they paid for made them happier than possessions they bought.
insight.step: This week, plan one small outing with someone you like: a new walk, or a meal somewhere you've never tried.

options.label: Quietly spending it on someone else

insight.reveal: Your best gifts are the ones nobody knows came from you. You remember the thing a friend mentioned wanting months ago, then turn up with it on an ordinary day. A quiet gift lifts you more than anything you'd buy yourself, which is a lovely kind of selfish.
insight.research: Spending money on other people lifted people's happiness more than spending the same money on themselves.
insight.step: This week, buy a small surprise for someone and don't tell anyone else.

questions.prompt: Where are you with volunteering?

options.label: I do it regularly

insight.reveal: Giving is part of your week, not a mood that comes and goes. Through it you've likely made friends of every age, people you'd never have met otherwise. On a slow, rainy weekend, you have somewhere to be and someone who's glad you came.
insight.step: Next time you volunteer, bring one friend along.

options.label: Now and then, when someone asks

insight.reveal: A friend's ask moves you more than any poster ever could. You help through people rather than causes, so your help tends to land exactly where it's needed. When someone's plans fall apart, they know they can call you.
insight.step: This week, ask one friend if there's anything they could use a hand with.

options.label: I keep meaning to start

insight.reveal: Your care is real, but 'someday' keeps winning. Full weeks push good plans to the back, and there may be a website or two you saved and never opened again. Picking an actual day, place and time is usually what turns 'soon' into a first visit.
insight.research: Across 94 studies, making a specific when-then plan ("When X happens, I will do Y") had a medium-to-large effect on reaching goals.
insight.step: This week, try a when-then plan: "When I finish breakfast on my day off, I'll look up one place nearby that needs help."

options.label: I help in private, informal ways instead

insight.reveal: Your kindness rarely comes with a name tag. You drive people places, drop off meals and fix things without fuss, and nobody keeps a list. That everyday kind of help is far more common than signing up to volunteer, and those close to you may only notice how much you carry once you're away for a week.
insight.research: In 2023, 28% of Americans volunteered through an organisation, but 54% informally helped neighbours, like running errands or lending tools.
insight.step: This week, keep up one quiet kindness and let it stay unseen.

questions.prompt: You helped someone a lot and nobody noticed. How do you feel?

options.label: Fine, that wasn't the point

insight.reveal: You'd help the same way with the lights off. Whether or not anyone's watching, you act the same, and people sense it. At work you get trusted with the sensitive stuff, and friends bring you the secrets they'd tell nobody else.
insight.research: A trait called Honesty-Humility predicts integrity and rule-breaking at work better than the classic five personality traits alone.
insight.step: Today, do one small helpful thing that nobody will ever trace back to you.

options.label: I find a way to mention it

insight.reveal: Wanting your effort to be seen is completely fair. You're good at making invisible work visible, the kind that otherwise vanishes into 'it just got done'. A hint can get missed, though, while a plain 'I worked hard on that' usually lands and feels better too.
insight.step: Next time you feel unseen, say simply: "I worked hard on that, I'd love a thank-you."

options.label: A little hurt, honestly

insight.reveal: That little sting shows how much care you put in. You put more thought into helping than ever shows: the timing, the details, the extra step nobody asked for. Hoping someone notices doesn't make it less generous. It just means you're human.
insight.research: People writing thank-you letters tended to underestimate how happy and surprised the receiver would be.
insight.step: This week, thank someone for an effort nobody else mentioned, and notice how it feels.

options.label: I remember it for a long time

insight.reveal: You keep a quiet record of the help nobody thanked. You notice what's unfair straight away, and you'd never short-change anyone yourself. Over the years, though, that record can grow heavier than the help ever was, and you're allowed to set some of it down.
insight.step: This week, pick one old unthanked effort and let it go with one sentence: "I did that because I wanted to."

questions.prompt: You're struggling with something. How easily do you ask for help?

options.label: Easily

insight.reveal: Asking for help feels as normal to you as offering it. That makes others feel trusted and useful, so they tend to show up fast. You sort out problems sooner because you don't struggle alone, and you rarely carry something heavy longer than you have to.
insight.research: In studies with over 14,000 strangers, people asking for help underestimated how many would say yes by about 48%, mostly because they forgot how awkward saying no feels.
insight.step: This week, ask someone for a small piece of advice, just to let them help.

options.label: Only for practical things

insight.reveal: You'll ask for help carrying boxes, but rarely for comfort. Help with jobs feels fair and easy to repay; help with feelings feels like owing too much. Yet the person who turns up to carry boxes would often happily sit and listen too.
insight.step: This week, tell one person how you're really feeling, not just what you need done.

options.label: Only when it's almost too late

insight.reveal: You hate the idea of your problems landing on anyone else. So you handle a surprising amount alone, and you're quick to help when someone else is struggling. Meanwhile your own pile keeps growing out of sight, and things are much easier to ask about while they're still small.
insight.step: This week, ask for help with one thing while it's still small.

options.label: I'd rather help someone else

insight.reveal: Giving care feels safer to you than needing it. In a crisis you're likely the steady one people call, knowing what to bring and what to say. Being on the receiving end can feel exposed, but the people who love you would welcome a turn at looking after you.
insight.research: Helping because you chose to tended to boost the well-being of both the helper and the person being helped.
insight.step: This week, let someone do one small thing for you, and simply say thank you.

questions.prompt: A coworker or classmate is clearly overwhelmed. What do you do?

options.label: Offer to take something off their plate

insight.reveal: For you, help means rolling up your sleeves. Your team leans on you more than they ever say. When a project gets rescued at the last minute, your name tends to come up, even if you'd rather it didn't.
insight.step: Next time you offer help, name one specific task instead of saying "let me know".

options.label: Bring them a coffee or snack

insight.reveal: A well-timed snack is your way of saying 'I see you'. You remember how each colleague takes their coffee, and who skips lunch when things get busy. Big rescues get the praise, but your small comforts often get someone through a long afternoon, and giving them probably lifts your mood too.
insight.research: Spending money on other people lifted people's happiness more than spending the same money on themselves.
insight.step: This week, surprise someone who's swamped with a small treat.

options.label: Wait until they ask

insight.reveal: You trust people to know what they need. You'd make the kind of manager who never hovers, and you give others the space you'd want yourself. Overwhelmed people rarely ask, though, which is partly how they got swamped, so one gentle question can open the door.
insight.step: Next time someone looks stressed, ask one gentle question: "How are you holding up?"

options.label: Keep my head down, I have my own pile

insight.reveal: You know your limits, and you're honest about them. You protect your energy so you can keep your own promises, and that isn't unkind. Still, a quick 'Rough week? Hang in there' takes ten seconds, and small kindnesses on busy days tend to steady your own mood too.
insight.research: In a daily diary study, on stressful days people who did more small helpful acts, like holding a door, kept their mood better than on stressful days when they helped less.
insight.step: This week, send one short kind message to a busy coworker or classmate.

questions.prompt: You find a wallet on the ground. What happens next?

options.label: Hand it in where it can be claimed

insight.reveal: Doing the right thing doesn't take you long to decide. You stay honest even when nobody would ever find out, and people pick up on it. You end up holding the spare key, the cash box or the sensitive file, without anyone quite saying why.
insight.research: A trait called Honesty-Humility predicts integrity and rule-breaking at work better than the classic five personality traits alone.
insight.step: Today, notice one small rule you keep even when no one is watching, and give yourself credit for it.

options.label: Look inside and contact the owner myself

insight.reveal: Passing a job on never feels quite finished to you. Lost emails get chased and forgotten tasks get closed when you're around. Secretly, you might enjoy the detective work a little, and the owner's relief when you track them down is half the reward.
insight.step: This week, finish one small task someone else started and forgot.

options.label: Leave it where it is, they may come back

insight.reveal: You picture the owner retracing their steps. You think from the other person's side first, which makes you patient and fair. Here, though, the wallet could wait a long time on the ground, and a nearby shop or front desk is often the kinder place to leave it.
insight.research: When 17,303 'lost' wallets were handed to staff at banks, hotels and offices in 40 countries, people returned 51% of those with money in them and 40% of those without.
insight.step: Next time you see something lost, ask a nearby shop or staff member what to do.

options.label: Return it, then wonder if they'd do the same

insight.reveal: You do the right thing, then wonder if it's a two-way street. You hold yourself to high standards and hope others will meet them too. That question isn't bitterness. It shows how much you want people to be good, and you light up a little every time a stranger proves you right.
insight.research: People tend to expect lost wallets to be returned about half as often as they really are.
insight.step: This week, notice one example of a stranger being kind and remember it.

questions.prompt: Which small kindness did you do most recently?

options.label: Held a door or let someone go first

insight.reveal: Little courtesies come so easily you've stopped counting them. You're part of what makes shops, buses and offices feel human. Over a year you've held a hundred doors, and at least one of them was for someone having a truly terrible day.
insight.step: This week, add one word to the gesture: a smile and "after you".

options.label: Checked on someone who'd gone quiet

insight.reveal: You notice who's missing, not just who's there. You spot the silence when someone stops replying in the group chat, or when a colleague is suddenly skipping lunch. Your message often arrives at exactly the right moment, and you may never find out how much it meant.
insight.research: People tend to underestimate how much someone will appreciate a quick message out of the blue, especially when it comes as a surprise.
insight.step: This week, check on one more person who has gone quiet for a while.

options.label: Gave a stranger a real compliment

insight.reveal: When you think something nice about someone, you say it. Waiting rooms and slow checkouts get brighter when you're in them. A sincere compliment from a stranger is the kind of thing people repeat to friends that evening, so some of yours are still being talked about.
insight.research: People about to give a compliment tend to underestimate how good it will make the other person feel.
insight.step: This week, give someone one specific compliment about a choice they made, not their looks.

options.label: I can't think of one

insight.reveal: Your kindness may be so automatic you've stopped seeing it. Or this season is so full there's barely room to notice anything. Either way, you do more for others than you give yourself credit for, and one day of paying attention would surprise you.
insight.research: Across 27 studies with over 4,000 people, doing acts of kindness gave the kind person a small-to-medium boost in well-being, whoever they were and whatever the kindness.
insight.step: Tomorrow, do one small kind thing on purpose, and notice how it feels.

questions.prompt: Someone asks a favour you really don't have time for. You…

options.label: Say no

insight.reveal: You trust a good friendship to survive an honest no. People may ask you a little less often, but when you say yes, they know you mean it. That makes your yes worth a great deal, and your calendar stays yours.
insight.step: Next time you say no, add one thing you can do, even if it's small.

options.label: Offer a smaller version

insight.reveal: Somewhere between yes and no, you always find a path. 'I can't help all day, but I can come for the first hour' is very you. You protect your time and the friendship at once, and you teach people, without a word, what's fair to ask.
insight.research: Helping because you chose to tended to boost the well-being of both the helper and the person helped, while helping under pressure did not bring the same benefits.
insight.step: This week, have one line ready: "I can't do all of that, but I can do this part."

options.label: Say yes and stretch myself

insight.reveal: Being useful is a big part of how you feel good about yourself. You're the dependable one in every group, which is lovely and also tiring. The same stretch shows up at work and at home, and the people who rely on you would cope with a 'not this time' now and then.
insight.step: Next time you want to say yes automatically, pause for one breath and ask: do I have time?

options.label: Say yes, then do it late or half-heartedly

insight.reveal: Your yes saves an awkward moment, then costs you later. You're warm and you hate letting people down, which is exactly why no feels so hard to say. A late, half-done job weighs more than a clear no ever would, and the person asking would honestly rather hear it early.
insight.step: Next time, say "Let me check" first, then answer within a day.

questions.prompt: Think of a really good day you had. What made it good?

options.label: Everything went to plan

insight.reveal: For you, a good day is one where nothing went wrong. With you around, tickets are booked and the charger is packed days ahead. The twist is that trips can feel oddly tiring, because every surprise lands on you as one more thing to handle.
insight.step: On one free day this week, leave one hour with no plan and notice how it feels.

options.label: I finally finished something hard

insight.reveal: You like to earn your good mood before you enjoy it. You get a lot done, and finishing gives you a glow nothing else quite matches. A lazy day with nothing crossed off, though, can leave you restless, as if you skipped a step before being allowed to relax.
insight.research: In about 12,000 daily diaries from 238 workers, the best days tended to be the ones where people made progress on work that mattered to them.
insight.step: One evening this week, note one good thing that happened that you did not have to earn.

options.label: A long talk with someone I like

insight.reveal: Your best days happen in conversation. You remember a trip less by the views and more by who said what over dinner. A good talk can keep you going for days, and losing track of time in one is your idea of an evening well spent.
insight.research: When 909 working women went back over their previous day, time relaxing with friends tended to feel the most enjoyable part of it.
insight.step: Before the week ends, invite one person for a talk with no other purpose: a walk, a call, a tea.

options.label: Hours alone where nobody needed me

insight.reveal: Bliss, for you, is a few hours when nobody needs anything. You give a lot all week, mostly without complaining, to family, work and friends. Often you only feel how much it cost when the house goes quiet and you can finally hear yourself think.
insight.step: This week, put a two-hour 'nobody needs me' block in your calendar and guard it like a meeting.

questions.prompt: Something small goes well for you. Who do you tell first?

options.label: Nobody, I just enjoy it quietly

insight.reveal: You hold good news like a warm drink, slowly and privately. You're steady and don't need applause. The hidden cost is that friends rarely learn what makes you happy, so they miss chances to help you get more of it.
insight.research: Telling someone about a good thing that happened tends to lift your mood beyond the good news itself, especially when they respond with real interest.
insight.step: Next time something small goes well, tell one person within the hour and watch their face.

options.label: My partner or closest friend

insight.reveal: Good news isn't finished for you until one person has heard it. You reach for your phone mid-moment, already typing their name. That reflex says a lot about the room this person holds in your life, and they'd be touched to know it.
insight.step: This week, ask your closest person about their small win before you share yours.

options.label: The group chat, with a photo

insight.reveal: Happiness gets bigger for you the more people it bounces off. You're the spark of your group chat and quick to cheer others on too. The flip side is that a silent reply can make a good moment feel smaller than it was, even when everyone's just busy.
insight.research: When people shared good news, an eager, interested reply tended to add to their joy, while a flat or dismissive reply took some of it away.
insight.step: Next time you share good news, notice if the joy peaks before the replies arrive, or after.

options.label: Someone whose approval still matters to me

insight.reveal: Your win feels fully real once a certain someone has seen it. You may carry one person from long ago whose nod still counts most: a parent, a teacher, an old boss. That can push you to great things, but it can also end up picking your goals for you, so it's worth asking if they're still yours.
insight.step: After your next small win, wait one minute and decide how proud you are before telling anyone.

questions.prompt: An unexpected free afternoon appears. What do you do with it?

options.label: Rest on the sofa, no guilt

insight.reveal: Switching off on purpose is a real skill, and you have it. It's an easy one to lose on the way into adult life. You come back to your week genuinely refreshed, and the 'no guilt' part is worth even more than the resting itself, so hold on to it.
insight.research: Across 91 samples and 38,000 people, mentally switching off from work in free time went with less exhaustion, better well-being and better sleep.
insight.step: Next free hour, rest fully, then name one thing that made it feel restful.

options.label: Go somewhere I've never been

insight.reveal: New places fill you up instead of wearing you out. One unfamiliar street can stay with you longer than a month of ordinary weeks. You're likely to know a few hidden corners of your own town, found simply by turning down a street you'd never tried.
insight.step: This week, take a different route home or eat somewhere new, and notice what you remember a day later.

options.label: Catch up on tasks I've been avoiding

insight.reveal: Free time feels like a debt you have to pay off first. You enjoy rest far more once that one nagging job is done, and that's fair. The trouble is that the list grows to fill every gap if you let it lead, and the afternoon can vanish without any rest at all.
insight.step: Next free afternoon, do exactly one task, then spend the rest on something you enjoy.

options.label: Scroll my phone and somehow lose it

insight.reveal: When choosing feels like work, your phone chooses for you. That's often tiredness, not laziness, and you may be more stretched than you let on. The free afternoons you end up remembering are usually the ones you decided on in the first few minutes.
insight.research: Across 94 studies, making a specific when-then plan ("When X happens, I will do Y") had a medium-to-large effect on reaching goals.
insight.step: Next free afternoon, try a when-then plan: 'When free time appears, I'll pick one thing to do before I unlock my phone.'

questions.prompt: A friend shares big news online. What's your first honest feeling?

options.label: Pure happiness for them

insight.reveal: Other people's good news doesn't take anything from you. You measure your life against your own past, not your friends' highlights, so scrolling rarely dents your mood. No wonder friends want to tell you their news first.
insight.step: This week, send one friend a message saying exactly why their news made you happy.

options.label: Happy, then I quietly check my own life

insight.reveal: Your happiness for them comes with a quick, quiet scorecard. That's very human, and it shows you're ambitious and paying attention. Notice which part of your life you check first: work, love, money, home. It often points at what you want most right now.
insight.step: Next time you compare, notice which part of your life you checked, and name it in one word.

options.label: A small sting I'd never admit out loud

insight.reveal: You're honest enough to feel the sting and name it. That little envy is a signpost, not a flaw. It usually points at something you want but haven't let yourself go after yet, which makes it oddly useful once you stop being embarrassed by it.
insight.research: A friendly kind of envy, wanting what someone else has without wishing them harm, tended to push people to work harder, but only when they believed they could improve.
insight.step: Next time you feel that sting, ask: what exactly do I want here? Then pick one tiny step towards it.

options.label: I scroll past fast or mute them

insight.reveal: Sometimes you protect your mood by letting less in. That can be wise, especially in a hard week. Your friend may read the silence as distance, though, even when it was only about what you were carrying, and a late reply is still a warm one.
insight.research: In a large experiment, people paid to stop using Facebook for four weeks became a little happier and spent more time with family and friends.
insight.step: If you scroll past someone's news this week, come back a day later and react when you feel ready.

questions.prompt: Someone does something kind for you. How do you respond?

options.label: A quick thank you, then move on

insight.reveal: You like kindness light and even, so nobody owes anyone. You're easygoing and gracious, and you never make a fuss. The same balance can make asking for help feel hard, because asking tips the scales the other way.
insight.research: People who wrote thank-you letters underestimated how happy and surprised the receivers would feel, and expected far more awkwardness than there really was.
insight.step: This week, thank someone with one specific detail about what their kindness changed for you.

options.label: I feel I must return it soon

insight.reveal: You keep a careful note of who did what for you. You're a remarkably reliable friend, and borrowed dishes come back from your house clean and fast. The only downside: a gift can feel like a task until it's repaid, which drains some of the warmth out of it.
insight.step: Next time someone is kind, wait a full week before giving anything back, and just enjoy receiving.

options.label: I feel awkward, like I don't deserve it

insight.reveal: Receiving is harder for you than giving. You're quick to say 'you didn't have to' and slow to just enjoy it. Part of your generosity may come from giving feeling safer, and letting a kindness simply land, with a plain thank you, gets easier every time you try.
insight.step: Next time someone is kind, try saying only 'Thank you, that means a lot', and leave out the 'you didn't have to'.

options.label: I wonder what they want from me

insight.reveal: You've learned that kindness sometimes comes with a price tag. That makes you hard to fool and sharp at reading motives. It's worth asking, gently, whether the people around you now have earned the same caution as the ones who taught it to you.
insight.research: Adults differ in attachment anxiety (worry about rejection) and attachment avoidance (discomfort with closeness), and both shape how relationships feel.
insight.step: This week, accept one small kindness without looking for the reason, and see what actually follows.

questions.prompt: You get some unexpected money. What would make you happiest?

options.label: Saving it

insight.reveal: Safe and steady is your kind of happy. A growing buffer quiets your mind in a way no purchase can. You check your savings the way other people check the weather, and a bigger safety net beats a bigger treat for you almost every time.
insight.step: This week, picture what 'safe enough' looks like for you, so saving has a finish line.

options.label: A trip, a concert or a great meal

insight.reveal: You spend on memories, and you get your money's worth twice. Once on the night, then again every time you tell the story. Long after the bill is forgotten, you're still describing that meal or that concert to friends, and it gets better with each retelling.
insight.research: People often report that experiences they paid for made them happier than possessions they bought.
insight.step: This month, plan one small outing you'll enjoy, then tell someone the story afterwards.

options.label: Treating someone I love

insight.reveal: Your happiness travels through other people's faces. You're wonderful at gifts and surprises, and you remember exactly what lights someone up. You may forget to treat yourself, though, and only notice after a generous month that your own cup has run low.
insight.research: Spending money on other people lifted people's happiness more than spending the same money on themselves.
insight.step: This week, do one small kind thing for someone else, and one for yourself.

options.label: The thing I've wanted for months

insight.reveal: You've been patient with this wish, and now it gets its turn. You compare options carefully rather than buying on a whim, so you probably know the exact model and the best price already. Half the pleasure was the wanting, so enjoy the getting slowly.
insight.research: In two diary studies, things people bought gave small bursts of happiness more often over two weeks, while experiences gave stronger but rarer moments.
insight.step: Before buying, picture using it on an ordinary weekday a month from now. Still exciting? Enjoy it.

questions.prompt: How do your mornings usually start?

options.label: Slowly, with something warm to drink

insight.reveal: Your first cup is a small ritual that sets the tone for your day. You arrive at the first meeting or class of the day already settled. When the ritual gets skipped, everything can feel slightly off for hours, and you might not connect the two until the afternoon.
insight.research: A review of ritual research found that set rituals, religious or everyday, tend to help people manage worry, feel more in control and feel bonded to the people they share them with.
insight.step: On a rushed morning this week, keep just two minutes of your ritual and see if the day feels different.

options.label: Phone first, before my feet touch the floor

insight.reveal: Other people's news gets to you before your own thoughts do. You're quick to reply and know what happened overnight before you've brushed your teeth. Moving the phone just out of reach makes mornings feel longer, and your best ideas may be waiting in that quiet gap.
insight.step: For three mornings, keep the phone out of reach until you've had water or daylight.

options.label: Rushing, already a bit behind

insight.reveal: Your mornings start in a hurry, owing time you never had. You probably guard your late evenings fiercely, because night is the only time that feels truly yours, and your mind can be at its sharpest after dark, which is great for ideas and rough on alarms.
insight.research: Many people go to bed later than they meant to for no outside reason, and this 'bedtime procrastination' was linked to too little sleep and next-day tiredness.
insight.step: For the next three mornings, try one when-then plan: 'When my alarm rings, I'll stand up and drink water.'

options.label: With a heavy feeling about the day ahead

insight.reveal: You feel the weight of the day before it has even started. That's tiring, and it says you take what's ahead seriously. The heaviness is often tied to one specific thing, and naming it can lighten the rest. The day doesn't have to be carried all at once.
insight.step: Tomorrow morning, name the one thing behind the heavy feeling, then do the smallest part of it first.

questions.prompt: Which of these has given you the most joy lately?

options.label: A really good meal

insight.reveal: Joy finds you through your senses, one bite at a time. You notice the weather, the smell of fresh bread and the sound of rain that other people walk straight past. Friends ask you where to eat, and you're rarely wrong.
insight.research: Training people to slow down and enjoy good moments, called savouring, moderately boosted good feelings and eased low ones across 20 trials with 4,805 people.
insight.step: At one meal this week, eat the first three bites with no phone and full attention.

options.label: Helping someone with a problem

insight.reveal: Nothing lifts you quite like fixing someone's problem. You're first in line when a friend is stuck, whether it's a broken phone or a broken heart. On a long break with nobody needing anything, you might feel oddly lost, so it helps to keep a little usefulness in your rest too.
insight.research: Across 27 studies with over 4,000 people, doing acts of kindness tended to give the kind person a small-to-medium boost in well-being.
insight.step: This week, offer help with something small that nobody asked for, and notice your mood after.

options.label: Getting better at something

insight.reveal: You enjoy the climb more than the view from the top. You pick up new skills fast and love the moment something finally clicks. Once you've mastered one, restlessness creeps in, and you're probably already eyeing the next hard thing to learn.
insight.research: In about 12,000 daily work diaries, people's best days tended to be the ones where they made progress on work that mattered to them; setbacks hit harder.
insight.step: This week, pick one skill and spend ten minutes on it on three different days. Missing one is fine.

options.label: Honestly, it's hard to say right now

insight.reveal: It sounds like you've been carrying a lot lately. When duty fills every corner, joy tends to go quiet rather than disappear. Small, specific pleasures, like a song you love or a few minutes in the sun, often bring it back sooner than big plans do.
insight.research: Across 26 trials, a method built on planning small enjoyable or meaningful activities, and noticing how they feel, lifted persistent low mood a lot.
insight.step: Each evening this week, notice one moment that was even a little bit good, however small.

questions.prompt: You reach a goal you worked hard for. How do you celebrate?

options.label: With people around me

insight.reveal: You celebrate in company, and you bring everyone along. You're just as good at cheering for others, sorting out the cake and the speech. All that celebrating builds the circle of people who'll show up for you when things go wrong.
insight.research: When someone shares good news, an interested, enthusiastic reply is linked to more trust and closeness, while a flat or distracted reply is linked to less.
insight.step: This week, celebrate someone else's small win as loudly as you would your own.

options.label: A small private treat

insight.reveal: Success sits calmly with you, no fireworks needed. Because you never pour all your joy into one big moment, you rarely get the slump that follows. Your treats tend to be small and oddly specific, like one particular pastry from one particular shop.
insight.research: A review of happiness research suggested money tends to bring more joy when spent on many small treats rather than one big one.
insight.step: This week, choose your next small treat before you reach the goal, and tie it to a clear finish line.

options.label: I'm already thinking about the next goal

insight.reveal: Your finish line moves the moment you touch it. You get a lot done and remember surprisingly little of it, because you rarely stop long enough for the good feeling to sink in. Ask yourself what you achieved last year and the list may surprise you.
insight.research: Across 20 trials with 4,805 people, savouring exercises, which train people to notice and enjoy good moments, moderately boosted good feelings and eased low ones.
insight.step: Next time you finish something, wait one full day before starting a new goal.

options.label: It feels oddly flat when I get there

insight.reveal: You found out the chase meant more than the prize. That flat feeling can be confusing, but it isn't failure. You're thoughtful and searching, and it often means the next goal needs a deeper reason behind it, not a bigger target.
insight.research: People whose biggest life goals were money, looks and fame tended to have less energy and more aches and pains, while those chasing close relationships, growth and community felt better.
insight.step: Before your next goal, say in one sentence why it matters to you, not only what it is.

questions.prompt: It's the last day of a holiday. What's on your mind?

options.label: Grateful it happened

insight.reveal: You close good chapters cleanly, with thanks. Because your happy memories aren't mixed with the sadness of endings, they tend to stay bright for years. You're good at goodbyes too, the guest who leaves on time without lingering at the door.
insight.research: Simple gratitude exercises, like writing down things you are thankful for, led to small improvements in mood and worry on average, though the evidence is uncertain.
insight.step: On the last day of your next break, tell someone your three best moments.

options.label: Already planning the next one

insight.reveal: Something on the calendar keeps you going. The weeks of waiting can hold as much joy for you as the trip itself, so the size of the plan matters less than having one. Even a dinner booked three weeks out can carry you through a dull month.
insight.research: Holidaymakers tended to be happier than others before their trip, mostly from looking forward to it, but once home most were no happier than people who stayed.
insight.step: This week, put one small thing to look forward to in your calendar, even just coffee with a friend.

options.label: Dreading normal life and messages

insight.reveal: Coming back to normal life feels heavy for you right now. Often it isn't the whole week that drains you, just one part of it: a certain meeting, a certain inbox, a certain person. Pinpointing that one piece can help more than any trip you could book.
insight.step: This week, notice which single part of your normal week you dread most. Just name it to yourself.

options.label: Sad that I never really relaxed

insight.reveal: You brought your to-do list along on the trip. Your body rested while your mind kept checking things. You spend the first days of any break learning how to switch off, and often unwind fully just as it's time to go home, which is worth planning around.
insight.research: Across 91 samples of 38,124 workers, people who mentally switched off from work in their free time reported less exhaustion and better sleep and life satisfaction.
insight.step: On your next day off, put your work apps out of sight for the whole day.

questions.prompt: After a bad day, what helps you first?

options.label: Food and a show

insight.reveal: You comfort the body first and save the thinking for later. You let a bad day be over before you try to understand it. Usually you're ready to talk it through the next morning, not that night, and you wake up seeing it more clearly.
insight.step: After your next bad day, take the comfort first, and give yourself until morning before thinking it over.

options.label: Telling someone the whole story

insight.reveal: You make sense of your day by talking it through. You think best in conversation, and you often find the answer halfway through the story, before the listener has said a word. For you, a good friend is mostly a good pair of ears.
insight.step: Next bad day, ask someone to just listen for five minutes, no advice needed.

options.label: Walking or moving until it fades

insight.reveal: Your feet sort out your feelings before your words do. You think more clearly in motion, and some of your best decisions arrive mid-walk or halfway through scrubbing the kitchen. A bad day often looks smaller to you by the end of the street.
insight.research: Across more than 1,000 trials, regular physical activity, from walking to yoga or weights, tended to give medium-sized relief from low mood and worry.
insight.step: On your next stressful day, take a ten-minute walk before replying to anything important.

options.label: Nothing really, I replay it in bed

insight.reveal: Your mind keeps trying to fix the day after it's over. You're careful and thorough, and you want to get things right. After the first replay, though, the loop rarely finds anything new. You've done enough thinking for today, and it can wait until morning.
insight.research: Going over and over a problem in your head without acting on it tends to deepen low mood and make problems harder to solve.
insight.step: Tonight, if the replay starts, write down the one thing you'd do differently, then close the notebook.

questions.prompt: When stress builds up, how do you usually notice it first?

options.label: My shoulders or jaw get tight

insight.reveal: Your body hears stress before your mind admits it. You have a built-in early warning, sometimes days ahead of the worried thoughts. Tight shoulders or a clenched jaw in the middle of something perfectly ordinary are worth listening to.
insight.step: Three times this week, check your jaw and shoulders and let them drop for one slow breath.

options.label: I snap at people over small things

insight.reveal: When you're stressed, it leaks out sideways onto whoever's near. It takes honesty to notice that about yourself. The snapping rarely has anything to do with the person in front of you, and a quick 'sorry I snapped, that was my stress' repairs more than you'd expect.
insight.research: Of six parts of an apology, admitting it was your fault mattered most to people, then offering to fix it; asking for forgiveness mattered least.
insight.step: Next time you snap, say 'Sorry I snapped. That was my stress, not you' within the hour.

options.label: Someone else tells me I seem stressed

insight.reveal: Others often see your strain before you do. You stay calm in a crisis and keep going while everything shakes. That's a gift, but it can hide your own tank running low, even from you, so the people who mention it are worth hearing.
insight.step: This week, ask one person you trust: 'What's the first sign you notice when I'm stressed?'

options.label: My sleep goes first

insight.reveal: Your worries wait until the house is quiet to speak up. In daylight you're busy and capable, so the thoughts only get their turn at night. They look huge at two in the morning and much smaller over breakfast, and nothing needs solving in the dark.
insight.step: Tonight, keep paper by your bed. If a worry wakes you, write it down so your mind can set it aside until morning.

questions.prompt: You don't get something you really hoped for. What happens next?

options.label: I shrug and move on quickly

insight.reveal: Setbacks slide off you, and you're soon moving again. You're resilient and easy to work with when things go sideways. Sometimes, though, you move on before learning what the hope was really about, then find yourself chasing something very similar a year later.
insight.step: Next disappointment, give it five minutes and ask: what did I actually want from this?

options.label: I look for what I did wrong

insight.reveal: You'd rather take a lesson than a loss. You improve quickly and turn disappointment into something useful. The risk is taking the blame for things that were mostly timing or luck, and being harder on yourself than you'd ever be on a friend.
insight.research: Across 27 trials, learning to treat yourself with kindness, as a good friend would, reduced self-criticism, dwelling on problems, stress and low mood by moderate to large amounts.
insight.step: Next time, name one part that was in your control and one part that was simply luck.

options.label: I tell myself not to hope so much next time

insight.reveal: Disappointment teaches you to want a little less. It's a way of protecting yourself, and it keeps you steady under pressure. Over time, though, you may notice you've stopped going after things you truly wanted, and some of those hopes still deserve a chance.
insight.research: Asked about their biggest regret, 76% of people named failing to become the person they hoped to be, rather than failing a duty, and these regrets lasted longer.
insight.step: This week, tell someone one thing you still hope for, even if it might not happen.

options.label: I feel low for days and keep it to myself

insight.reveal: You feel things deeply, and you carry them alone. From the outside you look fine, which makes it easy for others to miss and hard for you to bring up. Sharing even one small piece with someone you trust tends to make low days lighter, and if a low stretch lasts for weeks, tell a doctor too.
insight.research: People who usually hide their feelings tended to feel worse inside, share less with others and feel less close to friends than people who rethink what upset them.
insight.step: Next time you feel low for more than a day, tell one person one sentence about it.

questions.prompt: When do you feel most alone?

options.label: The last evening of the weekend

insight.reveal: The quiet end of a weekend can feel strangely empty to you. It's often less about missing people and more about the gap between free time and the week ahead. A small plan for that evening, like a call, a walk or a meal you love, tends to fill it nicely.
insight.research: Across 26 trials, planning small enjoyable or meaningful activities and noticing how they feel tended to lift persistent low mood.
insight.step: Next weekend, plan one small thing for its last evening: a call, a walk or a meal with someone.

options.label: In a crowd or at a party

insight.reveal: A room full of small talk can feel lonelier to you than an empty one. You need depth, not just people. You might slip out of parties early, then talk for an hour with one friend on the way home, and that one real conversation is the part you remember.
insight.research: In 12 experiments with over 1,800 people, conversations with strangers felt less awkward and more enjoyable than expected, especially deeper ones.
insight.step: At your next gathering, aim for one real conversation instead of many short ones.

options.label: When good news comes and there's no one to tell

insight.reveal: Loneliness finds you most in your happy moments. For you, sharing is what makes good news feel complete. The pang usually points straight at someone you wish you could call, and that person might be really glad to hear from you.
insight.research: People tend to underestimate how much someone will appreciate a quick message, call or small gift out of the blue, especially when it comes as a surprise.
insight.step: Next time you have good news, send it to one person you've drifted away from.

options.label: Sometimes even with my partner or family

insight.reveal: Even close to the people you love, you sometimes feel unseen. That's a painful feeling, and it doesn't mean the bond is weak. More often a part of you hasn't been shared yet. You deserve to be known, and it can start with one small sentence.
insight.research: Adults differ in attachment anxiety (worry about rejection) and attachment avoidance (discomfort with closeness), and both shape how relationships feel.
insight.step: This week, tell someone close one thing you care about that they may not know.

questions.prompt: Your to-do list is far too long. What do you actually do?

options.label: Do the easy things first

insight.reveal: Small wins warm you up for the big stuff. Ticking off a few quick ones gets you going, and that can genuinely help. The risk is a day full of crossed-off lines while the one thing that really mattered sits waiting at the bottom.
insight.step: Tomorrow, do one easy task, then the hardest one before lunch.

options.label: Rewrite the list in a better order

insight.reveal: You calm the chaos by putting it in order. Making a fresh list feels like progress, and sometimes it is. A list does the most for you when it starts with something doable in the next ten minutes and says when you'll do it.
insight.research: Across 94 studies, making a specific when-then plan ("When X happens, I will do Y") had a medium-to-large effect on reaching goals.
insight.step: Next time you rewrite a list, add one when-then plan: 'When I finish lunch, I will start task one.'

options.label: Freeze and scroll instead

insight.reveal: When everything feels urgent, you can't find a place to start. That freeze is overload, not laziness, and it tends to hit hardest when a task feels unpleasant or you doubt you'll manage it. Shrinking the list to one single thing often gets you moving again faster than you'd expect.
insight.research: People tend to put tasks off most when a task feels unpleasant and they doubt they will manage it; perfectionism did not predict delay.
insight.step: Next time you freeze, cover the list and do only the top line for ten minutes.

options.label: Work late until it's all done

insight.reveal: You trust effort more than limits. When something has to get over the line, people know to bring it to you. Past a point, though, extra hours tend to get less done, so late nights rarely keep the list short for long, and you deserve evenings that belong to you.
insight.research: Among British munition workers a century ago, output rose with hours up to a point, then more and more slowly as hours got longer.
insight.step: This week, pick a stop time for one evening and keep to it, even with tasks left.

questions.prompt: Something sad happens. What do you do with the feeling?

options.label: Keep busy so I don't think about it

insight.reveal: Busy hands get you through hard weeks. You keep life running through the worst of it, and that's a real strength. The feeling usually waits patiently, though, and may surface in a quiet moment, on a trip or late at night, asking for a few minutes of your attention.
insight.research: Grieving people tend to move back and forth between facing the loss and getting on with daily life, and taking breaks from grief is a normal part of coping.
insight.step: This week, give a sad feeling ten minutes on purpose, then go back to your day.

options.label: Music or a film that matches the mood

insight.reveal: You let sad feelings run their whole course. You know which songs to put on and which film to save for a good cry. Letting the feeling finish instead of fighting it often helps you feel better sooner than pushing it away would.
insight.research: Many people enjoy sad music because it feels safe, beautiful and comforting, and listeners often feel nostalgia or mixed feelings rather than real sadness.
insight.step: This week, while you feel fine, make a short playlist for low days.

options.label: Let myself cry if it comes

insight.reveal: Tears are a release for you, not a weakness. You tend to recover fully once the feeling has passed through. You're also the person others feel safe enough to cry in front of, because you never make it awkward.
insight.research: Crying often helps people feel better, though usually not straight away; comfort from one close person helps, while embarrassment or a big audience can cancel the relief.
insight.step: Next time someone near you is sad, sit with them for a minute before saying anything.

options.label: Hide it so nobody worries

insight.reveal: You keep your sadness tucked away to spare the people you love. That's a kind instinct, and it keeps you standing when everything around you falls apart. It also means they rarely get to care for you back, and many would welcome that chance. You don't have to hold it all by yourself.
insight.research: People who habitually hide their feelings tended to share less, feel less close to friends and be less satisfied with life than people who rethink what upset them.
insight.step: This week, tell one trusted person 'I'm a bit sad today' and let them respond.

questions.prompt: It's the night before a hard day. How do you spend it?

options.label: Go to bed early

insight.reveal: Sleep is your preparation of choice, and it serves you well. You trust that a rested mind will handle what a worried one couldn't plan. You arrive at big days looking calmer than you feel, and people may assume you weren't nervous at all.
insight.research: Among 88 students wearing sleep trackers, sleep in the month before exams went with better grades, while sleep the night before did not.
insight.step: In the week before your next hard day, set an alarm for bedtime, not just for waking up.

options.label: Prepare everything, then prepare again

insight.reveal: You turn worry into checklists, spare pens and backup files. You're impressively ready for almost anything. After the first round, though, the extra checking is mostly for comfort rather than catching anything you missed, and that time could go to rest.
insight.step: Next time, prepare once, then put everything in your bag and agree with yourself not to reopen it.

options.label: Distract myself with something fun

insight.reveal: You know worrying tonight won't change tomorrow. So you'd rather laugh, play or go out, and you show up fresh because of it. A good evening can be the best preparation you give yourself.
insight.step: This week, pick a fun thing to save for the night before your next hard day.

options.label: Lie awake running through what could go wrong

insight.reveal: Your mind tries to live tomorrow tonight, every version of it. It's trying to protect you, and you do end up ready for surprises. The real day is rarely like the ones you rehearse, and usually kinder. Let your shoulders drop and breathe out slowly.
insight.research: Young adults who spent five minutes writing tomorrow's to-do list before bed fell asleep in about 15 minutes, compared with about 25 for those who wrote about tasks already done.
insight.step: Tonight, write the worst case and one thing you'd do if it happened. Then put the paper away.

questions.prompt: A friend asks 'How are you?' during a hard week. What do you say?

options.label: "Fine, thanks!"

insight.reveal: You save the real answer for the right time and person. You come across as steady and composed, and you don't like to make a scene. The small cost is that friends may not know when to show up for you, because 'fine' looks the same on good weeks and bad ones.
insight.research: People tend to underestimate how often others feel low or upset, partly because others hide it, and those who underestimated it most felt lonelier.
insight.step: This week, answer 'How are you?' with one true detail, just once.

options.label: "A bit tired, but all right"

insight.reveal: You leave the door half open to see who notices. A little hint, then you wait. You feel closest to the friends who gently ask a second time, and you're good at catching hints in others too, which is why people open up to you so easily.
insight.step: Next time you hint, add one more sentence even if they don't ask.

options.label: I make a joke about how bad it is

insight.reveal: A joke lets you share the hard stuff without making it heavy. It invites people in while keeping them at a safe distance, and you can lift a room even in a rough week. The right friend laughs first, then asks what's really going on, and you deserve that friend.
insight.step: After your next joke about a hard week, add one serious sentence.

options.label: The real answer, even if it's messy

insight.reveal: You'd rather be honest than tidy. Your openness gives others permission to be real too, and that's how small talk turns into closeness. It's why people confide in you, sometimes before they've told anyone else.
insight.research: Strangers who spent 45 minutes taking turns answering slowly deeper personal questions felt closer than pairs who made small talk.
insight.step: This week, ask someone 'How are you, really?' and wait through the pause.

questions.prompt: Nobody has messaged you all day. What goes through your mind?

options.label: Nice, a quiet day

insight.reveal: Silence on your phone sounds like peace, not a message. You feel secure without constant proof of connection. In relationships you tend to stay calm too, and a slow reply rarely sends your mind racing.
insight.step: On your next quiet day, message someone you've been meaning to, just because.

options.label: I message someone first

insight.reveal: You start the conversation instead of waiting for it. Thanks to you, friendships that would have faded are still alive. You've probably wondered why you always write first, and part of the answer is that others are glad you do.
insight.research: People tend to underestimate how much others appreciate a quick message or call out of the blue, especially when it comes as a surprise.
insight.step: This week, notice who messages you first, and thank one of them for it.

options.label: I keep checking my phone

insight.reveal: A silent phone makes you wonder where you stand. You're tuned in to people and you care how they feel about you. The gaps you read meaning into are usually just busy days on the other side of the screen: people cooking, working or asleep.
insight.research: Adults differ in attachment anxiety (worry about rejection) and attachment avoidance (discomfort with closeness), and both shape how relationships feel.
insight.step: On your next quiet day, leave your phone in another room for one hour and notice what you feel.

options.label: I wonder if people have forgotten me

insight.reveal: You think of others often, and wonder if they think of you. Quiet days can feel like proof you've slipped from people's minds, but the gap is usually in messages, not in care. Someone has likely thought of you today and simply forgotten to say so. You matter to more people than your phone shows.
insight.research: After chatting with someone new, people tend to think the other person liked them less than they really did, and this 'liking gap' lasted for months between new roommates.
insight.step: This week, ask one friend: 'Do you ever think of messaging someone and then forget?'

questions.prompt: On a tired, low evening, what are you most likely to reach for?

options.label: Something warm and a blanket

insight.reveal: You comfort yourself the way you'd comfort a child. Warmth, softness and quiet tell your body it's safe before your mind has caught up. You look after yourself without fuss, and small comforts work on you faster than any pep talk.
insight.step: This week, set up one corner of your home as your low-day spot, ready before you need it.

options.label: An old favourite show I've seen many times

insight.reveal: On low nights, knowing the ending is the whole point for you. You rest best when nothing can surprise you. In hard weeks you lean on familiar food, places and faces too, and that steady sameness is how you recharge.
insight.research: Nostalgia often comes on when people feel low or lonely, and thinking back to fond memories tended to lift mood and make people feel closer to others.
insight.step: Next low evening, notice which old favourite you pick. It may point to a time you felt safe.

options.label: A call with someone who knows me well

insight.reveal: A familiar voice that needs no backstory brings you back. No advice, just someone who already knows the whole picture. You have one or two people like that, and they may have no idea how much those calls mean to you.
insight.research: People expected a phone call with an old friend to feel more awkward than a text or email, but calls built a stronger bond and weren't more awkward.
insight.step: This week, tell the person you'd call that they are your low-day person.

options.label: Online shopping I don't really need

insight.reveal: On your low nights, a parcel on the way feels like a small promise. You're great at spotting a bargain, and half the fun is waiting for the knock at the door, more than the thing itself. Something else to look forward to, like a plan with a friend, can meet the same need.
