insight.research: Waiting for an experience, like a trip, a concert or a party, tends to feel more pleasant and exciting than waiting for a new thing to arrive.
insight.step: Next low evening, put items in the basket but wait until morning to decide.

questions.prompt: Someone cuts in front of you in a queue. What do you do?

options.label: Let it go, not worth it

insight.reveal: Not worth it, you decide, and you actually mean it. In traffic, at family dinners or at a busy counter, you shrug and move on. Now and then a small slight sneaks back later, but it usually comes out as a funny story, not a grudge.
insight.step: Next time you let something go, check an hour later: is it still on your mind?

options.label: Point out where the line starts

insight.reveal: You say what's fair, and you keep it friendly. You probably send back a wrong order or question an odd charge, and nobody even feels told off. In meetings, colleagues hope you'll speak up, and you usually do.
insight.step: This week, practise one calm, short sentence for small unfair moments, like 'Sorry, the line starts here.'

options.label: Say nothing, but fume inside

insight.reveal: On the outside you look calm; inside, you're writing a speech. Staying quiet spares you a scene, and the speech gets sharper every time you replay it on the way home. That inner voice makes you a keen judge of how people treat each other; it just shouldn't cost you the whole evening.
insight.research: Across 154 studies with over 10,000 people, calming activities like slow breathing, meditation or relaxing the muscles tended to reduce anger, while revving-up ones mostly did not.
insight.step: Next time you fume silently, breathe out slowly three times, then decide: say it or drop it.

options.label: Tell them clearly, even if it gets loud

insight.reveal: You can't stand by and watch something unfair happen. You're likely first to challenge a rude waiter or a boss who crosses a line, and friends know you'll fight for them just as hard. The volume can make people defend themselves instead of listening, even when you're completely right.
insight.step: Next time you confront someone, lower your voice on purpose and notice whether they listen more.

questions.prompt: On the road, another driver nearly hits you. What's your reaction?

options.label: A deep breath, then I forget it

insight.reveal: You assume people mess up by accident, not on purpose. That's partly why a rough day rarely follows you to bed. When everyone in the car is shouting, you're the calm voice, and you bounce back from setbacks fast.
insight.research: People who tend to rethink what upset them, instead of hiding their feelings, felt better inside and closer to friends than habitual hiders did.
insight.step: Next time someone cuts you off, imagine one innocent reason they might be rushing.

options.label: The horn, and maybe a gesture

insight.reveal: Your temper flares fast and is gone just as fast. Your passenger may still be talking about it two streets later, while you've already forgotten it happened. People rarely have to guess how you feel, which is honest, though the person beside you can need longer to settle.
insight.step: On your next journey, notice how long the feeling lasts after you use the horn.

options.label: Shout at them where no one can hear

insight.reveal: The car might be the only place your frustration gets loud. At work and at home you're patient and polite, so the car is where it spills over. A rough drive often says more about your week than about the other driver.
insight.research: People who vented anger while dwelling on the person who annoyed them became angrier and more aggressive than people who did nothing.
insight.step: Next time you want to shout, try one long out-breath instead and compare how you feel a minute later.

options.label: Still angry about it hours later

insight.reveal: A scare like that stays in your body long after the road is clear. You probably feel it all over again each time you tell the story, and some of the tension can land on whoever's home first. That vivid memory is also what makes you such a careful driver.
insight.step: When you get home after a bad drive, tell the story once, then change the topic on purpose.

questions.prompt: In an argument with someone close, what do you tend to do?

options.label: Talk it through

insight.reveal: You believe a problem shrinks once it's put into words. At home you're often the steady one, finding words for the mess. A very calm reply can make an upset partner feel their feelings are too big, though, so letting a little of yours show really helps.
insight.step: Next disagreement, say what you feel in one word before you explain your logic.

options.label: I need space before I can talk

insight.reveal: You need a walk before you can find the right words. A drive, a tidy kitchen, a quiet hour: that's where your head clears. It works best if you say how long you'll be, so the other person doesn't feel shut out while you're gone.
insight.research: Across 74 studies of over 14,000 people, couples stuck in a pattern where one pushes to talk and the other goes quiet tended to be less satisfied and feel less close.
insight.step: Next time you need space, say 'Give me twenty minutes, then let's talk' and come back on time.

options.label: I need to fix it right now

insight.reveal: An argument left hanging won't let you rest. You might follow someone from room to room or send one more message, just to settle it. That urge to repair is a real gift in love, though it can push someone who needs space a little further away.
insight.research: Couples caught in a pattern where one partner pushes to talk and the other withdraws tended to feel less close, whichever partner played which role.
insight.step: Next argument, wait ten minutes before trying to fix it, and notice what the waiting feels like.

options.label: I get sarcastic or roll my eyes

insight.reveal: When you feel unheard, your wit gets sharp. On a good day that quick tongue makes friends laugh, and in a fight it saves you from saying the hurt plainly. An eye-roll tends to land as 'I look down on you', though, and that's rarely what you mean.
insight.research: In long-running studies of couples, contempt, such as mockery, sarcasm and eye-rolling, was the strongest single predictor of divorce.
insight.step: Next time sarcasm rises, say the real complaint underneath it in plain words instead.

questions.prompt: Someone wronged you years ago. How do you feel about them now?

options.label: I barely think about it

insight.reveal: They stopped being important to you, so you moved on. You tend to leave breakups, lost jobs and old rivalries behind cleanly. At a reunion you could be perfectly friendly while someone else is still bracing for drama.
insight.step: This week, notice one small annoyance you're still carrying and choose to drop just that one.

options.label: Forgiven, but I remember everything

insight.reveal: You can forgive someone and still keep the lesson. You'll be warm to them again, but they won't get the same key twice. That makes you smart about who to lend money to and who gets to hear your secrets.
insight.step: This week, think of one person you've forgiven and one small piece of trust you could safely give back.

options.label: It still stings when I think of it

insight.reveal: It still stings, maybe because you never got a real answer. Often what stings most isn't what they did, but that they never seemed to understand what it cost you. The same deep memory makes you a loyal friend who remembers what matters to people.
insight.research: People who looked back on an angry or upsetting moment as if watching from a distance, like a fly on the wall, tended to get less worked up.
insight.step: Tonight, write what happened as if you were a kind stranger watching, including what it cost you. Then put it away.

options.label: I'd still like them to admit it

insight.reveal: You still want them to own what they did, and that's fair. You notice unfairness, and you won't pretend it didn't happen. The hard part is that your peace ends up waiting on someone who may never act, and you deserve that peace sooner.
insight.research: Across 175 studies of 26,006 people, forgiving tended to be most likely when people felt empathy for the wrongdoer, felt the hurt wasn't meant and got an apology.
insight.step: This week, ask yourself: what would I feel if they never admit it? Let the answer sit for a day.

questions.prompt: A colleague takes credit for your idea in a meeting. What do you do?

options.label: Nothing. It's not worth it

insight.reveal: A calm team matters more to you than your name on the idea. You're easy to work with, and often the reason projects run smoothly. Just keep an eye on one thing: a few colleagues may slowly learn that your ideas are free to take.
insight.step: Next time you share an idea, send a short written summary afterwards.

options.label: Add a detail only the real author would know

insight.reveal: You set the record straight without raising your voice. One clever detail and the whole room works out whose idea it was. That same skill probably helps you negotiate, write sharp emails and win debates without getting heated.
insight.step: Before your next meeting, prepare one follow-up point about your own idea.

options.label: Talk to them privately afterwards

insight.reveal: You give people a quiet chance to put things right. It protects the work and the relationship at once, and it earns you a name for fairness. You'll also remember, very clearly, who took that chance and who didn't.
insight.research: People were most likely to forgive when they got an apology, felt the hurt wasn't intended and felt empathy for the wrongdoer, across 175 studies.
insight.step: Next time it happens, start the private talk with 'I noticed…' and describe only what happened.

options.label: Stay angry for days and avoid them

insight.reveal: It hurts this much because your work matters so much to you. Staying quiet in the meeting kept the peace, but you might carry it for a week while they don't even know. That means you end up paying the whole cost of something they did.
insight.research: In polls of 800 workers, among those treated rudely at work, 80% lost time worrying about it and 48% cut back their effort.
insight.step: This week, choose one sentence you could say to them, then decide whether to say it or let it go.

questions.prompt: At home, which small thing irritates you most?

options.label: Dishes left in the sink

insight.reveal: Those dishes in the sink aren't really about dishes for you. You spot what needs doing early and keep the house running. What usually stings is the message underneath: 'nobody sees what I do'.
insight.research: When couples each rated their share of household jobs, the two shares usually added up to more than the whole: we tend to notice our own effort more than other people's.
insight.step: This week, thank someone at home for one small thing they do, and see whether the dish issue softens.

options.label: Noise when I want quiet

insight.reveal: Quiet is how you recharge, like a phone on its charger. Early mornings, good headphones and the empty house after everyone leaves are probably your favourite things. When it stays loud too long, people can call you grumpy when you're simply running on empty.
insight.step: This week, agree on one quiet hour at home with everyone, and enjoy every minute of it.

options.label: Being interrupted when I'm focused

insight.reveal: Your focus takes ages to build and seconds to break. The irritation is really about the cost of starting over. You do your best work in long, protected stretches, and it shows: your jigsaws, reports and big projects actually get finished.
insight.research: In a study of 48 people, those interrupted while answering emails felt more stress, frustration and time pressure, even though they made no more mistakes.
insight.step: Next time you need focus, tell people at home: 'Give me 30 minutes, then I'm all yours.'

options.label: Feeling like I'm the only one who helps

insight.reveal: You carry the jobs nobody else even sees. Birthdays, the shopping list, noticing the soap has run out: you're the glue at home, whether anyone says so or not. That load gets heavier the longer it stays unspoken, and it's fair to ask for help carrying it.
insight.research: Interviews with 35 couples found that the mental work of running a home, like noticing what is needed and keeping track, often goes unseen and causes friction.
insight.step: This week, name one invisible task you do and ask someone to take it over for a week.

questions.prompt: You read an online comment that makes you angry. What do you do?

options.label: Close it and move on

insight.reveal: Your attention is precious, and you guard it well. You skip pointless fights with strangers and relatives alike, and you probably sleep better for it. All that saved energy goes to the people and plans that actually matter to you.
insight.step: This week, notice one moment your mood dropped because of something on a screen.

options.label: Read all the replies

insight.reveal: Down you scroll, hoping someone out there agrees with you. Wanting to know how others think is a real strength. The trouble is that the replies are usually packed with other angry people, so your anger tends to grow instead of settling.
insight.research: In over 560,000 tweets on hot political topics, each extra word mixing morals and emotion raised sharing by about 20%, mostly among people who already agreed.
insight.step: Next time, read only the first three replies, then close the app.

options.label: Write a reply, then delete it

insight.reveal: Your anger needs words, but it doesn't need an audience. Writing it out and then letting it go gives the feeling somewhere to land. The wait lets you cool down without the cost of a public fight, and people see you as level-headed because of it.
insight.research: Across 154 studies, calming down, such as slow breathing or taking a time-out, tended to reduce anger, while revving-up activities mostly did not.
insight.step: Next time, write the reply, wait an hour, then decide whether it's still worth sending.

options.label: Reply, then keep checking who answered

insight.reveal: If something online is wrong, you feel you have to fix it. You know your facts and care about getting things right. It's the checking back that keeps the anger alive, sometimes for a whole evening after the comment has scrolled away.
insight.research: People who vented anger while dwelling on the person who annoyed them became angrier and more aggressive than people who did nothing.
insight.step: This week, if you reply to a post, turn off its notifications straight after.

questions.prompt: Someone is 30 minutes late to meet you, with no message. How do you feel?

options.label: Fine, I find something to do

insight.reveal: Waiting hardly bothers you, because you come prepared. A book, a podcast, a short walk: you turn dead time into free time. You're likely the relaxed one at airports, and the friend people feel safe being a little late for.
insight.step: This week, keep one small time-filler with you and notice how waiting feels.

options.label: Annoyed. It's rude

insight.reveal: Turning up on time is your way of showing respect. You're probably early yourself, keep a tidy calendar and get trusted with deadlines. You also know exactly who's always late, and you plan around them without saying a word.
insight.research: People told to share honest feedback with someone close found it more pleasant and connecting than they expected, and listeners reacted better than feared.
insight.step: Next time someone is late, tell them kindly how it felt instead of staying quiet.

options.label: Worried something happened to them

insight.reveal: Your mind goes to danger long before it goes to rudeness. You text 'home safe?' after a night out. When the late one finally walks in, relief and anger often arrive together, and the anger can come out louder than you meant.
insight.step: Next time you wait, send one message asking if they're all right, then set a time to stop worrying.

options.label: Wondering if I matter to them

insight.reveal: A late friend can make you wonder where you stand. You notice every small signal, and friends feel truly seen by you. Most of the time the delay is about their messy day, not about you, even when the feeling insists otherwise.
insight.research: Adults differ in attachment anxiety (worry about rejection) and attachment avoidance (discomfort with closeness), and both shape how relationships feel.
insight.step: Next time, think of two other reasons they might be late before deciding what it means.

questions.prompt: You're blamed for something you didn't do. What's your first move?

options.label: Explain the facts

insight.reveal: Calm, clear facts are how you clear your name. You're often the steady voice in a crisis, the one a manager leans on when things get messy. Calm works, but now and then people also need to hear that it hurt, not just that you were right.
insight.step: Next time, add one sentence about how it felt, not just what happened.

options.label: Gather proof before I say anything

insight.reveal: Words alone don't feel like enough to protect you. You like the emails and the dates straight before you speak, and that care means you can always say who agreed to what. A habit like that can come from a time when your word wasn't enough.
insight.step: This week, try clearing up one small misunderstanding quickly, with words alone and no proof.

options.label: Take the blame to keep the peace

insight.reveal: You'd give up being right to keep the peace. You smooth over family tension, and you're easy to live and work with. Over time, though, people may start to see you through mistakes you never made, and your side of the story deserves airtime too.
insight.step: Next time, try: 'That wasn't me, but I can help fix it.' Both parts are true.

options.label: Get angry and defend myself hard

insight.reveal: Being wrongly blamed feels like an attack on who you are. Your sense of fairness wakes up fast, and you'd defend a friend just as fiercely. The heat can drown out the facts you're right about, so one pause before you answer often wins it for you.
insight.research: Calming activities like slow breathing or a short time-out tended to reduce anger across 154 studies, while revving-up activities like jogging mostly did not.
insight.step: Next time you feel blamed, take one breath and say one calm fact before anything else.

questions.prompt: After you lose your temper, what usually happens next?

options.label: I apologise quickly

insight.reveal: Until things are right between you again, you can't relax. You're usually first to send the 'sorry' message after a family fight. A quick apology mends a lot, though it can skip the part where the other person gets to say how it felt.
insight.research: Across 175 studies, people tended to forgive most readily when they got an apology, felt the hurt wasn't intended and felt empathy for the wrongdoer.
insight.step: Next time you apologise, add 'How did that feel for you?' and really listen.

options.label: I act normal and hope it's forgotten

insight.reveal: You say sorry with a cup of tea, not a speech. A small favour, a joke, their favourite snack: you show love by doing. One person reads that perfectly; another is still waiting to hear the words.
insight.step: Next time, pair your kind action with one short spoken sentence: 'Sorry about earlier.'

options.label: I feel bad about it for a long time

insight.reveal: Nobody judges you as harshly as you judge yourself. You may replay the moment at night long after the other person has forgotten it. That conscience is what makes you so careful with people's feelings, and you deserve a little of that care too.
insight.research: Across 65 samples with nearly 18,000 people, those better able to forgive themselves after doing wrong tended to have better well-being.
insight.step: Next time, ask the person directly: 'Are we all right?' Then believe the answer.

options.label: I explain why I was right to be angry

insight.reveal: You need your reasons heard before you can soften. Your anger usually had a fair point inside it, and you can argue it well. The trick is getting the point across without the heat, because people rarely hear reasons while they still feel stung.
insight.research: In apology studies, admitting it was your fault mattered most to people, then offering to fix it; asking for forgiveness mattered least.
insight.step: Next time, start with what you regret, and explain your reasons after that.

questions.prompt: A friend gives you a gift you don't like. What do you say?

options.label: "I love it!"

insight.reveal: A small white lie can be your gift back to them. You protect warm moments, and friends trust you with their feelings because of it. The present matters less to you than the person who chose it, and they can feel that.
insight.research: In 8 experiments, people trusted partners who told a kind lie for their benefit more than honest partners, but relied less on their word for facts.
insight.step: Next time, find one thing about the gift you can honestly praise, and say that.

options.label: Thank them for the thought, not the gift

insight.reveal: You find the words that are both kind and true. It's a quiet talent that shows up at work too, in feedback, references and tricky emails. You'd rather be gently honest than smoothly fake, and that makes your kind words worth trusting.
insight.step: This week, give one compliment that is completely true and very specific.

options.label: Hint later at what I'd really like

insight.reveal: Why correct this gift when you can steer the next one? You deliver honesty in small, careful doses. You're likely just as skilled at steering plans, menus and trips, without anyone noticing they were steered.
insight.research: People liked gifts they had asked for, and even money, more than surprise gifts, though givers expected surprise gifts to be valued more.
insight.step: This week, tell one close person about something you'd truly love to receive.

options.label: Tell them it's not really me

insight.reveal: Close friends get the truth from you, even about small things. It might sting for a second, but it makes your praise worth more. You're the one people ask 'does this really suit me?' before a big day.
insight.research: People asked to be fully honest for three days found it more pleasant and connecting than they expected, and listeners reacted better than feared.
insight.step: Before your next honest talk, choose the kind first sentence you'll open with.

questions.prompt: You promised to help a friend, but now you'd rather stay home. What do you do?

options.label: I go anyway

insight.reveal: Once you've said yes, your word is as good as signed. You turn up with a van on moving day. You're probably careful about promising in the first place, which can make you seem slow to commit.
insight.step: This week, before agreeing to something, say 'Let me check and confirm tomorrow.'

options.label: Go, but feel quietly grumpy

insight.reveal: Duty beats mood for you, nearly every time. Friends can count on you even on bad days, and they value that more than they say. They may still pick up on the grumpiness, though, and a simple 'I'm tired, but I'm here' often clears the air.
insight.research: Across four studies, helping because you chose to lifted the well-being of both helper and helped, while helping under pressure did not bring the same benefits.
insight.step: Next time you go anyway, pick one thing to enjoy on the way there.

options.label: Tell them honestly I'm too tired

insight.reveal: Showing up empty isn't kind, and you'd rather be honest. With you, 'no' is safe, which makes your 'yes' mean more. You likely guard your energy at work the same way, and people learn that when you're in, you're really in.
insight.research: In 8 experiments, people trusted kind liars' good intentions more than honest partners', but relied less on the liars' word for facts.
insight.step: Next time you cancel, offer one specific other time, so it feels like a change of plan, not a no.

options.label: Make up a reason I can't come

insight.reveal: You worry that 'I don't feel like it' won't sound good enough. The excuse comes from kindness: you want to spare their feelings, and yours. Over time, though, it can teach you that your real needs require a cover story, and they don't.
insight.research: People tend to expect honest talks to hurt their relationships more than they do; in tests, being honest felt better and more connecting than people predicted.
insight.step: Next time, try a short true reason: 'I'm out of energy today. Can we move it?'

questions.prompt: You make a mistake at work that no one has noticed yet. What do you do?

options.label: Fix it and tell my team

insight.reveal: You treat a mistake as news to share, not a secret to bury. Teams with you in them raise problems sooner, because you've made it feel safe. Managers likely hand you the projects where an early warning matters most.
insight.research: A trait called Honesty-Humility predicts integrity and rule-breaking at work better than the classic five personality traits alone.
insight.step: This week, mention one small mistake you made and what you learned, in a casual moment.

options.label: Fix it quietly, no need to say

insight.reveal: You'd rather fix it than make an announcement. You're efficient, low-drama and good at your job without making a show of it. The catch is that nobody sees how well you handle problems, so when a bigger one comes, a little visibility now will help you.
insight.step: Next small fix, mention it in one line: 'Found and fixed an error in this.'

options.label: Wait and see if anyone notices

insight.reveal: Looking bad can feel scarier to you than the mistake itself. You care how you come across, which keeps your standards high. It also means you might spend a whole weekend worrying about something a ten-minute fix would have settled.
insight.research: In a study of 281 scientists, colleagues who admitted a finding of theirs was wrong were judged at least as well as those who refused to, and on some measures better.
insight.step: Next time, set yourself a short deadline: if it isn't fixed by then, tell someone.

options.label: Hope it looks like a system problem

insight.reveal: At some point, you learned that mistakes at work get punished. That instinct protects you, and you've become a sharp reader of office politics. It often comes from the room more than the person, so it's fair to ask whether your room is really that unsafe.
insight.research: In interviews with 40 employees, most had stayed silent about a concern at work, and the top reason was fear of being seen or labelled negatively.
insight.step: This week, watch how your manager reacts to someone else's mistake. It shows how safe honesty is there.

questions.prompt: A shop gives you too much change by mistake. What do you do?

options.label: Give it back right away

insight.reveal: Keeping what isn't yours just feels wrong to you. You're probably quick to mention the item the cashier forgot to scan. The same instinct shows up with time and credit: you hate taking more than your share.
insight.research: Pooling 72 experiments where people could lie in private for money, people lied far less than they could have; wanting to be honest, and to look honest, explained it best.
insight.step: This week, notice one moment you got a little more than was fair, and decide what to do about it.

options.label: Small shop, I return it. Big company, maybe not

insight.reveal: Your honesty is about people, not about rules. You protect whoever would actually lose out, which makes you loyal to small local shops and cafés. When no single person seems to get hurt, rules may feel easier to bend than you'd admit.
insight.research: When 17,303 'lost' wallets were handed in across 40 countries, people returned 51% with money in them but 40% without, the opposite of what experts predicted.
insight.step: Next time you think 'it's a big company', picture the cashier who has to balance the till.

options.label: I'd notice later and not go back

insight.reveal: Honesty comes easy to you; going back is the hard part. That's an ordinary gap between meaning well and getting round to it. You'll probably follow through best with a simple plan, like popping in the next time you're passing that shop anyway.
insight.step: Next time you spot a mistake after you've left, fix it on your very next visit.

options.label: Keep it. Their mistake, not mine

insight.reveal: Life, to you, is a series of fair trades where luck cuts both ways. You're practical, hard to guilt-trip and unsentimental about money. It's easy to assume anyone in your shoes would keep it too, so it helps to picture the cashier who comes up short at closing time.
insight.research: People tend to overestimate how many others share their own choices and opinions (the false consensus effect).
insight.step: Next time luck goes your way, ask: would I want this back if I were the cashier?

questions.prompt: A friend tells you a secret. Who might you tell?

options.label: Nobody, ever

insight.reveal: Secrets go into you and never come out. When a friend is in trouble, you're probably their first call. The quiet cost is that you rarely share your own, because you know exactly how heavy a secret can be.
insight.research: Studying over 13,000 secrets, people's minds drifted to their secrets far more often than they had to hide them, and that drifting went with lower well-being.
insight.step: This week, share one small personal thing with someone you know keeps secrets well.

options.label: Only my partner

insight.reveal: Your partner feels like part of you, not a third person. You share almost everything at home and have built a close, private world together. Your friends might see it differently, though, and it's worth asking them once.
insight.step: Next time someone shares a secret, ask: 'Is it all right if my partner knows?'

options.label: Maybe one person, if it's not too serious

insight.reveal: You sort secrets into heavy ones and light ones. You're a lively storyteller who keeps conversations moving. Your friend may have sorted it differently, though, and people rarely say which kind it was.
insight.step: Next time you hear a secret, simply ask: 'Is this just for me?'

options.label: It sometimes slips out without meaning to

insight.reveal: Closeness, for you, means swapping stories. You're warm, open and easy to talk to, so a secret can end up feeling like a gift for the next person. Noticing the moment one reaches the tip of your tongue is often enough to slow it down, and to make your warmth feel safe too.
insight.step: When a secret is on the tip of your tongue this week, switch to a story about yourself instead.

questions.prompt: Splitting a group bill when you ordered much less. What do you do?

options.label: Split it evenly, no fuss

insight.reveal: An easy evening is worth more to you than an exact split. Small losses are a fair price for smooth friendships, and you get invited back a lot. You may also notice who orders the priciest dish every single time.
insight.step: Next group meal, notice how you feel when the bill arrives. That feeling is useful information.

options.label: Pay for exactly what I had

insight.reveal: For you, fair means exact. You're often trusted with group money and shared trip budgets, and sometimes called tight when you're really just precise. You probably know your bank balance to the penny.
insight.step: Next time, suggest your way kindly before the bill comes, not after.

options.label: Split evenly, but feel annoyed

insight.reveal: You pay twice: once with money, once with irritation. Putting the group's comfort first is why you're such a generous host and easy company. The money is often the smaller cost; the replay on the way home is what really adds up.
insight.research: Most diners in a restaurant experiment said they preferred paying for their own food, yet even splits led people to order more.
insight.step: Next time, try one light sentence: 'I'll just pay for mine tonight, if that's all right.'

options.label: Order more so it feels fair

insight.reveal: If the bill won't balance, you'll find a way to balance it. You've got a sharp eye and a creative streak with money, like finding the best deal on a trip. It shows how strongly fairness pulls on you, even when the fix ends up costing you more.
insight.research: In a restaurant experiment, diners ordered more when the bill was split evenly than when each paid for their own food, even though most preferred paying individually.
insight.step: Next group meal, try paying only for your share and see if anyone even notices.

questions.prompt: When is it hardest for you to tell the truth?

options.label: In small talk, like 'How was your day?'

insight.reveal: Your real answers are saved for moments that matter. To you, 'fine, thanks' is just how small talk goes, not a lie. You likely open up fully with a chosen few and keep it light the rest of the time.
insight.research: In a survey of 2,980 people in the UK, most said they are honest most of the time, and white lies were more common than big ones.
insight.step: Once this week, answer 'How was your day?' with one real detail.

options.label: When it would hurt someone I love

insight.reveal: With people you love, you'd pick kind over exactly right. You're the friend people go to after a bad haircut or a failed exam, because you listen well and go gently. You probably hear far more truth than you ever say.
insight.research: In week-long diaries, US students told about 2 lies a day and other adults about 1; most were minor, and about a quarter were told to protect or please someone else.
insight.step: Next hard truth, start with 'I'm telling you because I care' and see how it lands.

options.label: When it makes me look bad

insight.reveal: You know exactly where your honesty bends. That takes real self-knowledge, because that kind of blind spot is far easier to see in someone else. You tend to own up in the end, and that self-awareness keeps you fair with other people too.
insight.research: People tend to see bias in others much more than in themselves, and even after learning about a bias, they insisted their own judgement was objective.
insight.step: This week, admit one small thing that makes you look a little less perfect, and watch the reaction.

options.label: When I'm being honest with myself

insight.reveal: The hardest truths for you are the private ones. You question your own motives often, late at night or in a notebook. Seeing this is already a start, and honesty with yourself tends to grow one small admission at a time.
insight.research: Friends often judge traits like intelligence and creativity more accurately than we judge ourselves, while we know our own anxiety better than they do.
insight.step: This week, ask one trusted friend: 'What's one thing about me you think I don't see?'

questions.prompt: You realise you were wrong in an argument you 'won'. What do you do?

options.label: Go back and say I was wrong

insight.reveal: You'd rather get it right than win, and you know the difference. Being willing to lose is a strength, and it makes the people around you more open to changing their minds too. Your opinions carry extra weight precisely because you'll take them back.
insight.research: Scientists who admitted a finding of theirs was wrong were judged at least as well, and on some measures better, than colleagues who refused to admit it.
insight.step: This week, say 'I was wrong about that' about one small thing.

options.label: Mention it casually much later

insight.reveal: You get there in the end, once the heat has gone. Weeks later you'll slip a 'you were right about that' into a chat. The other person may have stopped waiting by then, yet it usually lands more warmly than you expect.
insight.step: Next time you realise you were wrong, say so within one day.

options.label: Let it stand. The moment has passed

insight.reveal: Once an argument's over, you close the file and move on. It keeps life light, and you hold few grudges. The other person may still be carrying the old version, though, and it can shape what they believe about you.
insight.step: This week, think of one argument you won but shouldn't have, and find a light way to mention it.

options.label: Look for a new reason I was still right

insight.reveal: Being wrong feels like losing a little piece of you. Most minds work this way, and a quick one like yours wins a lot of debates. Catching yourself hunting for new reasons is already the hard part, and you just did it.
insight.research: Even after learning about a bias, people tended to insist their own judgement was objective, while easily seeing bias in others.
insight.step: Next time you hunt for new reasons, ask: 'If they had said this, would I accept it?'

questions.prompt: When you post about your life online, how true is the picture?

options.label: I rarely post at all

insight.reveal: Your real life and your online life barely meet. You'd rather share news face to face, and you value your privacy. The flip side is that friends may miss the good things happening to you, from a new job to a new hobby.
insight.step: This week, share one small good moment directly with one friend, not online.

options.label: True, but only the best bits

insight.reveal: You share the best bits and keep the rest for yourself. Then, scrolling, it's easy to set your own behind-the-scenes against someone else's highlights and forget they're edited too. You have a good eye for what makes a moment worth sharing.
insight.research: People tend to underestimate how often others feel low and overestimate how often they feel good, partly because others hide it; those who did this most felt lonelier.
insight.step: Next time you compare yourself to a post, remember one thing you chose not to post.

options.label: I share the hard parts too

insight.reveal: You'd rather be known than admired. Sharing the hard parts invites 'me too' messages, and you've become a safe place for others without planning to. Your friendships are more honest because of it.
insight.step: This week, reply kindly to someone who shared something hard online.

options.label: A bit better than real life, honestly

insight.reveal: Even a small audience pulls on you, and you admit it. You've got real flair for style and storytelling. The gap between the post and the life can feel a bit lonely, though people tend to see more of the real you than you'd think.
insight.research: When strangers rated people's social media profiles, their impressions tended to match the person's real personality rather than the idealised self they wished to be.
insight.step: For one week, post nothing, or post one thing exactly as it is.

questions.prompt: A work rule seems pointless and no one would notice if you skipped it. What do you do?

options.label: Follow it anyway

insight.reveal: You trust that a rule has a reason, even when you can't see it. You're the colleague trusted with tasks where details really matter. You read the instructions first, not after something goes wrong.
insight.step: This week, ask the reason behind one rule you follow without knowing why.

options.label: Follow it, but ask to change it

insight.reveal: You respect a system enough to try to make it better. You improve workplaces slowly and without drama. Fixing a confusing form so nobody else has to struggle with it is your kind of good deed.
insight.step: This week, pick one pointless rule and suggest one clear fix to the person who can change it.

options.label: Depends on my mood that day

insight.reveal: Your rule-keeping is strongest on your good days. Tiredness can lower the bar for anyone, and you're honest enough to say so. You're flexible, easy company, and knowing what your tired self tends to do late in the week is half the battle.
insight.step: This week, notice one choice you made differently because you were tired.

options.label: Skip it quietly

insight.reveal: A rule has to earn your respect by making sense. That makes you quick and practical, happy to cut through red tape that slows the work down. It also means your own sense of 'pointless' becomes the rule, so check it now and then.
insight.research: A trait called Honesty-Humility predicts integrity and rule-breaking at work better than the classic five personality traits alone.
insight.step: Before skipping a rule this week, ask one colleague why it exists.

questions.prompt: It's 3 a.m. and something has gone badly wrong. How many people could you call?

options.label: Lots. I have a wide circle

insight.reveal: You've got someone for every kind of problem. You're the connector at parties, and no single friendship has to carry too much. The hidden cost: you may know a lot about others while the whole story of you is shared with no one.
insight.research: Across 148 studies of over 300,000 people, those with stronger social ties had about 50% better odds of survival.
insight.step: This week, tell one friend something real about your life that you usually keep light.

options.label: Two or three, and that feels like plenty

insight.reveal: A few deep friendships are plenty for you. You're the kind of friend people keep for decades. The same habit often shows up in how you shop and work: fewer things, chosen with care, kept for a long time.
insight.step: Today, send one of those two or three people a message with no question or request in it.

options.label: One, and I'd still hesitate to wake them

insight.reveal: You'd get up in the night for anyone, but you hate to ask. Asking, to you, feels too close to being a burden. Your friend would probably be glad you called, exactly the way you would be.
insight.research: In studies with over 14,000 strangers, people asking for help underestimated how many would say yes by about 48%.
insight.step: This week, ask that one person for a small favour and notice how they actually respond.

options.label: Honestly, I'd handle it alone

insight.reveal: You learned to rely on yourself, and it mostly works. In a crisis you're resourceful: you read the manual and fix the leak yourself. That skill is real, but it can make closeness feel like a risk instead of a rest.
insight.research: Adults differ in attachment avoidance, a discomfort with closeness, and it shapes how relationships feel.
insight.step: Next time something small goes wrong, tell one person about it the same day instead of after it's fixed.

questions.prompt: You open your wardrobe. What do you mostly see?

options.label: A few pieces I love and wear all the time

insight.reveal: You know what works for you, and you stick with it. Long menus probably tire you, and ordering the same favourite dish again and again is a quiet pleasure. Your mornings are quicker for it, because half the choices are already made.
insight.step: Tonight, pick tomorrow's outfit and notice whether your morning feels lighter.

options.label: Lots of choice, some never worn

insight.reveal: You buy clothes for the person you might become. The bold shirt, the fancy coat for a life you're still picturing: those unworn pieces are less about clothes and more about lives you're trying on. You're more open to reinvention than you let on.
insight.step: This week, wear one never-worn item just once, and see who you feel like in it.

options.label: Things I'm keeping for 'one day'

insight.reveal: You save the best things for a future version of you. 'One day' plans can pile up the same way: the trip, the class, the call you keep meaning to make. It's real hope, though sometimes the future you gets all the good stuff while today's you waits.
insight.research: Owning something tends to make it feel worth more: in classic experiments, people given a mug asked far more to sell it than others would pay for it.
insight.step: This week, choose one 'one day' item, then wear it or give it away before the week ends.

options.label: Things I bought to feel better on a bad day

insight.reveal: Your wardrobe is partly a diary of hard days. When a week gets heavy, a little treat helps, and you know it. Being this honest with yourself takes courage, and it's exactly where the pattern starts to loosen.
insight.step: Next time a bad day pulls you towards a shop, wait one night first and see if the wish is still there.

questions.prompt: You get one free week to travel. Which trip do you choose?

options.label: One place, slowly, like I live there

insight.reveal: A bakery and a bus ride tell you more than any famous sight. You judge a place by its ordinary moments, and you likely come home knowing a café owner by name. You bring the same instinct to friendships, where small routines often beat big events.
insight.step: This week, visit one place near home twice instead of trying somewhere new.

options.label: Five places. See as much as I can

insight.reveal: Missing the one great thing scares you more than being tired. You pack your days tight and come home with a camera roll full of stories. You collect moments, not things, and remember the rush more than the details.
insight.research: People's minds wandered almost half the time they were awake, and they tended to feel less happy then than when focused on what they were doing.
insight.step: On your next outing, pick one moment and stay with it for five full minutes before moving on.

options.label: The trip that will look best when I share it

insight.reveal: A trip feels even better to you once it's been shared. You have a good eye for beauty and a knack for telling a story. Admitting it takes honesty, because it's tempting to pretend other people's opinions don't shape your choices.
insight.research: In four studies, people free to take photos remembered more of what they saw but less of what they heard, even if they never looked at the photos again.
insight.step: This week, take one outing with no photos at all, then notice what you remember.

options.label: Stay home and finally do nothing

insight.reveal: You may be running on less fuel than you let anyone see. You carry a lot without a word, at work and at home. Wishing for a blank week often means your ordinary weeks hold more than they show.
insight.step: This week, block one evening with nothing planned, and protect it like a meeting.

questions.prompt: You arrive at a big buffet. What's your plan?

options.label: A little bit of everything

insight.reveal: Closing doors isn't your thing, even at dinner. The same pull shows up in work and hobbies, where you'd rather keep options open than bet it all on one. You'll probably order several small dishes for the table to share.
insight.step: At your next meal out, order the first dish that catches your eye without reading the rest.

options.label: Find the best dish and go back for it

insight.reveal: You're a scout first, then a loyal regular. You do the same with music, places and friends: a short search, then years of steady loyalty. Once you've found the best thing, you're happy to order it for years.
insight.research: A review of 268 tests found people tend to like things more the more often they see them, though liking can dip again after too many repeats.
insight.step: This week, go back on purpose to one favourite thing: a song, a café or a person.

options.label: Eat enough to make it worth the price

insight.reveal: You keep a quiet scoreboard to make sure things are fair. It makes you savvy and hard to cheat, and you know which deal is actually a deal. The same scoreboard, though, can turn a lovely evening into a test you feel you have to win.
insight.step: Next time you pay for something, judge it by how you felt after, not by how much you got.

options.label: Take more than I want, then feel bad

insight.reveal: Your fear of missing out is louder than your stomach. You're enthusiastic and up for anything, which people love about you. You might spot the same pattern in your calendar: saying yes to everything, then wishing you hadn't.
insight.step: At your next meal, serve half of what you think you want and go back only if you're still hungry.

questions.prompt: You're offered one more project at work. What do you do?

options.label: Say yes. More is more

insight.reveal: You run on momentum, not rest. You probably do your best work slightly overloaded, juggling side projects with ease. Quiet weeks and long breaks can leave you feeling strangely flat.
insight.step: Before your next yes, take ten seconds to name what you will do less of to make room.

options.label: Say no to protect the work I already have

insight.reveal: Finished work is how you measure a good day, not busy hours. Colleagues tend to admire the quality you turn out, and they trust a yes from you because they know you'll do it well. Your 'no' protects the very work that earned you that respect.
insight.research: In about 12,000 daily diaries from 238 workers, the best days were the ones where people made progress on work that mattered to them.
insight.step: This week, name the one task that deserves your best hours, and do it first thing one morning.

options.label: Say yes, even though I'm already stretched

insight.reveal: You feel you've earned your place when people can count on you. You protect everyone's deadlines except the ones for your own life, like the exercise plan or the trip you keep putting off. Being reliable is lovely; being reliable to yourself counts too.
insight.step: This week, move one small request to 'next week' and see if anything actually breaks.

options.label: Say yes because saying no scares me

insight.reveal: Saying no feels like a risk to you, not just a choice. You're generous, hard-working and quick to read other people's moods. That fear often runs even deeper at home than at work, and admitting it here takes a quiet kind of courage.
insight.research: Helping because you chose to lifted the well-being of both helper and helped, while helping under pressure did not bring the same benefits.
insight.step: This week, try one small, kind no, like turning down a meeting you don't need.

questions.prompt: How do you usually read books, or watch series?

options.label: One at a time, start to finish

insight.reveal: You like a story to end before the next one starts. An unanswered message or a half-made plan tugs at you until it's settled. It's also why you're the one confirming the time and place the day before.
insight.research: Unfinished tasks are not remembered better than finished ones, but people do tend to feel a pull to go back and finish what was interrupted.
insight.step: Tonight, leave one small thing unfinished on purpose and notice how long it nags at you.

options.label: Several at once, depending on my mood

insight.reveal: You pick your story to match your mood. Your tastes run wide, and you know which kind of story suits a tired night and which suits a lazy Sunday. Knowing what you need on a given day is a quiet skill.
insight.step: This week, notice which story you reach for on a hard day. It may tell you what you need.

options.label: I go back to the same favourites again

insight.reveal: A story you already know is a safe place for you to rest. When the rest of life is full of unknowns, a known ending can't surprise you. You likely stay loyal to favourite songs, cafés and people for years, and they're lucky to have you.
insight.research: Nostalgia often came on with low mood or loneliness, and recalling fond memories helped people feel more connected and better about themselves.
insight.step: This week, try one new show or book that someone who knows you well recommended.

options.label: I start many and finish almost none

insight.reveal: You love beginnings, when anything still feels possible. Ideas come easily to you, and starting is your gift. You might notice the same pattern with plans and projects, where the exciting start fades long before the slow middle.
insight.step: This weekend, pick one thing you started and finish just the next chapter or episode.

questions.prompt: How many photos are on your phone right now?

options.label: Not many. I delete as I go

insight.reveal: You trust your memory more than your phone. A tidy inbox and a clear desk are likely part of the same habit, and old arguments, old things and old versions of yourself don't hang around long either.
insight.step: Tonight, pick one photo you kept and send it to the person in it, no message needed.

options.label: Thousands. I'll sort them one day

insight.reveal: You keep everything, just in case it matters later. You're a curious collector of moments, and the 'one day' pile likely grows in other places too: inboxes, browser tabs, half-planned trips.
insight.step: Tonight, spend five minutes deleting photos from one single day, and stop when the timer ends.

options.label: Thousands, and I never look back at them

insight.reveal: You take the photo for the moment, not to look at it again. You live forward, and the past rarely holds you for long. Old mistakes don't tend to haunt you, because whatever comes next is simply more interesting.
insight.research: People free to take photos remembered more of what they saw, even if they never looked at the photos again, though they remembered less of what they heard.
insight.step: Tonight, open a photo from exactly one year ago and notice what you had forgotten.

options.label: I photograph moments instead of being in them

insight.reveal: You worry good moments will vanish if you don't catch them. That's because you treasure them deeply, which is a real strength. The camera is your way of holding on, even while it puts a screen between you and the moment you wanted to keep.
insight.research: Across 20 trials with 4,805 people, savouring exercises, which train people to notice and enjoy good moments, moderately boosted good feelings.
insight.step: At the next good moment, leave the phone in your pocket and describe it to someone later instead.

questions.prompt: Which sounds most like your hobbies?

options.label: One thing I've gone really deep on

insight.reveal: When you love something, you go all the way in. You lose track of time in your hobby and can get grumpy when someone interrupts. That same depth often shows up in love: you probably care for a few people, but very fully.
insight.step: This week, teach someone one small thing about your hobby and see how it feels to share it.

options.label: Lots of things tried, none mastered

insight.reveal: The first weeks of learning something are your favourite part. Progress is fast then, and you love that feeling. You're great company at dinner, and you often link ideas from different worlds in ways specialists miss.
insight.step: Over the next few days, spend twenty minutes on one past hobby, just to see what you still know.

options.label: I don't really have hobbies anymore

insight.reveal: Your hobbies slipped away one busy month at a time. You're responsible, and probably stretched thin. Here's the interesting part: you already know what you'd pick back up first if you had a free afternoon, and that answer is still in you.
insight.research: Across 93,263 people aged 65 and over in 16 countries, having a hobby went along with more happiness and life satisfaction.
insight.step: This weekend, spend thirty minutes on something you used to love, with no goal at all.

options.label: I quit once I'm not quickly good at it

insight.reveal: Being bad at something feels personal to you. You're capable and curious, just not used to feeling like a beginner. The first clumsy weeks feel harder than they really are, and the people you admire went through them too.
insight.research: People who believed passions are 'found' rather than built tended to lose interest faster when a new interest got hard.
insight.step: This week, try something new where the only goal is to be bad at it for ten minutes.

questions.prompt: Think about your group chats. Which is true?

options.label: One or two that really matter

insight.reveal: You treat messages as real conversations, not noise. You remember small things people told you weeks ago and ask how the job interview went. You also notice, a little sadly, when that care doesn't come back.
insight.research: Time spent side by side didn't, on its own, make people closer friends; catching up on each other's lives and joking did.
insight.step: Tomorrow, reply to one message with a question that shows you remembered something.

options.label: Many, and I keep up with all of them

insight.reveal: You're the quiet glue in a lot of friend groups. You know what everyone's up to, and you plan the next meet-up. Sometimes you'll notice that the checking-in rarely comes back your way.
insight.step: This week, notice who in your chats asks how you are, and spend a little more time with them.

options.label: Many, and the unread ones make me guilty

insight.reveal: You hold yourself to a standard nobody actually asked for. You're a thoughtful friend who replies properly, never with a lazy thumbs-up. That same rule, though, can make rest feel like something you have to earn first.
insight.research: When students kept phone alerts on for a week, they reported more trouble focusing and more restlessness than in a week with alerts off.
insight.step: Today, mute one busy chat for three days and notice whether anyone actually needed you.

options.label: Many, but no one I really talk to

insight.reveal: Your phone is busy, but you're missing someone to really talk to. You're good at keeping things light and friendly. You're likely closer to one real friendship than you think, and it usually starts with a single honest message.
insight.research: Across 148 studies, people with stronger social ties had about 50% better odds of survival, and rich, many-sided connection mattered more than just living with others.
insight.step: In the next few days, message one person outside the group and ask how they really are.

questions.prompt: Your ideal birthday dinner looks like…

options.label: A big party. Everyone's invited

insight.reveal: Half your friends probably met through you. You feel most like yourself with your whole world in one room. You're a generous host, and introducing people to each other can be more fun for you than talking to any one of them.
insight.step: This month, introduce two people you know who've never met but would get along.

options.label: A few close people around a long table

insight.reveal: Your best evenings are the ones where something real gets said. You care more about the talk than the noise. You're likely the last one still at the table long after dessert, asking one more question.
insight.research: In every world region, people who share more meals with others tend to report higher well-being.
insight.step: This month, invite two people for a simple meal, even if it isn't a special day.

options.label: Just one person who really knows me

insight.reveal: One person who truly sees you beats a room full of cheers. Big celebrations of you can feel a little uncomfortable, and on ordinary days you'd pick one deep talk over an evening of small talk. Someone probably came to mind as you answered.
insight.research: People who wrote thank-you letters underestimated how happy the receivers would feel, and expected far more awkwardness than there really was.
insight.step: Before the week is out, tell the person you thought of what they mean to you. No birthday needed.

options.label: Alone, with something great to eat

insight.reveal: Attention on your big day can feel more like pressure than a gift. You enjoy your own company and know how to treat yourself well. You often give generously on other people's birthdays while hoping your own passes softly.
insight.step: This week, treat yourself to one great meal alone, and let it be enough.

questions.prompt: You win a huge amount of money tomorrow. What do you do first?

options.label: Call my family and share the news

insight.reveal: Good news isn't real for you until someone you love hears it. You probably tell your people before you've even put your bag down, and you cheer loudest when they have news too. A win you couldn't share would feel strangely flat, like cake eaten alone.
insight.research: Telling someone about a good thing that happened tends to lift your mood beyond the good news itself, especially when they respond with real interest.
insight.step: Today, share one small piece of good news with someone, even if it feels too small to mention.

options.label: Stay calm, make a plan, change little

insight.reveal: Even a fortune wouldn't rush you, and that steadiness is worth a lot. You read the small print, keep the routines that already work, and friends tend to phone you first when things go wrong. The flip side: exciting news can take a while to actually feel exciting.
insight.research: Swedish lottery winners, on average, cut their work earnings only modestly after winning, and that small drop lasted for years.
insight.step: Tonight, write down three things in your life you'd keep exactly the same, whatever happened.

options.label: Quit my job that same week

insight.reveal: The real prize for you would be getting your time back. You already know which part of your week you'd cut first, down to the day. Once a door opens you move fast, and you bring real energy to fresh starts instead of planning them to death.
insight.step: This week, name the part of your work week you'd drop first, and find one small way to shrink it.

options.label: Tell no one, afraid of how people would change

insight.reveal: You want to be loved for who you are, not for what you've got. You notice who stays close when life shifts, and big news stays inside a very small circle. It can make you seem guarded, but once someone earns your trust, you're about as loyal as a friend gets.
insight.step: This week, notice who you'd trust with big news. That short list is worth knowing.

questions.prompt: Do brand names on clothes and bags matter to you?

options.label: Not at all. I want comfort

insight.reveal: You dress for how it feels, not for what it says. Your most-loved clothes probably stay in rotation long after they've earned retirement. How someone treats a waiter tells you far more than their bag ever could.
insight.step: This week, notice one sign of status you do care about that has nothing to do with things.

options.label: Quality yes, logos no

insight.reveal: You like nice things that whisper, not things that shout. You compare before you buy, check the stitching and read the reviews, then keep it for years. Being underestimated by someone who only notices loud labels secretly amuses you.
insight.research: Wealthy buyers with little need for status tended to prefer luxury goods with quiet logos, while status-seekers chose loud ones.
insight.step: Tomorrow, use one 'good' thing you've been saving, on a completely ordinary day.

options.label: A little. I notice what others wear

insight.reveal: Your eye goes straight to the details. You'd spot a friend's new haircut straight away and might remember what someone wore to a party months ago. On a wobbly day, that same sharp eye can slide into quiet comparing, and it's rarely kind to you when it does.
insight.step: Next time you notice what someone wears, also notice one thing about them that cost nothing.

options.label: Yes. I feel more respected in them

insight.reveal: The right clothes let you walk into a room already accepted. Somewhere along the way you learned that respect gets decided on sight, so you take real care with how you show up. Friends likely call you before a big interview, though you deserve that respect in your plainest shirt too.
insight.research: People overestimate how much others notice them: students in an embarrassing T-shirt guessed about 46% of the room noticed, but only about 23% did.
insight.step: This week, wear your plainest outfit somewhere ordinary and notice how people actually treat you.

questions.prompt: A close friend suddenly becomes rich. Your honest first feeling?

options.label: Pure happiness for them

insight.reveal: With the people you love, you never keep score. You're first to raise a glass at a friend's promotion, with no edge in your voice at all. Friends call you early with good news because they know your joy will be real, and that's a kind of wealth too.
insight.research: When someone shares good news, an interested, enthusiastic reply is linked to more trust and closeness, while a flat reply is linked to less.
insight.step: Next time a friend shares good news, ask which part of it they're proudest of.

options.label: Curious how they did it

insight.reveal: A friend's sudden luck is a puzzle you want to solve. You learn more from friends than from books, and you ask the questions that politeness usually swallows. You often leave dinners like that with a new idea for your own life, typed into your phone on the way home.
insight.step: This week, ask someone you admire one specific question about how they got where they are.

options.label: A small sting of envy

insight.reveal: Admitting that sting takes honesty, and you've got plenty. You'd probably tell a friend the truth about a bad haircut, too. And envy works like a compass for you: it points straight at something you want for yourself, which is useful, not shameful.
insight.research: A friendly kind of envy, wanting what someone has without wishing them harm, pushed people to work harder, but only when they believed they could improve.
insight.step: Next time you feel envy, finish the sentence 'I wish I had…' in your head. That's the real goal.

options.label: Worry they'll leave me behind

insight.reveal: When a friend's life changes fast, you wonder where you fit. You stay loyal for years and likely keep track of who reached out last. The worry says more about how much you care than about them, and a friend with a changed life often still wants the old friends close.
insight.research: Adults differ in attachment anxiety, a worry about rejection, and it shapes how relationships feel.
insight.step: Over the next few days, reach out to a friend whose life has changed lately, and talk about anything but the change.

questions.prompt: Which life pulls at you more?

options.label: A small home, lots of free time

insight.reveal: You count your wealth in hours, not things. A slow morning with nothing booked feels richer to you than any shopping trip. A promotion that eats your evenings might not tempt you at all, and a tight budget can still feel like plenty to you.
insight.step: This weekend, give yourself one slow morning with nothing scheduled before ten.

options.label: Comfort, plus a few real luxuries

insight.reveal: Some luxuries are worth it to you, and you know exactly which. A great bed, really good coffee or one proper trip a year gets your money, and little else does. Choosing your splurges this carefully makes everything stretch further, and you enjoy the chosen few more for it.
insight.research: In over 76,000 bank transactions, people whose spending matched their personality were more satisfied with life, a stronger link than total income or spending.
insight.step: This week, enjoy your one 'worth it' luxury slowly, with no rushing and no guilt.

options.label: Big success, whatever it takes

insight.reveal: It's proof you're after, more than possessions. Proof you were right, proof you could, and that hunger probably started long before money was the reason. Give you a bold target and a scoreboard everyone can see, and you'll rally a whole team around it.
insight.step: Tonight, write down who you'd most want to see your success. Then ask yourself: why them?

options.label: I want simple, but I keep chasing more

insight.reveal: Part of you wants enough, and part of you can't stop running. You might look at little houses by the sea on your lunch break, then go back to pushing harder at work. Seeing both pulls this honestly is the first real step to choosing between them.
insight.research: In Gallup data from over 1.7 million people worldwide, extra income stopped lifting life ratings beyond a certain point, which was higher in richer regions.
insight.step: This month, picture an ordinary week in your 'enough' life, and claim one small piece of it now.

questions.prompt: Dinner with friends who earn more than you. The bill comes. You…

options.label: Split it evenly, no fuss

insight.reveal: You'd rather keep the evening warm than keep the numbers exact. You remember who was fun, not who ordered the pricey bottle, and group plans run smoother with you in them. Just check now and then that easygoing hasn't turned into always paying more than your share.
insight.research: In a restaurant experiment, diners ordered more when the bill was split evenly than when each paid for their own food.
insight.step: Next time you eat out, suggest one place that you choose, and see how it feels to lead.

options.label: Quietly do the maths in my head

insight.reveal: There's a quiet calculator running behind your smile. You're scrupulously fair, and you probably know your monthly spending almost to the coin. When a split comes out uneven, you feel the pinch, then say nothing to keep the peace.
insight.research: People tend to expect honest talks to hurt their relationships more than they do; in tests, honesty felt better and more connecting than predicted.
insight.step: Next time it feels uneven, say so lightly once and watch how little drama it causes.

options.label: Order less so I don't overspend

insight.reveal: You protect your friendships by making yourself smaller. You're modest with money and generous with attention. The same habit may show up elsewhere too: the worse seat, the smaller room, the last turn, taken without a word and rarely noticed.
insight.step: At your next meal out, order the thing you actually want, just once.

options.label: Act fine, then stress about it later

insight.reveal: You'd rather pay with worry than risk one awkward moment. You're generous at the table, then you replay the evening all the way home. Hardly anyone sees what it cost you, which is kind of you, and also a bit lonely.
insight.step: Next time you make plans, suggest a cheaper one to a friend, like a walk or cooking together.

questions.prompt: You walk into a very fancy hotel lobby. How do you feel?

options.label: At ease. I enjoy places like this

insight.reveal: Fancy rooms don't shrink you one bit. You chat with the front desk like old friends and help a nervous companion relax without making a show of it. Most rooms feel like yours, which is exactly why the rare one that doesn't is worth noticing.
insight.step: This week, go somewhere you're a beginner, and notice how you carry yourself there.

options.label: Excited, like it's a special treat

insight.reveal: Nice things still give you a little thrill, and that's precious. You let a special place feel special instead of shrugging it off. A rare treat gives you more joy than daily luxury ever could, and ordinary outings feel like an occasion when you come along.
insight.research: A review of happiness research suggested money brings more joy when spent on many small treats rather than one big one, and on things to look forward to.
insight.step: Today, plan one small treat for later this week, and enjoy the waiting as much as the treat.

options.label: A bit bored. It's all for show

insight.reveal: You can spot a performance from across the room. You'd pick the small family-run place over the grand chain, and marketing tricks rarely get past you. The catch: that same radar can make a sincere compliment hard to enjoy without checking whether it's real.
insight.step: Next time someone compliments you, just say 'thank you', with no checking and no brushing it off.

options.label: Like someone will notice I don't belong

insight.reveal: A small voice asks whether you're allowed to be here. You likely hear it in meetings and new groups too, even when you're clearly welcome. The upside is real: it can make you a kind guest in any room, quick to spot who else feels out of place.
insight.research: Using luxury goods can make people feel like impostors, as if the luxury were an unearned privilege, which can leave them acting less confidently.
insight.step: This week, ask a friend what kind of room they think you shine in. Their answer may surprise you.

questions.prompt: You meet someone wearing a very expensive watch. First thought?

options.label: Nice watch. That's it

insight.reveal: You let people start with a clean slate. You judge someone by what they do next, not by what's on their wrist, and you take your time deciding who a person is. That's likely why your friends are such a wonderfully mixed bunch.
insight.step: Next time you meet someone new, guess one thing about them, then check it later.

options.label: I wonder what they do for work

insight.reveal: You look at a watch and see a life story. You're the one asking strangers how they ended up in their job, and other people's paths pull you right in. You probably hold those paths up against your own a little more than you let on.
insight.step: This week, ask one person how they ended up in their job, and listen for the turning point.

options.label: They're trying to impress someone

insight.reveal: Showing off makes you itch, and you spot it fast. People at work trust you because you play it straight and play down your own wins. The cost is that even your own nice things can come with a flicker of guilt, as if enjoying them were bragging.
insight.research: A trait called Honesty-Humility predicts integrity and rule-breaking at work better than the classic five personality traits alone.
insight.step: Today, tell someone one thing you're proud of, plainly, without a joke to soften it.

options.label: I quietly compare myself and come up short

insight.reveal: Someone's expensive watch can turn into a scoreboard you're losing. You're ambitious and you notice details, so the comparing likely runs on many fronts, not just money. What you rarely do is count the things you have that someone else would wish for.
insight.research: Life satisfaction tracked where people's income ranked among others like them more than the amount itself, and comparing upward counted more than downward.
insight.step: Tonight, write down three things someone might envy about your life, and reread them each day this week.

questions.prompt: Growing up, how did money feel in your home?

options.label: Rarely talked about. It was just there

insight.reveal: Money sat in the background of your childhood. Bills don't rattle you much, and money surprises roll off. Funny thing is, you probably know more about your friends' love lives than their money lives, because money talk still feels a bit awkward.
insight.step: This week, ask someone you trust one simple money question, like what they most enjoy spending on.

options.label: Tight, but we managed

insight.reveal: You learned early how to make a little go a long way. You check prices out of habit even when you don't need to, and nobody stretches a budget like you. Spending generously on yourself probably still feels a little like breaking a rule.
insight.step: Sometime this week, buy yourself one small thing without checking the price first.

options.label: Money caused arguments

insight.reveal: Money talk can still make your shoulders tighten. You might steer around money talk with the people closest to you, just to keep the peace. Yet you could also be the one keeping money calm and open in your home now, which is no small thing given where you started.
insight.research: In a 2022 US survey, 66% named money as a major stress, and of those, 55% said it caused fights or tension in the family.
insight.step: This week, at a relaxed moment, start one calm, short money chat with someone close.

options.label: Something I still feel uneasy about today

insight.reveal: Some of your money worries are older than your bank account. Your unease probably doesn't rise and fall with your balance, a clue that it's about feeling safe more than about numbers. Seeing that clearly is a big deal, and it's often where feeling settled begins.
insight.step: Next time money worry rises, ask: 'Is this about today, or about back then?' and just notice the answer.

questions.prompt: You get some unexpected extra money this month. Where does it go?

options.label: Put aside for later

insight.reveal: Feeling safe beats a quick thrill for you, every time. You build a cushion before friends have even made a plan, and money scares don't knock you over. The catch is that small joys can wait for years, long after you could easily afford them.
insight.step: This weekend, do one small thing you've been 'saving up' to enjoy, even a tiny one.

options.label: A meal or trip with people I love

insight.reveal: You turn money into memories with people in them. You're likely to get the group trip off the ground, and you can describe a shared meal from years ago in detail. Those stories get retold every time you meet, so the spending keeps paying you back.
insight.research: People often report that experiences they paid for made them happier than possessions they bought.
insight.step: This week, suggest a simple shared plan to someone, like a picnic or a cheap dinner.

options.label: Something just for me

insight.reveal: A treat for yourself is your way of saying your wants count too. You may put others first most of the year, so this is your moment to come first. Enjoy it while it's fresh, and skip the guilt.
insight.step: Today, notice one want of your own and tell someone about it.

options.label: It's gone before I even notice

insight.reveal: Money slips through your fingers into a hundred small joys. You're spontaneous and generous, quick to get the coffees and say yes to last-minute plans. 'Later' just feels very far from 'now' for you, which makes saving seem a bit unreal.
insight.research: People with stronger present bias, preferring smaller rewards now over bigger ones later, are more likely to carry credit card debt.
insight.step: For three days, write down one small thing you spent on each evening, just to see the pattern.

questions.prompt: Your income doubles overnight. Would you be happier?

options.label: Yes, clearly

insight.reveal: More money would erase a few daily stresses, and you can name them. You're practical about trade-offs and keep a mental list of upgrades ready to go. Better still, you can usually tell which problems are really about money and which only look like it.
insight.research: On average, happiness kept rising with income even at high salaries, though for the unhappiest group it levelled off at moderate incomes.
insight.step: This week, name the one daily stress more money would fix, and find one free way to soften it.

options.label: A bit, then I'd get used to it

insight.reveal: You already know how fast a new comfort turns normal. Things rarely impress you for long, but surprises delight you every single time. You'd likely spend on new experiences over new stuff, because that's what keeps life feeling fresh.
insight.research: Swedish lottery players who won large prizes were more satisfied with their lives for over a decade, but day-to-day happiness changed much less.
insight.step: Tomorrow, surprise someone with a small unexpected gesture, and notice your own mood after.
