options.label: No. My real problems aren't about money

insight.reveal: There's one problem in your life no amount of money could touch. It might be a relationship, a choice or a feeling, and you know exactly which one keeps you up at night. You think deeply about what matters, so quick fixes rarely fool you.
insight.research: Extra money did not lift people who were well-off but unhappy, even though on average happiness kept rising with income.
insight.step: This week, spend ten quiet minutes on the problem money can't fix, just thinking it through.

options.label: I'd mostly worry about losing it

insight.reveal: For you, having more mostly means having more to lose. You plan carefully, check your accounts often and insure what you own. The middle feels safest to you, where nothing can fall too far, and good news may need a day before you trust it.
insight.step: Next time you get something good, say 'this is good right now' before your mind jumps to losing it.

questions.prompt: If money and fear disappeared tomorrow, what would you do first?

options.label: Travel far, for a long time

insight.reveal: You're hungry for distance as much as adventure. Unfamiliar streets light you up, and you'd order the dish you can't pronounce. Part of the pull is a place where nobody expects you to be the usual you, so you can try on someone new for a while.
insight.step: This weekend, spend one afternoon somewhere nearby where no one knows you.

options.label: Start the thing I keep talking about

insight.reveal: Your dream already has a name, and that's a real head start. You may already have notes, sketches or a half-built plan. The usual snag is the perfect start date, the one that slides a little further away every time you get close.
insight.research: Across 94 studies, making a specific when-then plan had a medium-to-large effect on reaching goals.
insight.step: This week, write one when-then plan: 'When it's Saturday morning, I'll spend 20 minutes on my idea.'

options.label: Honestly, I don't know what I'd want

insight.reveal: You've been so good at what was needed that your own wants went quiet. You're the dependable one at work and at home, and your wishes speak in a whisper. Not knowing isn't emptiness, though, just a sign those wants have been waiting for some room.
insight.step: Each evening this week, note one moment that made you feel more alive than usual.

options.label: Leave a job or relationship I've outgrown

insight.reveal: You know exactly what you've outgrown, and that clarity matters. What's holding you back is fear, not confusion, and you've likely rehearsed the conversation in your head more than once. Naming it, even silently, is a real first step.
insight.research: People stuck on a big decision, like quitting a job, let a coin toss decide; those told to make the change were happier six months later than those told to stay.
insight.step: This month, write down one small thing you could change about that situation, without leaving it.

questions.prompt: Which kind of regret visits you most often?

options.label: Something I said

insight.reveal: You care a lot about how your words land. You replay conversations in the shower and you're quick to say sorry. Funny how the person you forgive last is you, even for things the other person forgot by lunchtime.
insight.research: People overestimate how much others notice them: in one test, only about half as many people noticed an embarrassing T-shirt as the wearer guessed.
insight.step: Next time a sentence replays in your head, ask the person directly if it bothered them.

options.label: A chance I didn't take

insight.reveal: The roads you didn't take still feel open in your mind. Missed chances bother you more than mistakes do. That's good news, honestly: it can make you braver than you think when the next chance shows up.
insight.step: This week, say yes to one small invitation you'd normally talk yourself out of.

options.label: Someone I lost touch with

insight.reveal: Old friendships stay alive in your heart long after contact fades. A birthday or an old joke can bring someone back to you in an instant. You assume they've moved on, when they may be waiting for the very same first message you keep not sending.
insight.research: People tend to underestimate how much someone will appreciate a quick message, call or small gift out of the blue, especially when it comes as a surprise.
insight.step: Today, send that person one short message. You don't need to explain the gap.

options.label: Years spent being who others wanted

insight.reveal: You can see the gap between who you were and who you showed. You're deeply tuned in to others, which is how the gap opened in the first place. You may already have started closing it, choosing honesty in small moments that once would have slipped by.
insight.research: Asked about their biggest regret, 76% of people named failing to become the person they hoped to be, and these regrets lasted longer.
insight.step: Tomorrow, make one small choice purely because you want it, not because it pleases anyone.

questions.prompt: Two offers: a safe job, or a risky one doing what you love. You…

options.label: Take the safe job

insight.reveal: Stability is the ground everything else in your life stands on. You'd keep your passion as a side project, where no boss can touch it. That's a smart way to protect what you love, as long as it still gets real hours and not just leftovers.
insight.step: This week, give one hour to the thing you love, with no plan to turn it into money.

options.label: Ask for time and make long lists

insight.reveal: Your gut often decides before your list is even half done. At work your choices are thorough and careful, and people rely on that. But sometimes the pros-and-cons list is really a way to talk yourself out of something you already want.
insight.research: People stuck on a big decision who let a coin toss decide, and were told to make the change, were happier six months later than those told to stay put.
insight.step: Next time you're stuck on a big choice, flip a coin. Notice which side you hope for while it's in the air.

options.label: Take the risk, sort it out later

insight.reveal: You trust yourself to land on your feet, almost wherever you fall. You'll change cities, jobs or haircuts with little warning, and you adapt fast when plans fall apart. Just check now and then whether you're leaping to reach a dream or to escape boredom.
insight.step: Before your next leap, write one line on what you're running to, not just from.

options.label: Take the safe one and always wonder

insight.reveal: You know your heart well, and you know your fear even better. Fear often wins the vote, yet you cheer with your whole heart when a friend takes the bold road. You'd happily talk someone else into the very risk you won't take, which tells you the courage is in there.
insight.research: Across 51 economies in 2024, nearly half of adults who saw a good business opportunity said fear of failure would stop them starting.
insight.step: This week, take one tiny risk for yourself, the kind you'd happily cheer a friend into.

questions.prompt: Who knows about your biggest dream?

options.label: Everyone. I talk about it a lot

insight.reveal: Telling everyone is how you make a promise you can't back out of. You gather cheerleaders easily, and your excitement gets a whole group going. One sneaky trap: talking about the dream can feel so good that it starts to stand in for doing it.
insight.research: When other people took note of someone's plan to become a certain kind of person, they tended to work less at it, as if being noticed already felt like getting there.
insight.step: This week, take one step towards your dream before telling anyone about it.

options.label: One or two close people

insight.reveal: You guard your dream like something that could break. You choose your audience with care, the few who'll believe in it without asking for proof. In return you're fiercely loyal to other people's dreams, sometimes more openly than to your own.
insight.step: This week, give one of those people an update on your dream, even if there's little to report.

options.label: No one. Saying it would make it real

insight.reveal: It's the look on someone's face you fear, more than failing. You work in private and show things only when they're finished, which can be really impressive. The trouble is, a dream nobody knows about is also a dream nobody can help with.
insight.step: This week, tell one kind person a small part of your dream. One sentence is plenty.

options.label: I've stopped admitting it even to myself

insight.reveal: Your dream went quiet to protect you from wanting it. It still sneaks up on you, in a song, a book or someone's success that stings more than it should. Oddly enough, that sting is good news: it means the wish is still alive.
insight.step: Next time someone else's success stings, pause and ask what it reminds you of.

questions.prompt: Someone your age achieves exactly your dream. You feel…

options.label: Inspired. It's possible!

insight.reveal: Someone else's win is proof to you that there's room for yours. You're a great friend to ambitious people, who often feel judged elsewhere. You'll likely look up how they did it and turn their path into a rough map for your own next move.
insight.step: This week, look up how that person started, and find one step they took that you could take too.

options.label: Fired up to catch up

insight.reveal: A rival fires you up more than any goal on paper. You do your best work when someone is just ahead, and you'll glance at who's winning even at the gym. Out in front on your own, though, your energy can start to drift.
insight.research: A friendly kind of envy pushed people to work harder and do better, but only when they believed they could improve.
insight.step: This week, choose a friendly 'rival' and share one small goal with them.

options.label: Quietly crushed for a day or two

insight.reveal: There's a clock in your head for where you should be by now. You hold high standards and feel things deeply, so the hurt is less about them and more about that inner clock. The good news is that you set the clock, so you can reset it too.
insight.step: Tonight, write down where you thought you'd be by now. Then cross out the date and keep the goal.

options.label: Relief. Now I don't have to try

insight.reveal: Relief tells you that dream was carrying a heavy load. Sometimes a dream turns out to be partly someone else's, picked up from a parent, a teacher or an old plan. Setting it down can free a surprising amount of energy for something that's truly yours.
insight.step: This week, ask yourself which of your goals you chose, and which ones you inherited.

questions.prompt: It's Sunday night. What's mostly on your mind?

options.label: Plans for the week ahead

insight.reveal: You relax once the week ahead has a shape. Sunday is when you check the calendar, sort out meals and pick your clothes, so deadlines rarely sneak up on you. A weekend with no plan at all, though, can feel more stressful than fun.
insight.research: Young adults who spent five minutes writing tomorrow's to-do list fell asleep about 10 minutes faster than those writing about tasks already done.
insight.step: This week, leave one evening totally unplanned and see what you choose to do with it.

options.label: Not much. I'm relaxed

insight.reveal: Sunday evening doesn't scare you, and that's worth a lot. Either your work fits your life well or you've built a solid wall between the two. You sleep easily and bounce back from bad days fast, and that's a skill worth protecting.
insight.research: Across 91 samples and 38,000 people, mentally switching off from work in free time went with less exhaustion, better wellbeing and better sleep.
insight.step: This week, notice what keeps your Sunday calm, and protect that one habit.

options.label: A quiet 'is this it?'

insight.reveal: It's less that you're unhappy, more that you feel unfinished. You crave growth and fresh challenges, and that question may visit at the same hour every week. If it does, that's a clue it's about your routine more than your whole life.
insight.research: In Gallup's 2025 worldwide data, only 1 in 5 employees felt engaged at work, and about a third were thriving in life overall.
insight.step: Next Sunday evening, add one new thing, even a small one, and see if the feeling shifts.

options.label: The life I'd live if I were braver

insight.reveal: A braver version of your life plays in your head, clear as day. You probably already know its first step, even the day you'd take it. The risk is that it keeps waiting for the right Monday, and the right Monday never announces itself.
insight.step: This Monday, do one five-minute action from that braver life.

questions.prompt: When you set a big goal, what usually happens?

options.label: I make a plan and stick to it

insight.reveal: Once you commit, you follow through. You finish courses, hit savings targets and keep your streaks alive, so goals come easy and rest is the hard part. That can make it tricky to drop a goal you've outgrown without noticing.
insight.research: Long-term studies show personality traits predict how far people get at work about as well as family background and intelligence do.
insight.step: This week, look at one goal and ask: do I still want this, or do I just want to finish it?

options.label: Start strong, fade by week three

insight.reveal: You're a brilliant starter, and week three is your weak spot. New projects get your full energy, and that spark is a real gift. You'll do best when the goal is tiny and the first step is almost too easy to skip.
insight.research: In one study, new daily habits took 66 days on average to feel automatic, with a wide range, and missing one day did little harm.
insight.step: Today, restart a goal you dropped, at a size so small it feels silly.

options.label: I keep it vague so I can't fail

insight.reveal: Keeping goals vague is how you protect yourself from missing them. A loose goal feels safe because nobody can say you failed. Trouble is, nobody can say you made it either, and one small, named target could unlock a lot for you.
insight.research: Picturing a goal, then the main obstacle inside you, then an if-then plan to beat it, helped people reach goals more often, a small-to-medium effect across 24 studies.
insight.step: This week, make one vague goal specific, name what in you might block it, then plan: 'When that happens, I'll do Y.'

options.label: I avoid setting goals. They stress me

insight.reveal: Goals can feel like a test you might fail, so you skip the test. You grow through curiosity instead, following whatever catches your interest. That winding path often takes you surprisingly far from where you started, and in good ways.
insight.step: This week, skip the goal: pick one question you're curious about and explore it for 20 minutes.

questions.prompt: Whose life do you secretly envy a little?

options.label: Someone who travels with no fixed home

insight.reveal: What you're craving is lightness, as much as travel. You've probably daydreamed about selling most of what you own, and a weekend with no plans feels like heaven. The wish points at whatever feels heaviest in your life right now.
insight.step: This week, drop one small duty that no one would really miss.

options.label: Someone who makes things for a living

insight.reveal: Making things with your own hands looks like freedom to you. Jobs where the work vanishes into emails and meetings can leave you restless, because you want something to show for your days. There may be a creative side project that matters more to you than you let on.
insight.step: This weekend, make one small thing with your hands: a meal, a drawing, a repair.

options.label: An old friend who chose differently

insight.reveal: You once stood at the same fork in the road they did. You notice how old classmates' lives turned out. The envy is often less about them and more about a version of you who might have gone along, which makes it a useful clue.
insight.research: People tend to underestimate how much someone will appreciate a message or call out of the blue.
insight.step: This month, get in touch with that friend and ask what they miss about the road you took.

options.label: A version of me who made another choice

insight.reveal: You keep a detailed picture of a life you didn't choose. Your imagination is generous, so that other life probably comes with its problems edited out. The useful question isn't whether you chose wrong, but which piece of it you could still bring into this life.
insight.step: This week, pick one quality of that 'other you' and try living with it for a day.

questions.prompt: At 90, looking back, what would hurt most?

options.label: Places I never saw

insight.reveal: You feel most alive when everything around you is new. You plan the next trip before you've unpacked from the last and try new routes just because. Routine drains you fast, so a little newness each week isn't a luxury for you.
insight.step: Tomorrow, take a different route to somewhere you go every day.

options.label: Work I never finished or made

insight.reveal: Leaving something behind with your name on it matters to you. You feel the clock keenly and judge a good day by what got built. You're likely still tinkering on a project long after the lights should be off.
insight.step: This week, spend 25 minutes on the thing you'd most hate to leave unmade.

options.label: Love I didn't say out loud

insight.reveal: Your love runs deep, but it travels sideways. It comes out as help, jokes or simply showing up. You'd fix a friend's shelf before telling them how much they matter, and you may keep waiting for the right moment for the bigger words.
insight.research: People about to give a compliment tended to underestimate how good it would make the other person feel, and overestimate how awkward it would be.
insight.step: Today, tell one person, in plain words, one thing you love about them.

options.label: Knowing I played it safe on purpose

insight.reveal: Caution has a cost, and you can already feel it. That price is easy to miss until much later. Seeing it now makes you honest with yourself, and probably a lot closer to changing than you give yourself credit for.
insight.research: Asked about their biggest regret, 76% of people named failing to become the person they hoped to be, rather than failing a duty, and these regrets lasted longer.
insight.step: This week, do one thing your 90-year-old self would be glad you did.

questions.prompt: When you really want something from someone, what do you do?

options.label: Ask for it directly

insight.reveal: To you, a 'no' is just information, not a verdict. You'll ask for more pay, a better seat or a hand with something, without much fuss. That ease can catch others off guard, so a little warm-up helps your ask land.
insight.step: Next time you ask for something, add one sentence about why it matters to you.

options.label: Drop hints and hope

insight.reveal: You hope people will notice what you want without you saying it. Part of you treats it as proof they care. You read other people's needs beautifully, but a hint that seems obvious to you is easy to miss, so the test gets failed unfairly.
insight.research: People asking strangers for help guessed they would need to ask about 50% more people than they really did: others say yes more than we expect.
insight.step: This week, turn one hint into a plain request, starting with 'I'd love it if…'

options.label: Wait until someone offers

insight.reveal: Taking more than your share feels wrong to you. You're a thoughtful guest and a fair colleague. The quiet cost is that good things often go to whoever simply asked first, and you've probably watched that happen more than once.
insight.step: This week, ask for one small thing you'd normally wait to be offered.

options.label: Tell myself I didn't want it anyway

insight.reveal: Not wanting feels safer to you than wanting and not getting. Others see you as easygoing and wonderfully self-sufficient. Meanwhile, a private list of shrugged-off wishes keeps growing, each one filed under 'never mind'.
insight.research: Adults differ in attachment avoidance, a discomfort with closeness, and it shapes how relationships feel.
insight.step: Next time you catch yourself saying 'never mind', say the real wish instead.

questions.prompt: How do you most often show a partner affection, or how would you?

options.label: Small touches during the day

insight.reveal: Your affection lives in your hands as much as your words. You reach for a partner's arm while walking and touch their back as you pass. A day without that contact can feel colder to you than a missed call, and it's the first thing you miss.
insight.research: A review of research on adults found that receiving affectionate touch, like hugs and holding hands, tends to support closeness, calmer stress responses and well-being.
insight.step: Next time your partner walks past, give them a light touch for no reason at all.

options.label: Saying it out loud, often

insight.reveal: Saying 'I love you' feels like a promise to you, not decoration. You leave sweet notes and voice messages that make a partner feel openly cherished. When they say it less than you do, you might worry, even when every other sign is right there.
insight.step: This week, notice one way your partner shows love without words, and tell them you saw it.

options.label: I show it, but rarely say it

insight.reveal: You say it with actions far more than with words. The fixed tap, the charged phone, their go-to snack waiting at home: you give more than a partner may notice, in ways they don't always spot. The words themselves can feel oddly heavy.
insight.research: A review found little support for the popular 'five love languages': most people value all five kinds of affection, and couples who 'speak the same language' are not happier.
insight.step: This week, pair one thing you do for your partner with one sentence about why.

options.label: I wait for them to show it first

insight.reveal: You hold your affection back until it feels safe to show. Going first can feel like risking not being met, so it waits behind a door for proof. Once you feel safe, you're a deeply devoted partner, and the person on the other side may be surprised how much was waiting.
insight.step: This week, make the first warm move once, small and simple, and notice what comes back.

questions.prompt: What does a truly romantic evening look like to you?

options.label: Dinner somewhere new

insight.reveal: Newness itself feels romantic to you. The place nobody has tried yet is usually the one you book. Seeing a partner somewhere unfamiliar, with a few happy nerves in the air, tends to make the attraction rise all over again.
insight.research: In a 21-day study of 122 long-term couples, days when partners did something new and exciting together went with more desire and satisfaction.
insight.step: For your next evening together, suggest one place neither of you has been.

options.label: Cooking together at home

insight.reveal: Romance, for you, happens side by side. Chopping vegetables together or painting a room can make you feel closer than candles ever could. You feel most drawn to a partner when you're a team, and a shared task can turn into a date without anyone planning it.
insight.step: This week, cook one meal together with both phones in another room.

options.label: A long talk with phones away

insight.reveal: For you, desire follows closeness, not the other way round. You remember what a partner said long after you've forgotten what they wore. Being truly listened to can feel more intimate to you than any candlelit setting, and a late talk may be the best part of the night.
insight.research: Strangers who took turns answering slowly deeper personal questions for 45 minutes felt closer than pairs who only made small talk.
insight.step: Tonight, ask your partner one question you've never asked them before.

options.label: Honestly, we've stopped planning these

insight.reveal: Romance has slipped behind daily life, and you've noticed. Noticing usually means you miss it, and that's hopeful: the wish is still alive in you. One small planned evening, even a walk, can wake it back up faster than you'd think.
insight.step: This week, plan one small evening, even just a walk, and call it a date.

questions.prompt: What usually draws you to someone first?

options.label: They make me laugh

insight.reveal: A quick laugh tells you there's a quick mind and a safe heart. You flirt through teasing and in-jokes. If a partner stops being playful, your interest can fade fast, even when everything else looks fine on paper.
insight.step: This week, start something playful with your partner or a friend, just to see who joins in.

options.label: Their confidence

insight.reveal: You're drawn to people who seem settled in their own skin. Part of the pull is relief: with someone that steady, you can finally stop holding everything together. And you bring plenty of your own spark, so it's rarely a one-sided match.
insight.step: This week, notice one moment when you feel fully at ease with someone, and ask yourself what made it so.

options.label: The way they look at me

insight.reveal: Being wanted is what lights the spark for you. You're a warm, responsive partner who notices every glance. Because your desire often starts as a reflection of theirs, it can cool fast when that look of interest fades, even for a day.
insight.step: Tonight, look at your partner a few seconds longer than usual, and see what changes.

options.label: Someone a little hard to read

insight.reveal: Not knowing where you stand can feel thrilling to you. You feel intense, vivid chemistry, and it's easy to mistake that rush for a deeper match. Calm, kind people may seem a little flat at first, then turn out to be the ones worth staying for.
insight.research: In one small study, women who were unsure whether a man liked them thought about him more and felt more attracted than women told he liked them a lot.
insight.step: Next time someone feels 'too easy', give it one more conversation before deciding.

questions.prompt: With a partner, now or in the past, what happens when one of you leaves the house?

options.label: Always a kiss or hug goodbye

insight.reveal: You keep closeness alive with small daily habits. A goodbye kiss, a goodnight message: these rituals matter to you more than big gestures. You build steady relationships, and you'd notice straight away the one morning the goodbye got skipped.
insight.research: A review of research on adults found that receiving affectionate touch, like hugs and holding hands, tends to support closeness, calmer stress responses and well-being.
insight.step: Tomorrow, make your goodbye last five seconds longer than usual.

options.label: Sometimes, if we remember

insight.reveal: The love between you is clearly there, just running on autopilot. Big moments still bring you close. It's the ordinary days in between where the little gestures slip, without either of you meaning them to.
insight.research: A review of 32 studies found regular family routines and rituals, like shared meals and holiday traditions, go with happier marriages.
insight.step: This week, pick one daily moment, leaving or arriving, and turn it into a small ritual.

options.label: Rarely. We're deep in routine

insight.reveal: Your relationship feels comfortable right now, more than close. Routine is a real sign of trust, and you're a dependable partner. Small touches are usually the first thing to slip away, and the good news is they're also the easiest to bring back.
insight.step: Tomorrow, surprise your partner with a goodbye hug, no explanation needed.

options.label: I'd like to, but feel shy starting it

insight.reveal: Even with someone close, reaching out can leave you feeling exposed. You're tender and attentive, and you may assume your partner doesn't want the hug. They could well be standing at the door thinking the exact same thing about you.
insight.step: This week, start one goodbye touch yourself. Keep it small, and let it be enough.

questions.prompt: When do you feel the strongest desire for a partner?

options.label: After we've laughed together

insight.reveal: Laughter is what opens the door to desire for you. You flirt through shared jokes and bring playfulness into the bedroom. A stressful week may dim your desire more than you'd guess, simply because there's been nothing to laugh about.
insight.step: Today, share something funny with your partner on purpose, and notice the mood after.

options.label: Seeing them confident in their element

insight.reveal: Seeing your partner shine on their own is what lights you up. Watching them give a talk or fix something tricky can give you a real jolt. A little distance and admiration may do more for your desire than closeness alone, because you see them as their own person.
insight.step: This week, watch your partner do something they're good at, and tell them what you noticed.

options.label: After some time apart

insight.reveal: You need a little space to miss someone before you want them. Reunions after a few days away can feel electric, and you keep a healthy life of your own. Constant closeness may feel loving but less exciting, and that's normal, not a warning sign.
insight.step: This week, spend an evening apart doing your own thing, then notice how you feel when you're back together.

options.label: Oddly, after we've had tension

insight.reveal: Closeness feels most urgent to you right after it felt at risk. Relief and desire can arrive together, so making up may feel more intense than the calm days. That shows how much you care about repair, and the same heat is possible without the fight first.
insight.research: In a 21-day study of 122 long-term couples, days when partners did something new and exciting together went with more desire and satisfaction.
insight.step: This week, on a calm day, try something new together, like an unfamiliar walk or recipe, and notice the spark.

questions.prompt: With a partner, now or in the past, who usually starts things in the bedroom?

options.label: Pretty equal, it goes both ways

insight.reveal: You feel wanted without having to keep checking, and that's lovely. Chores and plans are probably shared just as evenly in your home. The only quiet risk is assuming the balance will hold forever without anyone ever talking about it.
insight.step: Tonight, tell your partner one thing you love about how they show they want you.

options.label: Mostly me

insight.reveal: You're confident, and happy to make the first move. You likely plan the dates and start the big conversations too. Now and then you can wonder whether anything would happen if you stopped, and wishing to be pursued sometimes is completely normal.
insight.research: Across 48 studies with 12,145 people, couples who talked more openly about sex tended to have better sex lives; for women it also went with more desire.
insight.step: This week, tell your partner, kindly and outside the bedroom, that you'd love them to start things sometimes.

options.label: Mostly my partner

insight.reveal: Your desire tends to answer rather than spark, and that's normal. You're warmly receptive once things begin. The catch is that a partner can read your waiting as wanting less than you do, so even a small first move from you can mean a lot.
insight.step: This week, make one small first move, even just a lingering kiss, and see how it lands.

options.label: Neither of us, lately

insight.reveal: You and your partner may each be waiting for the other to go first. In a pause like this, both people often miss being close and each assume the other has stopped wanting it. Naming the pause, gently, can break it far more easily than you'd expect.
insight.research: Across 48 studies with 12,145 people, couples who talked more openly about sex tended to have better sex lives; for women it also went with more desire.
insight.step: This week, start a gentle chat: 'I miss us being close. Do you?' Nothing more is needed.

questions.prompt: How do you honestly feel about how often you and a partner are, or were, intimate?

options.label: It feels about right

insight.reveal: You measure intimacy by how close you feel, not by counting. You trust the relationship enough not to keep score, and you roll with busy seasons. Your calm helps a partner relax too, which keeps the whole thing easy.
insight.research: In large samples, couples' well-being rose with how often they had sex up to about once a week, then levelled off.
insight.step: This week, tell your partner about one recent moment of closeness you enjoyed, in or out of bed.

options.label: I'd like more

insight.reveal: Wanting more, for you, is partly a wish to feel chosen. You're openly affectionate and generous with attention. Because desire doubles as reassurance for you, a quiet week can feel like a message, even when it's really just tiredness or a full calendar.
insight.research: Among 229 people in long-term relationships, those who dealt with mismatched desire together with their partner were more satisfied than those who coped alone.
insight.step: This week, ask your partner what helps them feel in the mood, and simply listen to the answer.

options.label: I'd honestly like less

insight.reveal: You're honest about wanting less, and you're far from alone. You might feel guilty about it, yet desire often rises and falls with stress, sleep and feeling heard, not only with the partner. That's worth knowing before you blame yourself or them.
insight.research: In a study of 366 couples, partners with matching levels of sexual desire were not more satisfied than couples whose desire differed.
insight.step: This week, notice which kinds of closeness you do want, and share one with your partner.

options.label: We never talk about it, so I'm not sure

insight.reveal: In your relationship, intimacy happens, or doesn't, in silence. When nobody talks about it, both people guess, and often both guess wrong in the same careful direction. The care behind that caution is real, and it's a strong base for one honest conversation.
insight.research: Across 48 studies, couples who talked more openly about sex tended to have better sex lives, though many of the effects were small.
insight.step: This week, pick a relaxed moment and ask, lightly: 'Are you happy with how close we are?'

questions.prompt: Could you tell a partner plainly what you enjoy in bed?

options.label: Easily. We talk openly

insight.reveal: Talking openly about pleasure comes easily to you. That ease likely spills into other hard topics too, like money, family and fears. It can be one of the deep roots of your relationship's strength, even on days you don't think about it.
insight.research: Across 48 studies, couples who talked more openly about sex tended to have better sex lives, especially around orgasm.
insight.step: This week, ask your partner one open question about what they've been enjoying lately.

options.label: Only if they ask first

insight.reveal: You're open, you just need to be invited first. Generous and attentive, you assume they'd ask if they wanted to know. Meanwhile they may be assuming you'd simply say, so you both end up politely waiting.
insight.step: This week, do the inviting: ask your partner what they enjoy, and let them ask you back.

options.label: I hint or show instead of saying

insight.reveal: Closeness comes easily to you, but naming it doesn't. You communicate beautifully through touch and timing. Here's the twist: putting it into words can feel more exposing to you than the closeness itself, and that's more common than you might think.
insight.step: Next time you're close, say one short, warm sentence about something you enjoyed together.

options.label: I've never really said it

insight.reveal: Your pleasure has stayed private, even from people you trust. You put a partner's comfort first and tuck your own wants somewhere quiet, which shows real care. One honest, gentle sentence often opens more than you'd expect, and it's allowed to be about you.
insight.research: In a US survey of 52,588 adults, women who asked for what they wanted and praised their partner tended to reach orgasm with a partner more often.
insight.step: This week, think of one thing you enjoy and find a kind, simple way to tell your partner.

questions.prompt: A partner suggests trying something new together in bed. You feel…

options.label: Curious. Let's talk about it

insight.reveal: To you, intimacy is something two people keep building. You like talking things through and asking good questions first. The conversation itself is probably part of the excitement for you, not just the warm-up.
insight.research: Across 48 studies, couples who talked more openly about sex tended to have better sex lives; for women it also went with more desire.
insight.step: This week, ask your partner one 'what if we…' question, about anything, and see where it goes.

options.label: Excited. I've wanted that too

insight.reveal: You've been carrying a few wishes you hadn't put into words. You're adventurous and playful, and you may have been waiting for a partner to open the door. Once it's open, walking through can feel much easier than you'd imagined.
insight.step: This week, open the next door yourself by sharing one small new idea with your partner.

options.label: Nervous, but willing to talk

insight.reveal: Trust matters more to you than novelty, and that's a strength. You like a pace that feels comfortable, and you care about getting it right together. With that trust in place, new things often turn out to feel safe, and even fun.
insight.step: This week, tell your partner what would help you feel at ease trying something new. Only a clear yes means yes.

options.label: Worried I'm not enough as I am

insight.reveal: A new idea can sound to you like a review of you. You care deeply about a partner's happiness, so 'let's add something' can land as 'something's missing'. Most of the time it's an invitation, not a complaint, and often a sign they feel safe with you.
insight.step: This week, ask your partner: 'What do you love about us as we are?' Then let the answer land.

questions.prompt: When do you feel most desirable?

options.label: After a day where I did well

insight.reveal: Feeling capable and feeling attractive go hand in hand for you. You feel your best after nailing a presentation or finishing something big. Your confidence may rise and fall with your work week more than with the mirror, so a hard week can dim it without your noticing.
insight.research: A large review found that self-esteem tends to grow from doing things well, while trying to boost it directly does little for grades or work.
insight.step: On your next good day, tell your partner about it, and notice whether closeness follows.

options.label: When I've made an effort to dress up

insight.reveal: Getting dressed up switches on a bolder version of you. You love any excuse to dress for an occasion. You may enjoy being seen more than you'd ever admit, and there's nothing wrong with that at all.
insight.step: Tomorrow, dress up a little for no special reason, and see if your mood follows.

options.label: When someone can't stop looking at me

insight.reveal: Another person's gaze is what makes you feel desirable. You respond warmly to attention and give plenty back. On days the looks don't come, though, you may feel oddly invisible, which is why your own view of yourself deserves a vote too.
insight.step: This week, find one moment when you feel attractive on your own, with no one watching.

options.label: Rarely. I wait to be told

insight.reveal: You judge your looks more harshly than you'd ever judge a friend's. Others likely find you far more attractive than you believe. You're modest and unshowy, and compliments bounce off before they can land, which is a shame, because people usually mean them.
insight.research: After chatting with someone new, people tend to underestimate how much the other person liked them.
insight.step: Next time someone compliments how you look, say 'thank you' and let it land, no arguing.

questions.prompt: Something goes wrong at work and the room goes quiet. You…

options.label: Start fixing it before anyone asks

insight.reveal: Solving the problem matters more to you than finding the culprit. Before the explaining is done, you're usually halfway into the fix, and later nobody is quite sure how much trouble you saved them.
insight.step: When you fix something without fuss this week, send one short line so people know it's sorted, and by whom.

options.label: Say which part was mine

insight.reveal: Owning your share comes easily to you. When you say it first, others often find the nerve to own theirs, and the meeting gets shorter. Bosses tend to remember who did that long after the mistake.
insight.research: Pooling 136 samples of over 22,000 people, feeling safe to speak up and take risks in a team went with more learning, better performance and more engagement at work.
insight.step: When someone else owns a mistake this week, thank them in front of the team for saying it.

options.label: Quickly check it wasn't my fault

insight.reveal: Your first instinct is to make sure you're safe. That reflex often comes from being blamed unfairly once, though owning a slip usually costs far less than it feels. Once you know you're in the clear, you put your whole weight into helping.
insight.research: In a study of 281 scientists, colleagues who admitted a finding of theirs was wrong were judged at least as well, and on some measures better, than those who refused.
insight.step: Next time something breaks, ask 'How can I help?' before you check your own part.

options.label: Take the blame, even for parts that weren't mine

insight.reveal: A tense room bothers you more than carrying blame that isn't yours. You may be the peacemaker at home too. Colleagues love working with you, though a few learn they can leave you holding more than your share.
insight.step: Next time, say only the part that's truly yours, then stop and let someone else speak.

questions.prompt: Your boss sends you a message late in the evening. You…

options.label: Leave it until the morning

insight.reveal: Your evenings belong to you, and you protect them calmly. You probably walk in fresher for it, and bosses learn your rhythm fast. When something is truly urgent, you somehow still catch it.
insight.step: Tomorrow, make that late message the first thing you answer, so the rhythm feels fair to you both.

options.label: Reply quickly, then put the phone away

insight.reveal: Open loops keep you up, so you close them. A two-line reply buys you a quiet evening, and it mostly works. The line between work and home just moves a little each time, so it's worth noticing where it sits now.
insight.research: In a study of 297 working adults, the expectation of answering work emails after hours, more than the time spent on them, went with more exhaustion and worse work-life balance.
insight.step: Tonight, if a work message comes in, wait ten minutes and see whether it still needs you.

options.label: Read it, then think about it all night

insight.reveal: A late message keeps working in your head long after you put it down. You may draft three replies in bed and send none. By morning it usually turns out smaller than the night made it, which is worth remembering at bedtime.
insight.research: Young adults who spent five minutes writing tomorrow's to-do list before bed fell asleep about 10 minutes faster than those writing about tasks already done.
insight.step: Tonight, if a message stirs you up, write your reply in a note, not the chat, and send it in the morning.

options.label: Reply right away. I never really switch off

insight.reveal: You've become the person who always answers. Colleagues love this about you, and bosses come to rely on it without saying so. The cost shows up somewhere else first, like a dinner you ate without tasting or a story you half heard.
insight.research: Across 91 samples of 38,124 workers, people who mentally switched off from work in their free time reported less exhaustion and better sleep and life satisfaction.
insight.step: Tonight, mute work chats for one hour and see what, if anything, actually happens.

questions.prompt: You believe you've earned a pay rise. What do you do?

options.label: Wait for the next review

insight.reveal: You trust that good work gets noticed in time. That patience makes you steady and easy to manage. It also means your pay can hang on how well your boss remembers, so a small written record of your wins helps more than it seems.
insight.step: Start a note of your wins today, and add one line each Friday until your next review.

options.label: Book a meeting and ask

insight.reveal: To you, asking is part of the job, not a favour. You likely arrive with examples and leave with a clear answer at the very least. Even when the answer is 'not yet', you've put your case on the table for next time.
insight.step: Before your next pay talk, write down three results with dates, and the figure you'd be glad to hear.

options.label: Quietly start looking elsewhere

insight.reveal: Showing your worth feels better to you than arguing for it. You probably know your market well and leave places on good terms. Sometimes, though, the job you're leaving would have matched the offer, and pay is only loosely tied to how much people enjoy a job.
insight.research: Across 92 samples, how much people were paid was only weakly linked to how satisfied they were with their job.
insight.step: This month, have one honest pay conversation where you are now, before you decide anything.

options.label: Nothing. Asking feels like begging

insight.reveal: Asking for more feels heavier to you than the work itself. That modesty makes you lovely to work with, and it can leave money on the table that your work has earned. Asking isn't proof of being better at the job, just of being used to hearing no.
insight.research: Among about 4,600 Australian workers, men who asked for a pay rise got one 20% of the time and women 16%, though women asked just as often.
insight.step: Practise this at home a few times this week, until it feels ordinary: 'I'd like to talk about my pay.'

questions.prompt: A meeting runs long and nobody remembers the point any more. You…

options.label: Wait it out

insight.reveal: You give people room, even when time is short. Colleagues feel safe talking around you, which is why you hear things first. The price gets paid in the evening, when you finish whatever the meeting ate.
insight.step: In your next long meeting, ask one kind question: 'What do we need to decide today?'

options.label: Steer it back to the point

insight.reveal: Other people's time matters to you as much as your own. Steering a meeting rarely earns thanks in the room, yet it tends to get you invited to more of them, because things move when you're there.
insight.research: Across 136 samples of over 22,000 people, feeling safe to speak up in a team went with more learning, better performance and more engagement.
insight.step: Next meeting, invite the quietest person to speak before you steer things back.

options.label: Quietly get on with other work

insight.reveal: You've found a quiet way to rescue the hour. You get real work done in time that would otherwise be lost. Once in a while, though, the one sentence that would have changed your week slips past while you're typing.
insight.step: In your next meeting, put the phone face down for the first ten minutes and listen for one useful thing.

options.label: Look calm, but feel my whole day slipping away

insight.reveal: Lost time weighs on you more than it shows. You plan your days tightly, and a day always holds less than the plan says, so one long meeting can knock over the whole row. A protected hour later in the day can bring back much of the calm.
insight.research: People underestimate how long tasks take: students' everyday tasks took nearly twice as long as they predicted.
insight.step: Block one hour in this week's calendar that no meeting can take, and guard it kindly.

questions.prompt: How close are you to the people you work with?

options.label: Friendly, but it stays at work

insight.reveal: You keep work warm, and you keep it at work. That spares you most of the office drama and makes you the colleague people trust for a neutral view. When you move jobs, you'll leave very few loose ends behind.
insight.research: Time spent side by side at work or school didn't, on its own, turn people into closer friends; catching up on each other's lives and joking did.
insight.step: Over lunch tomorrow, ask one colleague about their life outside work, and really listen.

options.label: I have one real friend there

insight.reveal: One trusted person makes the whole place feel safer to you. Bad days shrink after a two-minute chat by the kettle or the door. That person probably counts on you more than you know, too.
insight.research: In a 2022 survey of 16,586 US workers, about 2 in 10 said they had a best friend at work; those who did tended to be more engaged and get more done.
insight.step: Today, tell your work friend one specific thing they make better about your job.

options.label: Some of my closest friends are colleagues

insight.reveal: For you, work is also where your people are. Long days feel lighter and hard projects feel shared. The flip side: leaving, or disagreeing with a friend who's also a colleague, can hit you hard, and work can tire you in ways that feel personal.
insight.research: In two US workplaces, employees whose colleagues were also friends got better performance ratings, but having many such friendships also went with more emotional exhaustion.
insight.step: This week, make one plan with a work friend that has nothing to do with work.

options.label: I keep everyone at a careful distance

insight.reveal: You draw a careful line between colleagues and the people you trust. That line exists for a reason, perhaps a time when closeness at work went wrong. People see you as fair, and like you more warmly than you guess.
insight.research: After chatting with someone new, people tended to underestimate how much the other person liked them, a 'liking gap' that lasted months among new roommates.
insight.step: On Monday, share one small, safe thing about your weekend with a colleague and see what comes back.

questions.prompt: You've been stuck on a work task for an hour. You…

options.label: Ask a colleague right away

insight.reveal: Your time matters more to you than looking clever. You learn new jobs fast, since each question saves you an afternoon. And colleagues like being asked more than you'd think; it tells them they know something.
insight.research: In experiments, people who asked for advice on a hard task were seen as more competent by the person they asked, though not when the task was easy.
insight.step: Next time someone helps you, tell them a day later how it turned out.

options.label: Look it up first, then ask

insight.reveal: You like to bring a better question than the one you started with. Because you've done the first steps, people rarely brush you off. The risk is the extra hour, spent when two minutes with someone would have done.
insight.step: Tomorrow, if you get stuck, give it fifteen minutes on your own, then ask someone, ready or not.

options.label: Stay late and figure it out alone

insight.reveal: You'd rather pay with your evening than with your pride. That streak makes people deeply skilled, because they've solved everything the hard way. Your team may not know how much it leans on you, since you never show the struggle.
insight.research: In studies with over 14,000 strangers, people asking for help underestimated how many would say yes by about 48%.
insight.step: This week, ask one colleague for help with something small, just to see how it feels.

options.label: Hope nobody notices I'm stuck

insight.reveal: Being seen stuck feels riskier to you than being stuck. Plenty of capable people feel like this, more than you'd guess. Often the first person you ask is relieved, because they've been stuck on the same thing.
insight.research: Feeling like a fraud who will be 'found out' despite real success is common: across 62 studies, between 9% and 82% of people reported it, depending on the measure.
insight.step: Tomorrow, ask one small question at work that you'd normally keep to yourself.

questions.prompt: A customer or client is rude to you. You…

options.label: Stay polite and sort it out

insight.reveal: When someone else loses their head, you keep yours. Customers notice, even if they never say so, and some come back asking for you by name. Just watch the cost: a forced smile tends to drain you more than a calm you actually feel.
insight.research: Across 95 studies, workers who faked feelings they didn't have, like a forced smile at a rude customer, tended to feel more drained; trying to really feel it cost far less.
insight.step: After your next hard customer, take one slow breath before you start the next thing.

options.label: Stay calm, but draw a firm line

insight.reveal: Kind and firm can live in the same sentence for you. Calm limits mean fewer repeat performances, because word gets around about who won't be walked over. Newer colleagues often watch how you do it and borrow your words.
insight.step: Next time a newer colleague is struggling, share the exact words you use to set a calm limit.

options.label: Smile, then vent to a colleague afterwards

insight.reveal: You hold it together, then let it out where it's safe. Telling a colleague can feel like relief, but going over the anger again tends to keep it going rather than drain it. A quick word, then something calming, usually helps you bounce back faster.
insight.research: People who let off steam by hitting a punching bag while thinking about the person who annoyed them got angrier; simply doing nothing calmed them better.
insight.step: Next time, tell the story once, then add what you'd do differently. Then let it go.

options.label: Stay kind, then carry it all the way home

insight.reveal: A rude moment stays with you long after the customer has gone. You're probably very good at your work, because you care how it lands. That same care can make one bad conversation louder than ten good ones.
insight.research: Bad events, bad feedback and bad moods usually affect people more strongly than good ones of the same size, though good can win when it clearly outnumbers bad.
insight.step: Tonight, write down one good customer moment from today, so the rude one isn't the only story.

questions.prompt: Two colleagues start gossiping about a third. You…

options.label: Change the subject

insight.reveal: Keeping the peace matters more to you than knowing the gossip. People trust you with real secrets, precisely because you don't trade in small ones. You might miss a bit of news, and you rarely lose sleep over it.
insight.step: Next time, try one kind fact about the person being discussed. It often turns the talk around.

options.label: Listen, but add nothing

insight.reveal: Ears open, words kept to yourself: that's your way. Hearing every side, you often understand the office better than it understands itself. Others see you as safe, which brings you more stories than you'd ever ask for.
insight.step: Over the next few days, notice which stories reach you twice, and let them stop with you.

options.label: Join in a little. It's how you fit in

insight.reveal: You know a bit of gossip is how groups stick together. That's very human, and it often makes you good company at work. The quiet risk is that colleagues start to assume their own stories travel the same way.
insight.research: Recording snippets of 467 people's daily talk, researchers found they gossiped about 52 minutes a day, mostly neutral chat about people they knew rather than nasty talk.
insight.step: Next time gossip starts, ask, 'Has anyone actually talked to them?'

options.label: Wonder what they say about me

insight.reveal: Gossip makes you wonder what's said about you. That watchfulness often makes you a careful, considerate colleague who gives nobody material. Most of the time, people are thinking about you far less than the worry suggests.
insight.research: People tend to overestimate how much others notice them: students guessed about half the room noticed their embarrassing T-shirt, but only about a quarter did.
insight.step: Today, when the worry comes, name one colleague you know speaks well of you.

questions.prompt: You get a new boss. In the first week, you…

options.label: Carry on as usual and see

insight.reveal: You let new people show you who they are. You rarely rush a first impression, and new bosses find you a relief: steady, unfussy, already doing the work. Within a month you'll know whether you get along.
insight.step: This week, ask your new boss one question about how they like to work.

options.label: Introduce myself and ask what they need

insight.reveal: Shaping a first impression suits you better than waiting for one. You'll learn the new boss's priorities in days rather than weeks, and they'll soon know they can turn to you. A warm welcome tends to help newcomers settle, and it works just as well with new neighbours.
insight.research: Across 70 samples of new starters, feeling clear about the role, confident and accepted by colleagues went with more satisfaction, better performance and less quitting.
insight.step: Next week, follow up on one thing you promised in that first conversation.

options.label: Miss the old boss more than I expected

insight.reveal: You're loyal to people, not just to job titles. Small endings can hit you hard, like losing a boss who finally understood how you work. That loyalty usually transfers, given a little time and a fair chance.
insight.step: This week, send your old boss a short thank-you, then give the new one a fair first month.

options.label: Worry they won't see what I've done here

insight.reveal: You worry your good work will get lost in the change. Often the work that holds everything up is the kind that makes no fuss, like yours. A new boss tends to see that fast, especially if you hand them a short summary instead of waiting to be noticed.
insight.research: In lab and workplace studies, women were asked more often than men to take on helpful but unrewarded tasks, like committee work, and they said yes more often.
insight.step: By Friday, write five lines on what you handle and share them with your new boss.

questions.prompt: A colleague keeps passing you bits of their work. You…

options.label: Help out. It's quicker than arguing

insight.reveal: Ten minutes lost is better to you than a standoff. You keep teams running smoothly and are often loved for it. You're also easy to ask, so small favours pile up without anyone deciding they should.
insight.research: Women were asked more often than men to take on helpful but unrewarded tasks and said yes more often; in all-men groups men volunteered as often, so expectations seem to drive who gets asked.
insight.step: Next time they ask, try 'I can after lunch' instead of 'sure', and see what happens.

options.label: Tell them it has to stop

insight.reveal: Saying no without a fight is one of your quiet skills. Things get said before they sour, so you carry few grudges at work. The colleague may grumble once, then respect you more for it.
insight.research: People tend to expect honest talks to hurt their relationships more than they do. In tests, being honest felt better and more connecting than predicted.
insight.step: Next time, offer one thing you can do instead, so your no comes with an open door.

options.label: Mention it to the boss

insight.reveal: Fair rules feel safer to you than awkward chats. You see the whole team, not just the moment. A quick private word with the colleague first keeps things warmer, and a good boss will ask if you tried.
insight.step: Before going to the boss next time, try one honest sentence with your colleague first.

options.label: Keep helping, and resent it a little more each time

insight.reveal: You keep saying yes while a quiet no builds up inside. It comes from a big heart and a real dislike of letting anyone down. The resentment tends to leak out somewhere smaller, like a shorter reply or a skipped coffee.
insight.research: Helping because you chose to boosted the well-being of both helper and helped, while helping under pressure did not bring the same benefits.
insight.step: This week, say no to one small extra task, kindly and without a long reason.

questions.prompt: The night before a big exam or test, you're usually…

options.label: In bed early. It's done

insight.reveal: You trust the work you've already put in. You walk into big moments rested, and the steady nights in the weeks before probably help even more than the last one. Being done the night before is a kind of confidence you've earned.
insight.research: Among 88 students wearing sleep trackers, sleep in the month before exams went with better grades; sleep the night before did not.
insight.step: Before your next big day, lay out what you need the night before, then do something gently fun.

options.label: Going over my notes one last time

insight.reveal: One last look is what lets you let go. That final pass turns up a forgotten detail now and then, and with it just enough calm to sleep. It works best with a firm stopping time, because 'one last look' has a way of becoming three.
insight.step: Before your next exam, set an alarm for when the last look ends, and stop when it rings.

options.label: Cramming until the small hours

insight.reveal: Pressure is when your brain finally switches on. You can do surprisingly well on the day, which is exactly why the habit sticks. The catch is that crammed facts tend to fade within weeks; spreading the same hours out is what makes them stay.
insight.research: A review of 10 study methods rated self-testing and spreading study over time as most effective; rereading and highlighting helped least.
insight.step: For the next exam or deadline, do one short session three days early, just to start the engine.

options.label: Awake, picturing everything that could go wrong

insight.reveal: Your mind runs every bad version of tomorrow before it arrives. You prepare hard and still feel unready. Yet the worry tends to shrink the moment the paper is in front of you, which is worth remembering the night before.
insight.step: The night before your next big day, write your three biggest worries on paper and leave it outside the bedroom.

questions.prompt: When there's homework at home, yours or a child's, it gets done…

options.label: Right away, before anything fun

insight.reveal: You'd rather earn your rest than borrow it. Evenings feel freer to you with nothing hanging over them. If there are children in your home, they're likely picking up that rhythm without anyone telling them.
insight.step: Tonight, once the work is done, mark it with something small you enjoy.

options.label: After a break and a snack

insight.reveal: A tired mind needs a moment first, and you respect that. Starting on a full tank means less fuss once the work begins. The only trick is making sure the snack doesn't turn into the whole evening.
insight.step: Tomorrow, set a short timer for the break, so starting feels decided, not debated.

options.label: At the last minute, in a rush

insight.reveal: Deadlines are what get you moving. Some of your sharpest thinking seems to happen in a rush, which is why the habit sticks around. The cost tends to land on sleep, and on anyone else in the house who has to rush with you.
insight.research: Students predicted a thesis would take about 34 days; it took about 56, and only 30% finished by the time they had predicted.
insight.step: This week, do just the first five minutes of one task as soon as you get it.

options.label: Eventually, after an argument or tears

insight.reveal: In your home, homework carries more feeling than the homework itself. Those battles are usually about tiredness, fear of failing or wanting company, rarely laziness. A fixed time and a calm adult nearby can change more than any lecture.
insight.step: Tonight, try sitting nearby with your own quiet task while homework happens, and make no comments.

questions.prompt: In a group project, you usually end up…

options.label: Doing my part, and only my part

insight.reveal: Fair shares matter to you, and you stick to yours. You rarely burn out on group work and rarely let anyone down. What you sometimes miss is the fun bit, when a whole group catches an idea at once.
insight.step: In your next group task, offer one idea beyond your own part, just to see where it goes.

options.label: Organising everyone

insight.reveal: A drifting group is something you can't just watch. You end up leading without being asked, at school, at work and in family plans. Funny thing: you know everyone's deadline except your own.
insight.step: Next time, ask someone else to run one part of the plan, and let them do it their way.

options.label: Doing most of it, so it's done right

insight.reveal: Carrying the load feels safer to you than risking a weak result. The final work is strong because of you, but the extra hours can slowly turn into resentment. The others may not even know they were allowed to try.
insight.step: In your next group task, hand one piece fully to someone else and don't redo it.

options.label: Going along, and keeping my best ideas quiet

insight.reveal: You keep the peace, and you keep your best ideas to yourself. Your ideas are often well thought through, and they often go unheard. The idea you held back is usually better than you give it credit for.
insight.research: Most of 40 employees interviewed had stayed silent about a concern at work, mostly for fear of being seen or labelled negatively.
insight.step: In your next group chat or meeting, say your idea first, before you hear anyone else's.

questions.prompt: You have to speak in front of a class or group. Beforehand, you…

options.label: Feel fine. I quite like it

insight.reveal: Attention gives you energy instead of draining it. You're the one asked to speak at weddings and farewells. The trick worth learning is the pause: a quiet second can land better than the next joke.
insight.step: Next time you speak, pause for one full second after your main point.

options.label: Practise it over and over

insight.reveal: Nerves become preparation in your hands. Because your words are already worn in, you come across as calm even when you're not. The audience rarely knows how many times you said it to the mirror.
insight.step: Next time, practise only your first and last lines until they're easy, and trust the middle.

options.label: Feel nervous, then get through it

insight.reveal: Your nerves show up, and you go anyway. That's the most common kind of courage there is. Speakers who feel this often sound warmer than the confident ones, because the audience can tell it matters to them.
insight.step: Before your next talk, tell yourself 'I'm excited' instead of 'I'm calm'. It's closer to the truth.

options.label: Look for any way to get out of it

insight.reveal: Being watched feels far bigger to you than the talk itself. You can have plenty to say in a small group and freeze only at the front. That fear tends to shrink fastest with tiny practice runs, not big brave ones.
insight.research: Students in an embarrassing T-shirt guessed about 46% of the room noticed; only about 23% did. People overestimate how much others notice them.
insight.step: This week, say one thing in a group, even just a question. That's the whole task.

questions.prompt: School fees, books, uniforms: when they come due, it feels…

options.label: Calm. It's already planned for

insight.reveal: You see big costs coming and meet them halfway. You likely give money a named pot and a purpose, which keeps it safe until it's needed. Fee season feels calm for you, and the people you pay for notice the calm more than the planning.
insight.research: People tend to sort money into mental 'pots' and judge each spend by its pot; such pots can help people protect their savings.
insight.step: Tonight, tell someone in your home what the planning made possible. It teaches more than numbers.

options.label: Tight, but we manage

insight.reveal: Tight numbers don't stop you making it work. You're likely resourceful in quiet ways: swapping books, finding second-hand uniforms, knowing who sells cheapest. The juggling it takes rarely gets seen, even by the people it's for.
insight.step: This month, find one cost you could share or swap with another family or classmate.

options.label: Worth any sacrifice it takes

insight.reveal: Learning is the one thing you believe is worth going without for. Often that belief comes from going without yourself, or watching a parent do it. The ones you pay for may not see the cost now; many understand it years later.
insight.step: Before the week ends, do one small thing just for you that costs nothing, and don't explain it.

options.label: Like a worry I hide from the people I'm paying for

insight.reveal: You carry the worry so others can carry their books. You may smile through fee season and lie awake after. Sharing even part of the plan with someone you trust usually makes it feel lighter, not heavier.
insight.research: People who usually hid their feelings tended to feel worse inside, share less and feel less close to friends than people who rethought what upset them.
insight.step: This week, share one piece of the money plan with someone you trust, even a small one.

questions.prompt: A teacher says the work, yours or your child's, isn't good enough. You…

options.label: Ask what would make it better

insight.reveal: Criticism sounds like directions to you, not a verdict. You improve fast because you leave with something concrete to do. Teachers warm to that, and the next round of feedback tends to come out kinder.
insight.research: Across 435 studies, feedback that explained how to improve helped students far more than rewards or punishment did.
insight.step: Next time you get feedback, pick the one change that matters most and do only that first.

options.label: Feel stung, then quietly fix it

insight.reveal: It stings, and you put the sting to work. You rarely argue in the moment, and you come back with work that's clearly better. The hurt fades faster once the fix is done, as you may have noticed.
insight.step: Next time it stings, wait an hour, then write down the one point you agree with.

options.label: Defend the work. They've missed something

insight.reveal: You won't let good work be dismissed without a word. You spot real unfairness, and you don't swallow it. Starting with a question before the defence is how you win a teacher over instead of losing them.
insight.step: Next time, start with 'Can you show me what you mean?' before you defend anything.

options.label: Feel small, like I'm back in school myself

insight.reveal: A teacher's red pen can still make you feel ten years old. A classroom moment from long ago can set the volume on every comment since. Remembering you're the grown-up now helps you hear the useful part.
insight.research: A large review found bad feedback and bad events usually affect people more strongly than good ones of the same size.
insight.step: Next time feedback lands hard, tell yourself: 'This is about the work, not about me.'

questions.prompt: When you have to learn something for a test, you mostly…

options.label: Read my notes again and again

insight.reveal: Seeing it all laid out in front of you feels steadying. Rereading is real comfort the night before a test. Mix in a little quizzing yourself with the book closed, and the same hours tend to stick far better.
insight.research: Testing yourself beat rereading: a week later, students who practised recalling a text remembered 56% versus 42%, though rereading looked better after 5 minutes.
insight.step: Next time you revise, close the notes after each page and say out loud what you remember.

options.label: Do old questions until it sticks

insight.reveal: Rehearsing the real thing suits you better than reading about it. You walk into tests feeling you've been there before. The same habit shows up elsewhere, like practising a hard phone call before you make it.
insight.research: A review of 10 study methods rated self-testing, like doing past papers, and spreading study over time as the most effective.
insight.step: Next session, try one question you're sure you'll get wrong, and learn the most from that one.

options.label: Explain it out loud to someone

insight.reveal: Things click for you once you've said them to someone. You probably help friends as much as yourself, and learn it twice in the process. Talking a problem through, even on a walk, is how you think best.
insight.research: Students who studied expecting to teach the material later remembered more of it, even though nobody actually taught.
insight.step: Tonight, explain one thing you learned today to someone at home, in under two minutes.

options.label: Make perfect notes, then run out of time

insight.reveal: For you, getting it neat feels like getting it right. Beautiful notes can help, but they can also eat the hours meant for the harder part: checking what's actually stuck. You may spot the same pattern before trips or big projects.
insight.research: Students who practised recalling a text remembered more a week later than students who reread it, yet the rereaders expected to remember more.
insight.step: For your next test, give the notes a time limit, then spend what's left testing yourself.

questions.prompt: Going back to school or a course as an adult. Your honest first thought?

options.label: I'm doing it, or I already have

insight.reveal: Age doesn't get a say in what you learn. You can outdo your teenage self, because now you know exactly why you're there. The people around you may be taking notes.
insight.step: Tell one person tonight what you're learning and why. Saying it to someone keeps it alive.

options.label: I'd love to, someday

insight.reveal: There's a subject waiting for you, and you know which one. 'Someday' usually means the wish is real and the first step is fuzzy. You may be one short, free course away from finding out if the spark is still there.
insight.step: This week, look up one short course in that subject and save the link. That's all.

options.label: Where would I find the time or money?

insight.reveal: You can be practical about a dream without giving up on it. You need a plan that fits real life: evenings, weekends, small fees. Once you find one, you'll likely stick to it, because you planned for real life from the start.
insight.step: By the weekend, find out the real cost and hours of one course, so it becomes a fact, not a fog.

options.label: I'd feel out of place, too old to start

insight.reveal: Part of you worries the classroom has moved on without you. That worry is loudest before you walk in, and it tends to fade once you're sitting down with a pen. Your life experience is often what younger classmates end up leaning on.
insight.research: In the EU, about 47% of adults aged 25 to 64 took part in some learning in a year, from over 65% in Sweden to under 25% in Greece.
insight.step: This month, sit in on one free class or online session, just to see who else is there.

questions.prompt: Results come back, yours or your child's, lower than hoped. You…

options.label: Shrug and plan for next time

insight.reveal: One result doesn't get to tell your whole story. You bounce back quickly and are often the calm voice in a tense room. The only thing to watch for is shrugging off a pattern that keeps coming back.
insight.step: Today, write one thing you'll do differently next time, and put it where you'll see it.

options.label: Look closely at what went wrong

insight.reveal: A bad result reads like a map to you. You improve most between one test and the next, because you know exactly where the marks went. You probably ask to see the marked paper, too.
insight.step: Today, find one thing in the results that went right, and plan to keep doing it.

options.label: Check how everyone else did

insight.reveal: You want to know whether it's you or the test. Hearing that everyone struggled brings real relief, and hearing they didn't brings an extra sting. Comparing helps for a minute, and rarely much longer.
insight.research: Across 33 studies of 1.28 million students, being in a higher-achieving class or school was linked to feeling less able yourself.
insight.step: Next time results arrive, read them twice on your own before you check anyone else's.

options.label: Feel it says something about me

insight.reveal: A low mark lands on you, not just on the paper. That's what caring deeply and working hard feels like. Separating the score from the person is a real kindness to yourself or your child, and kindness after a setback tends to fuel the next try.
insight.research: People encouraged to treat a failure with kindness, not harsh self-criticism, studied longer for a retest and were more motivated to improve.
insight.step: Tonight, name one thing you or your child did well this year that no exam measures.

questions.prompt: A classmate asks to copy your homework. You…

options.label: Offer to explain it instead

insight.reveal: Lifting someone up suits you better than handing over answers. Explaining sharpens your own grip on the work, so you end up knowing it best. Friends keep coming back to you long after school, for advice too.
insight.research: Students who studied a text expecting to teach it remembered more, and in a better order, than those expecting a test.
insight.step: Tomorrow, explain one hard thing to someone in under two minutes. It sharpens you too.

options.label: Let them. That's what friends do

insight.reveal: Loyalty to friends comes before the rules for you. You're probably generous in every direction, with notes, food and lifts home. Sometimes the friend learns less than they could have, and that can sit with you later.
insight.step: Next time, offer ten minutes going through it together before they copy anything.

options.label: Say no, even if it's awkward

insight.reveal: An awkward moment is better to you than a quiet compromise. People end up trusting you with important things, because they know where your line is. The friend may sulk for a day, and usually respects you more for it.
insight.step: Next time you say no, follow it with a small yes, like checking their first answer together.

options.label: Say yes, then feel used

insight.reveal: Saying no is hard for you, even when yes costs you. You're kind and well liked, and somewhere inside you keep track of who takes without giving. A small no early on saves a bigger hurt later.
insight.research: Helping because you chose to boosted the helper's well-being, while helping under pressure did not bring the same benefits.
insight.step: This week, practise one gentle no out loud: 'I'd rather not, but I can help you start.'

questions.prompt: By mid-morning, who has decided how your day goes?

options.label: Me. I had a plan and I'm on it
