options.label: Shared out fairly, more or less

insight.reveal: A home works, in your book, when everyone pulls a little. Fair shares usually start with a plain talk about the bins or the dishes, and you're not one to dodge it. Fairness at home rarely happens by luck.
insight.research: Even in US marriages where both partners earn about the same, wives spend about 4.6 hours a week on housework and husbands about 2.
insight.step: This week, thank someone at home for one job they do that nobody ever mentions.

options.label: Honestly, others do more than me

insight.reveal: It takes honesty to admit you're the lucky one at home. You probably notice more than you do, and a small guilt follows you past the sink. Admitting it already puts you one step from fixing it: one job, claimed for good, changes the picture.
insight.research: When couples each rated their share of household jobs, the two shares usually added up to more than the whole: we notice our own effort more than other people's.
insight.step: Choose one chore today and make it yours for good, without waiting to be asked.

options.label: I do more, and it's quietly building up

insight.reveal: You keep the house going, and much of it goes unseen. You spot jobs before they're even jobs, which is exactly what makes your work invisible. Resentment at home rarely grows from one big thing; it's the small, unthanked jobs, and naming just one can lighten the load fast.
insight.research: In interviews with 35 couples, the mental work of running a home, like noticing what is needed and keeping track, often went unseen and caused friction.
insight.step: This week, hand over one specific job by name, like 'Could you take the rubbish out on Thursdays?'

questions.prompt: Something at home breaks, and fixing it is your landlord's or someone else's job. You…

options.label: Report it the same day

insight.reveal: Small problems don't get to settle in around you. You likely report the broken light, the late delivery and the dripping tap, and people come to rely on you for it. Fixing things early saves you whole weeks of low-level irritation.
insight.step: Next time you report something, add a friendly line of thanks for whoever comes to fix it.

options.label: Fix it myself; asking takes longer

insight.reveal: Waiting on others costs you more than doing it yourself. Your toolbox, real or improvised, gets plenty of use, and you rarely sit stuck for long. Just notice the day 'quicker' turns into 'I always end up doing it.'
insight.step: This week, let someone else handle one small fix, even if you could do it faster.

options.label: Live with it for longer than I should

insight.reveal: You can make your peace with almost anything. You can step around the same loose tile for weeks and tell yourself it's fine, because it nearly is. That easygoing streak keeps you calm, and it can also leave you putting up with too much.
insight.research: Putting things off is very common: an estimated 15-20% of adults do it chronically, and people delay most when a task feels unpleasant.
insight.step: Today, write down one thing at home you've been living around, and send one message about it.

options.label: Delay asking so I don't seem like trouble

insight.reveal: You'd rather go without than be a bother. Requests get rehearsed in your head and softened until they barely ask for anything. Here's the thing: asking for what you're owed doesn't make you difficult, and a clear request is more likely to get a yes than you expect.
insight.research: People asking strangers for help guessed they would need to ask about 50% more people than they really did: others say yes more than we expect.
insight.step: Next time something needs fixing, send the request in one plain sentence, with no apology in it.

questions.prompt: A door handle at home comes loose. When does it actually get fixed?

options.label: That day, with whatever tool is nearby

insight.reveal: Broken things don't stay broken long around you. Whatever tool is within reach will do, and it usually does the job. Friends and family bring you whatever's wobbling, because you make problems look smaller than they are.
insight.step: This week, show someone at home how to do one small repair you know well.

options.label: I look up how, and enjoy learning it

insight.reveal: Every broken thing is a small lesson to you. You'll watch a ten-minute video and end up knowing more about hinges than you ever planned to. That curiosity shows up elsewhere as well: you'd rather understand something than just get it done.
insight.step: Next time something breaks, try fixing it for five minutes before you look anything up.

options.label: When someone else gets round to it

insight.reveal: You know your strengths, and fixing handles isn't one of them. That's fair. Your energy goes to the things only you can do, while home repairs wait in a gentle queue. Just watch that the queue doesn't quietly turn into a list.
insight.research: Delaying jobs that feel dull or unpleasant is very common; an estimated 15-20% of adults put things off chronically.
insight.step: Today, pick one small repair and either do it or ask someone, by name, to do it this week.

options.label: Never. I've learned the trick to open it

insight.reveal: You're brilliant at living around problems. The handle you wiggle, the tap you turn just so: you learn the trick and move on. It's a real kind of resourcefulness, though the same habit can keep bigger things 'nearly fine' for years.
insight.step: This week, fix one thing you've learned to work around, and notice how it feels to stop.

questions.prompt: There's a drawer or corner at home full of things you never use. Why is it still full?

options.label: I just haven't got round to it

insight.reveal: Clutter is simply low on your list, and fair enough. Bigger things compete for your time, and a drawer doesn't shout. When you do get to it, you're the type to clear the lot in one satisfying afternoon.
insight.step: This week, empty that one drawer onto a table and only put back what you've used this year.

options.label: Those things might be useful one day

insight.reveal: You're the person people come to for a spare cable. Planning ahead is part of how you feel safe, and sometimes it pays off spectacularly. The catch is that 'one day' things can crowd out the things you use every day.
insight.research: People tend to value things more once they own them: in classic experiments, people given a mug wanted far more to sell it than others would pay for it.
insight.step: Today, pick three 'one day' things and give them to someone who needs them now.

options.label: Throwing things away feels wasteful

insight.reveal: Waste bothers you more than clutter does. You probably learned early to mend, reuse and pass things on, and it stuck. That instinct is generous to the planet; it just means your things need somewhere to go other than the bin.
insight.step: This week, find one person or place that would actually use something from that drawer, and take it there.

options.label: Some of it holds memories I'm not ready for

insight.reveal: You keep memories in objects, not just in your head. A ticket, a note or an old phone can hold a whole chapter of your life. Keeping them isn't a problem. When you're ready, you may find it feels good to keep just the one that matters most.
insight.research: Thinking back to fond memories tended to lift people's mood and help them feel closer to others, though nostalgia can also feel bittersweet.
insight.step: Next time you open that drawer, hold one object for a minute, let yourself remember, then decide.

questions.prompt: It's dinnertime at home. Who usually ends up cooking?

options.label: Me, and I enjoy it

insight.reveal: The kitchen is one of your happy places. You taste as you go, change recipes without asking, and feel proud when the plates come back empty. Cooking, for you, is often how love gets said without words.
insight.step: This week, teach someone one dish you make well, from start to finish.

options.label: Whoever gets hungry first

insight.reveal: Appetite, not a schedule, runs your kitchen. Good days bring proper meals and busy ones bring creative ones, and nobody minds much. Easygoing kitchens like yours work well, as long as the same person isn't always the hungriest.
insight.step: Tonight, cook a little extra so tomorrow's first hungry person has something ready.

options.label: Someone else, and I'm thankful

insight.reveal: Being looked after is something you never take for granted. Washing up, fetching the bread or saying 'that was lovely' is how you give back, and small thanks like those are exactly what keep someone happy at the stove.
insight.research: People who wrote thank-you letters underestimated how happy and surprised the receivers would feel, and expected far more awkwardness than there was.
insight.step: This week, cook one simple meal for the person who usually cooks for you.

options.label: Me, every time, even when I'm worn out

insight.reveal: You feed everyone, even on the days you're running on empty. 'I can't tonight' rarely leaves your mouth, so nobody thinks to offer. You're allowed a night off, and asking for one will likely go better than you expect.
insight.research: People asking for help underestimated how many others would say yes, by about 48%, mostly because they forgot how awkward saying no feels.
insight.step: Pick one evening this week to say 'I'm not cooking tonight,' then let someone else sort it.

questions.prompt: Someone you live with leaves their dirty dishes out again. You…

options.label: Wash them; it's quicker than talking

insight.reveal: You'd rather have peace than prove a point. Mess gets cleared around you, often before anyone notices there was a problem. It keeps things smooth, though the house may be learning that dishes wash themselves.
insight.step: Next time, wash yours and leave theirs for one evening, and see what happens.

options.label: Say something light about it

insight.reveal: You say things before they turn into things. A quick joke or a 'hey, the dishes' is your style, and it usually works better than silence. Saying it early tends to keep big arguments out of your home.
insight.step: This week, suggest one simple house rule, like 'we wash up before bed.'

options.label: Leave them there until they get the message

insight.reveal: Grown-ups, you feel, should notice their own mess. Fair enough, though a silent message often lands as a puzzle rather than a point. Your own sense of fairness is strong, which makes it hard to understand a housemate who doesn't share it.
insight.research: People tend to expect honest talks to hurt their relationships more than they do; in tests, being honest felt better and more connecting than predicted.
insight.step: Next time, swap the silent message for a short, plain one: 'Could you wash these tonight?'

options.label: Say nothing, but it stays on my mind all day

insight.reveal: Small things at home take up more room in your head than you'd like. You replay the moment, plan what you'll say, and then say nothing at all. That isn't pettiness; you care about fairness and peace at once, and they can pull in different directions.
insight.research: Going over and over a problem in your head without acting on it tends to deepen low mood and make the problem harder to solve.
insight.step: Today, say the one sentence you've been rehearsing, kindly, and let the rest of the story go.

questions.prompt: Rent or another big home payment is due this week. How does it feel?

options.label: Like any other week; it's sorted

insight.reveal: You've built a home that doesn't keep you up at night. Paying early is one of the steady routines you rely on, and routines do the heavy lifting so willpower doesn't have to. People may never notice the planning, only that you always seem unhurried.
insight.research: Across 102 studies, self-control showed up more in steady, automatic routines than in one-off choices: self-controlled people tend to lean on good habits.
insight.step: This week, share one of your little systems with someone who'd find it useful.

options.label: A small sigh, then it's done

insight.reveal: You feel the weight, then you put it down. That's a healthy rhythm: you notice the cost without letting it run your week. Most grown-up jobs seem to go this way for you: a moment of grumbling and then straight on with it.
insight.step: On the day you pay it, do one small thing that makes your home feel more like yours.

options.label: I check my account more than once

insight.reveal: Keeping a roof over your head matters to you a great deal. Checking twice is how you reassure yourself, and it shows how seriously you take it. Often the money is already there; it's the not-knowing that wears on you.
insight.research: In a lab game, people felt most stressed when a bad outcome was uncertain, more than when it was very likely: not knowing can feel worse than knowing.
insight.step: This week, check once, write the number down, and let that note do the worrying for you.

options.label: It hangs over my whole week

insight.reveal: Your home feels safe, but never quite settled. When a payment is coming, it follows you into other conversations and dims the good bits of the week. That weight is real, even when you carry it without saying a word.
insight.research: In a 2022 US survey, 66% of adults named money as a major stress, and among them more than half said it caused tension in the family.
insight.step: Tonight, write down the date, the amount, and one thing you'd do if it went wrong. Worries often look smaller on paper.

questions.prompt: When does a proper deep clean happen at your place?

options.label: On a set day, most weeks

insight.reveal: You clean by the calendar, and it suits you. Knowing what each day is for gives you a steadiness that spills into the rest of your life. On the rare week the clean gets skipped, you'll feel it by midweek.
insight.research: Self-control tends to show up in fixed routines more than in one-off choices; people who seem steady and disciplined often lean on good habits.
insight.step: This week, let one part of your cleaning day go and put something fun in its place.

options.label: When guests are coming

insight.reveal: Visitors are your best cleaning motivation. You want people to feel comfortable in your home, and a deadline makes the work feel worth it. Your home probably looks its best on exactly the evenings you most want to share it.
insight.step: Next time you clean, invite someone over that same evening, so you get to enjoy it together.

options.label: When I'm avoiding something else

insight.reveal: Your home is never cleaner than when you're avoiding something. Scrubbing the stove suddenly feels urgent the moment a hard message or task is waiting. It isn't laziness: you're picking a job you can finish over one that feels bigger than it is.
insight.research: Across 94 studies, making a specific when-then plan ("When X happens, I will do Y") had a medium-to-large effect on reaching goals.
insight.step: Next time, try a when-then: 'When I finish this shelf, I'll do five minutes of the real task.'

options.label: When I'm upset; scrubbing helps me think

insight.reveal: When your mind is a mess, you put the house in order. Scrubbing, sorting and sweeping give your hands a job while your head catches up. It can be a wise habit: by the time the floor is clean, you often know what you want to say.
insight.research: In a small experiment, people made nervous about giving a speech spent longer cleaning an object, with more repeated hand movements, than calmer people did.
insight.step: Next time you clean to calm down, finish by writing one line about what was really on your mind.

questions.prompt: What does your breakfast usually look like?

options.label: The same thing most days

insight.reveal: You've solved breakfast, and you're not going back. One less decision in the morning leaves more room for the ones that matter. A few other quiet routines like this probably carry you through busy weeks, too.
insight.research: About a third to almost half of everyday actions are habits, done nearly every day in the same place, often while our thoughts are elsewhere.
insight.step: This week, swap one ingredient in your usual breakfast and see if the morning feels new.

options.label: Tea or coffee, and that's it

insight.reveal: Your morning starts with a warm cup, not a plate. Breakfast is more ritual than meal for you, a few calm minutes before the day begins. Hunger may well arrive all at once by mid-morning, when you'll eat whatever's closest.
insight.step: Tomorrow, add one small thing to your cup, like fruit or bread, and notice how the morning goes.

options.label: Whatever I can grab on the way out

insight.reveal: Your mornings move fast, and food has to keep up. You eat with one hand while sorting the day with the other. That's a real talent for getting going, though breakfast may get eaten without ever really being tasted.
insight.step: Tonight, set out something for tomorrow's breakfast, so the grab is a good one.

options.label: Everyone else eats first; I get what's left

insight.reveal: You feed others before yourself, even first thing in the morning. Making sure everyone has eaten and left on time is probably your job, official or not. It's a big kind of love, and you're allowed a proper plate too.
insight.research: Worldwide, unpaid care work like cooking, cleaning and looking after others is shared very unevenly: women do about three quarters of it.
insight.step: Tomorrow, sit down for five minutes with your own breakfast before you serve anyone else.

questions.prompt: You're hungry and there's no plan for dinner. What happens?

options.label: Cook something simple at home

insight.reveal: You can make a meal out of almost nothing. A few eggs, some rice, whatever's left in the cupboard, and you're fine. That calm, practical streak shows up when other plans fall through too: you just start with what's there.
insight.step: This week, cook one dish you've never made, using only what's already in your kitchen.

options.label: Buy something ready on the way

insight.reveal: You value your evening more than the washing up. After a long day, you'd rather spend your energy on rest than on chopping, and that's a fair trade. Buying back a little time like this tends to show up as more satisfied days.
insight.research: People who spend some money to save time, such as paying for help with chores, tend to be more satisfied with life, and this held at every income level.
insight.step: One evening this week, cook something easy instead, and see whether you enjoy the slower evening.

options.label: Go out; I need a change of scene

insight.reveal: Eating out, for you, is as much about the change of air as the food. A new room, other voices and someone else's cooking can reset your whole mood. 'Let's just go somewhere' is often your line, and it's usually the right call.
insight.step: This week, ask someone you don't see often to join you next time you eat out.

options.label: Look around the kitchen, then just eat bread

insight.reveal: At the end of a long day, bread is your easy answer. By evening, choosing dinner can feel like one question too many, so you take the simplest option. That isn't laziness; it's a full head asking for a break.
insight.research: Self-control was linked more to automatic, routine behaviour than to one-off decisions: people who seem disciplined tend to lean on good habits.
insight.step: Tonight, write down three easy dinners you like and keep the list where you'll see it tomorrow evening.

questions.prompt: Someone at the table asks to try some of your food. You…

options.label: Push the plate over: help yourself

insight.reveal: Food tastes better to you when it's shared. You order with the table in mind and enjoy watching someone love a bite of what you chose. Meals with you feel generous and loose, never measured.
insight.research: Tasting the same chocolate at the same moment as another person made good chocolate taste better: sharing an experience tends to make it feel stronger.
insight.step: Next time you eat with someone, order one thing just for sharing.

options.label: Cut them a proper piece myself

insight.reveal: You share, but on your terms, and neatly. You'll hand over the best bite, served properly, rather than watch a fork wander across your plate. That same care likely shows in how you give gifts and lend things.
insight.step: This week, offer someone a taste before they ask, and see how it changes the meal.

options.label: Share, while quietly guarding the best bit

insight.reveal: You're generous, with one small exception. Everyone has a corner of the plate they've been saving, and you're honest enough to admit yours. In the rest of your life, you're probably more open-handed than you think.
insight.step: Next time, give away the best bite on purpose and notice how you feel a minute later.

options.label: Say no: my plate is my plate

insight.reveal: You know what you want, and you ordered it. A friendly no to a small request takes confidence, and you have it. Your other boundaries are likely clear too, and the people close to you always know where they stand.
insight.research: People asking for help underestimated how often others would agree, mostly because they forgot how awkward saying no feels.
insight.step: Next time you say no, add an offer, like 'Shall we get you one?' You keep the no and the warmth.

questions.prompt: You open a packet of something tasty. When does it get put away?

options.label: After a handful or two

insight.reveal: A handful, enjoyed, and you're happy to stop. That easy rhythm shows elsewhere too: one episode, one coffee, then on with the evening. Pleasure doesn't have to be all or nothing for you.
insight.research: Across six studies, short breaks made pleasant experiences more enjoyable afterwards, yet people tended to avoid interrupting the things they enjoy.
insight.step: Next time you open a treat, put some in a bowl and really taste the first bite.

options.label: When it's been passed around

insight.reveal: A packet, to you, is something to pass around. You open snacks with others in mind, and a shared bag gets a room talking. You barely notice how much you had yourself, because the fun was in the sharing.
insight.research: Across 42 studies, people tended to eat more when dining with friends or family than when eating alone, but not when eating with strangers.
insight.step: This week, bring something small to share with people you see every day.

options.label: When it's suddenly empty, somehow

insight.reveal: Your hands are faster than your attention. When you're absorbed in a show, a chat or a task, the packet just melts into the moment. That's often habit and setting at work, not greed, and a sign of how fully you sink into things.
insight.research: Cinema-goers with a strong popcorn habit ate stale popcorn about as much as fresh, but not in a meeting room: habits are set off by places, not just taste.
insight.step: Next time, pour some into a bowl before you sit down, and enjoy every bit of it.

options.label: It's hidden where nobody else will find it

insight.reveal: You keep a little private treat, and that's allowed. In a home where everything gets shared, one hidden packet might be the only thing that's just yours. That says more about how much you give than about how much you take.
insight.step: This week, notice what else you'd like that's just for you, and give yourself one small piece of it.

questions.prompt: After a really hard day, what do you most want to eat?

options.label: Whatever's there; food is food

insight.reveal: Your mood doesn't rewrite your menu. You eat what's there and save comfort for other things, like a call, a walk or an early night. That steadiness may help hard days pass through you a little faster.
insight.step: Tonight, notice what does comfort you after a hard day, even if it isn't food.

options.label: Something warm and simple

insight.reveal: Warmth is your shortcut back to feeling all right. Soup, tea, porridge, rice: something soft that asks nothing of you. You probably look after others the same way, with a hot drink before any advice.
insight.step: This week, make a big pot of your favourite warm dish and save some for the next hard day.

options.label: A dish that tastes like home or childhood

insight.reveal: On hard days, you reach for where you came from. A familiar dish can feel like a hand on your shoulder from people who aren't in the room. You carry those people with you more than they know.
insight.research: Nostalgia often comes on when people feel low or lonely, and thinking back to fond memories tended to lift mood and make people feel closer to others.
insight.step: This week, call or message someone who used to make that dish and tell them you still crave it.

options.label: Nothing. My appetite disappears

insight.reveal: When life gets heavy, your body quietly closes the kitchen. Stress lands in your stomach first, and eating can feel like one more task. Often you only realise how hard the day was when you finally get hungry again.
insight.research: Across 54 studies, stress shifted eating only a little on average, and people differed: some ate more under stress, while others ate less.
insight.step: Next hard day, keep something small and easy nearby, like fruit or bread, and take a few bites anyway.

questions.prompt: Someone offers you a food you've never seen before. You…

options.label: Take a small bite to be polite

insight.reveal: You'll try anything once, at least a little. Kindness to the host comes first, and curiosity often follows a bite later. That's likely why you settle into new places quickly: you're willing to meet people where they are.
insight.step: This week, ask someone about a dish from their family and listen to the whole story.

options.label: Ask what's in it first

insight.reveal: A few questions first, then you're in. You like knowing what you're getting into, and once you do, you're usually happy to go for it. That same care shows up whenever you sign something, book something or meet someone new.
insight.step: Next time you're offered something new, try it before asking, then guess what's in it.

options.label: Dig in. New food is half the fun

insight.reveal: Your curiosity starts at the plate. Unfamiliar food feels like a small adventure, and you're the one at the gathering asking for the recipe. You probably travel, read and make friends the same way: hungry for what's next.
insight.step: This week, cook or buy one dish from a place you've never been.

options.label: Say no thanks

insight.reveal: You know what you like, and you're gentle about it. Familiar food means comfort and safety, and there's nothing wrong with that. Liking tends to grow with each taste, which is why your favourites feel so good, and why a second try can surprise you.
insight.research: Across 268 tests, people tended to like things more the more often they came across them, though liking dipped again after too many repeats.
insight.step: Next time something new is offered, take the smallest taste, then decide. One bite is enough.

questions.prompt: A family meal is coming up. What are you most looking forward to?

options.label: The food, honestly

insight.reveal: You're in it for the cooking, and nobody could blame you. Family meals hold dishes that taste like nowhere else, and you know exactly which ones you'll go back for. A love of the food is often a love of the people who made it.
insight.step: At the next family meal, ask the cook how they learned to make your favourite dish.

options.label: Catching up with everyone

insight.reveal: For you, the table is where the family news really happens. You drift between conversations, collect the updates and leave knowing who's doing what. People like having you there, because you make everyone feel caught up.
insight.research: In every world region, people who share more meals with others tend to report higher wellbeing, though happier people may simply share more meals.
insight.step: At the next family meal, ask one quiet relative a real question and listen to the whole answer.

options.label: Seeing one person in particular

insight.reveal: There's someone at that table who makes the meal worth it for you. You may spend most of the meal near them, half-listening to the rest of the table. It's worth telling them; people rarely know they're the reason someone comes.
insight.research: People tend to underestimate how much someone will appreciate a quick message out of the blue, especially when it comes as a surprise.
insight.step: Before the next family meal, send that person a message saying you're looking forward to seeing them.

options.label: Getting through it without old tensions

insight.reveal: You love your family, and family meals still take effort. You arrive with a quiet plan to steer around certain topics and leave more tired than you'd admit. That care for keeping the peace is real, even when nobody notices it.
insight.step: Before the next family meal, choose one topic you'll happily talk about, and one you'll politely skip.

questions.prompt: Picture a day of fasting, for faith or tradition. How do you get through it?

options.label: Keep busy and let it pass

insight.reveal: Keeping busy is your answer to hunger, and to plenty else. A full day leaves less room to notice what's missing. You probably use the same trick on other hard days, filling the hours until the worst has passed.
insight.step: Next time you fast, plan one quiet, restful hour in the day as well as the busy ones.

options.label: Count the hours until the meal

insight.reveal: You're honest about wanting the good part. You probably know exactly what you'll eat first and who you'll eat it with. Looking forward is its own pleasure, and the meal that breaks the fast tastes better to you than almost any other.
insight.research: Waiting for an experience, like a trip or a concert, tends to feel more pleasant and exciting than waiting for a new thing to arrive.
insight.step: Next time you're waiting for something good, plan the moment itself: who'll be there, what you'll say.

options.label: I get short with people, then feel bad

insight.reveal: Hunger finds your patience faster than you'd like. You might snap at something small, then spend an hour wishing you hadn't. That guilt says a lot about how much you care about the people around you.
insight.research: When 64 adults rated their feelings five times a day for three weeks, they felt more irritable and angry at times when they were hungrier.
insight.step: Next time you fast, warn one person kindly: 'I might be short today. It's not you.'

options.label: It makes me calmer and more thankful

insight.reveal: You find something quieter beneath the hunger. Going without seems to sharpen what you value, and you notice the people, prayers or thoughts that usually get lost in a busy day. You may be someone who grows most when things are a little harder.
insight.research: A review found that set rituals, religious or everyday, tend to help people manage worry, feel more in control and feel bonded to those they share them with.
insight.step: This week, keep one small moment of quiet each day, even when you're not fasting.

questions.prompt: There's one piece left on the shared plate. What happens?

options.label: I offer it to everyone else

insight.reveal: You'd rather give the last piece than eat it. You notice who hasn't had enough and make sure they do, without a fuss. People feel looked after around you, often without knowing why.
insight.research: Across 27 studies with over 4,000 people, doing small acts of kindness tended to give the kind person a small-to-medium boost in well-being.
insight.step: Next time there's a last piece, take it yourself and enjoy it. Someone has to.

options.label: I cut it in half

insight.reveal: Peacemaking comes naturally to you. Splitting the last piece is a small version of how you handle bigger things: everyone gets something, nobody feels left out. Friends may call you when a disagreement needs a fair middle.
insight.step: This week, notice one time you split the difference, and ask yourself what you actually wanted.

options.label: I take it before I overthink it

insight.reveal: You don't wait around for permission. While the plate is still being politely circled, you've already enjoyed it. That quickness serves you elsewhere too, grabbing chances before you can talk yourself out of them.
insight.step: Next time you're about to grab something, pause for one second and offer it first. Notice who says yes.

options.label: Nobody takes it, and it bothers me a little

insight.reveal: You notice the small dances people do around each other. That lonely last piece, left out of politeness, is exactly the kind of thing you see. It's part of why you read rooms well, sensing what people want but won't say.
insight.step: Next time the last piece sits there, say 'Shall we split it?' and watch how quickly people relax.

questions.prompt: When you eat a meal on your own, what's usually happening?

options.label: A screen keeps me company

insight.reveal: Company at mealtimes matters to you, even if it's on a screen. A favourite show turns a quick meal into a small break. Don't be surprised if your meals have started lasting exactly one episode.
insight.step: Tomorrow, eat the first five minutes of one meal with the screen off, then turn it back on.

options.label: I eat while getting other things done

insight.reveal: Meals, for you, get fitted into the gaps. You answer messages or finish work with one hand, and lunch is fuel for the next thing. You get a lot done this way; you just may not remember what you ate.
insight.research: In diary studies, a large share of everyday actions were habits done in the same place, often while people's thoughts were somewhere else.
insight.step: This week, take one meal away from your work, even ten minutes, and just eat.

options.label: Just me and the food, and I like it

insight.reveal: You're good company for yourself. Eating alone doesn't feel lonely to you; it feels like a pause the day owes you. Being able to sit happily with your own thoughts makes quiet stretches of life much easier.
insight.research: Across 11 studies, most people did not enjoy sitting alone for 6 to 15 minutes with only their thoughts, and many chose a mild electric shock instead.
insight.step: This week, take yourself somewhere nice to eat alone, and enjoy every bite.

options.label: I eat quickly; eating alone feels lonely

insight.reveal: Meals feel like they're meant to be shared, at least to you. Eating alone can remind you of who isn't at the table, so you get through it quickly. That longing says something lovely: food is how you connect, and you deserve more meals with company.
insight.research: People who share more meals with others tend to report higher wellbeing in every world region, while eating alone has become more common in the US.
insight.step: This week, invite someone to share a meal, or call someone while you eat.

questions.prompt: It's the last evening before your week starts again. What are you doing?

options.label: Getting clothes, bag and plans ready

insight.reveal: You like to meet the week halfway. Laying things out the night before is how you buy yourself a calmer morning. The week goes better when it starts on your terms, and the people around you benefit from that head start.
insight.research: Young adults who spent 5 minutes writing a to-do list before bed fell asleep in about 15 minutes, versus about 25 minutes for a comparison group.
insight.step: This week, add one thing to your evening routine that's purely for fun, not preparation.

options.label: Squeezing in one last bit of fun

insight.reveal: You'll take every drop of free time you're given. A late film, a long call, one more visit: you stretch the evening as far as it goes. That appetite for life makes you great company, even if the next morning arrives a little fast.
insight.research: Going to bed later than planned for no outside reason was common and linked with getting too little sleep.
insight.step: Tonight, give your fun an end time, and notice how tomorrow morning feels.

options.label: Already checking work or school messages

insight.reveal: Your week starts before it officially begins. Checking ahead feels like getting control back, and often it does. It can also cost you the last quiet hours that were meant to be yours.
insight.research: Across 91 samples and 38,000 people, mentally switching off from work in free time went with less exhaustion and better sleep.
insight.step: Next free evening, choose a time after which messages wait until morning, and keep to it once.

options.label: Feeling a heaviness I can't quite name

insight.reveal: Something about the week ahead sits on your chest. That evening heaviness is often less about one task and more about how much of the coming week doesn't feel like yours. Noticing it is the first step to working out what would make it lighter.
insight.step: Tonight, write down the one thing you're dreading this week, and one thing to look forward to.

questions.prompt: You get a whole hour with nothing to do. What does doing nothing look like?

options.label: Easy. I'm good at it

insight.reveal: Rest comes easily to you, no reason required. An hour on the step, at the window or lying flat with your eyes closed feels like time well spent. That ease is worth more than it looks, and it keeps you calm on frazzled days.
insight.research: Across 11 studies, most people did not enjoy spending 6 to 15 minutes alone with just their thoughts, and many chose a mild shock instead.
insight.step: This week, invite someone to do nothing with you: a slow walk, a long sit, no plan.

options.label: It lasts a while, then I find a job

insight.reveal: You rest for a bit, then your hands get restless. Ten minutes in, you've spotted the plant that needs water or the shelf that needs sorting. Your best rest probably comes mixed with small jobs, and that's fine.
insight.step: Next free hour, set a timer for twenty minutes of doing nothing, and only then start a job.

options.label: Only if my phone is in my hand

insight.reveal: Your hands like to hold something, even when your mind wants a rest. The phone fills the silence before it can get too loud. Afterwards, the hour may feel less restful than you hoped, and you're not quite sure where it went.
insight.step: Next free hour, leave your phone in another room for the first fifteen minutes.

options.label: Stillness makes me restless

insight.reveal: When you stop, your thoughts get louder. That's why doing nothing feels like hard work for you, not rest. Gentle movement may be your real recharge: a walk, cooking, tidying, anything where your body is busy and your mind can finally settle.
insight.research: A review covering 1,039 trials found physical activity reduced low mood and anxiety by a moderate amount.
insight.step: Next free hour, try resting on the move: walk with no destination for twenty minutes.

questions.prompt: Someone asks what you did on your day off. The honest answer: rested. You say…

options.label: 'I rested,' and I'm happy about it

insight.reveal: You don't need a productive story to justify a good day. Rest is part of your life, not a prize you have to earn. Just hearing you say it may help the people around you relax a little.
insight.step: This week, encourage one friend to take a proper rest day, and ask them afterwards how it went.

options.label: 'Oh, not much,' with a laugh

insight.reveal: You rest, but you keep it a little quiet. 'Not much' is easier than explaining how much you needed it. Your downtime matters more to you than you let on, and you guard it gently.
insight.research: Telling someone about a good thing that happened tends to lift your mood beyond the good news itself, especially when they respond with real interest.
insight.step: Next time someone asks, name one thing you enjoyed, like 'I slept in and it was great.'

options.label: I list the few useful things I did

insight.reveal: You rest like someone who has to earn it. Even on a day off, you want a few jobs to show for it, and you'll mention the errand before the nap. It comes from caring about being reliable, but rest doesn't need a receipt.
insight.step: This week, take one rest day without a single useful task, then tell someone exactly that.

options.label: Make it sound busier than it was

insight.reveal: Somewhere along the way, rest became something you hide. One errand can stretch into a whole busy day when you tell it. That's less about honesty than about worrying what people think, and the people who love you would be glad you rested.
insight.research: People tend to expect honesty to go worse than it does; in tests, being honest felt more pleasant and connecting than people predicted.
insight.step: Next time someone asks, tell them the plain truth about your rest, and notice how they react.

questions.prompt: When did you last take a few days fully off from work or daily duties?

options.label: Recently, and it did me good

insight.reveal: Stepping away is something you're genuinely good at. You take breaks before you're desperate for them, which probably helps them feel restful, and the people around you get a calmer, kinder version of you because of it.
insight.research: Holidaymakers were happier than others before their trip, mostly from looking forward to it, but once home most were no happier.
insight.step: This week, put the date of your next few days off in your calendar, even if it's months away.

options.label: A while ago; I keep meaning to

insight.reveal: You want a break; you just haven't let yourself take it. There's always one more thing to finish first, and the break slides a little further away. The right moment rarely arrives on its own; you'll have to choose one.
insight.step: Today, pick two days in the next month and tell one person you're keeping them free.

options.label: I honestly can't remember

insight.reveal: You've been running for a long time without a proper stop. You're the dependable one, keeping things going through every season. That's admirable, and it's exactly why a few days off could do you more good than you expect.
insight.step: This week, take one full afternoon off, phone away, as a test run for something longer.

options.label: Things would fall apart if I stopped

insight.reveal: Everything leans on you, or at least it feels that way. You've likely become the safety net for a lot of people, and stepping back feels risky. Most things survive a few days without you, and seeing that can be a quiet relief.
insight.step: This week, hand one small responsibility to someone else for a single day, and see what happens.

questions.prompt: Think of a hobby you love, or used to love. Where is it now?

options.label: Still part of my week

insight.reveal: You've kept something that's just yours. Holding on to a hobby through busy seasons takes quiet determination. It gives you a side of yourself that work and family rarely see, and probably keeps you steadier than you realise.
insight.research: Across 93,263 people aged 65 and over in 16 countries, those with a hobby tended to report better health and more happiness and life satisfaction.
insight.step: This week, share your hobby with one person who's never seen you do it.

options.label: Squeezed in when I can

insight.reveal: You fit the things you love into the cracks. It isn't the perfect amount, but you haven't let it go, and that matters. You can feel the difference in the weeks you manage it: a little lighter, a little more you.
insight.step: This week, give your hobby one fixed slot, even thirty minutes, and treat it like an appointment.

options.label: On hold until life calms down

insight.reveal: You've put yourself on the waiting list. It makes sense when life is full, but 'when things calm down' has a way of never arriving. The good news: small, planned moments tend to bring a hobby back faster than waiting for a free month.
insight.research: Across 94 studies, making a specific when-then plan ("When X happens, I will do Y") had a medium-to-large effect on reaching goals.
insight.step: This week, finish the sentence 'When ___ happens, I'll spend ten minutes on my hobby,' then do it once.

options.label: I miss it, and who I was when I did it

insight.reveal: You miss the hobby, and the person who had time for it. That version of you isn't gone; they're just waiting for a bit of room. Even a small return can bring back more of yourself than you'd expect.
insight.step: This week, do the smallest possible version of that hobby for ten minutes, just to say hello to it.

questions.prompt: Friends invite you out on your only free evening this week. You…

options.label: Go, of course

insight.reveal: For you, rest often looks like people. A loud table, good stories and late goodbyes leave you more refreshed than a quiet night in. You make plans actually happen.
insight.research: When 909 working women went back over their previous day, time relaxing with friends felt the most enjoyable part of it.
insight.step: This week, send the invitation yourself, to someone you haven't seen in a while.

options.label: Go for an hour, then head home

insight.reveal: You've found the middle ground between friends and rest. Showing up matters to you, but so does your own evening. Leaving while everyone's still having fun tends to mean people remember you at your best.
insight.step: Next time, tell your friends at the start when you'll leave, so leaving feels easy.

options.label: Say no and enjoy my evening

insight.reveal: A quiet evening is a real plan to you, not an empty slot. You can say no without feeling you owe anyone an explanation. Protecting your rest like this probably makes you more present when you do turn up.
insight.step: This week, suggest a different day to the friend you turned down, so the no comes with a yes.

options.label: Say yes, then wish I'd said no

insight.reveal: You'd rather lose your evening than let someone down. Saying no can feel like risking the friendship, so yes slips out first. Your real friends would likely understand a no far better than you imagine.
insight.research: Across four studies, helping because you chose to boosted well-being for both people, while helping under pressure did not bring the same benefits.
insight.step: Next time you're invited, say 'Let me check and get back to you,' and give yourself an hour to decide.

questions.prompt: A plan falls through and your afternoon is suddenly empty. Your first feeling?

options.label: Relief, like a little gift

insight.reveal: A cancelled plan can feel like found treasure to you. You love a full calendar in theory and an empty one in practice. That relief is a gentle hint that you may be saying yes to a little more than you need.
insight.step: This week, leave one afternoon empty on purpose, instead of waiting for a plan to fall through.

options.label: Excited. Now I can do my own thing

insight.reveal: There's always something waiting in the wings for you. A book, a walk, a project you've been itching to start: free time never stays empty for long. You fill a sudden gap quickly and happily.
insight.step: This week, keep a short list of things you'd love to do with a free hour, ready for the next one.

options.label: A bit lost without the plan

insight.reveal: Structure is where you feel most at ease. Without a plan, the afternoon can feel shapeless, and you're not sure where to put yourself. Your best rest may be the scheduled kind, and that's a perfectly good way to rest.
insight.research: Across 11 studies, most people did not enjoy 6 to 15 minutes alone with only their thoughts, and many preferred a mild shock.
insight.step: Next time a plan falls through, give the free time a quick shape: one thing to do, then rest.

options.label: Disappointed, and a little left out

insight.reveal: You were really looking forward to those people. A cancelled plan stings, because it was the company you were counting on, not the activity. That warmth is a strength: when plans do happen, you show up fully.
insight.step: Today, message the person who cancelled and suggest a new date, so the plan isn't lost, just moved.

questions.prompt: Your days off: what usually fills them?

options.label: Rest first, then I see how I feel

insight.reveal: You treat days off as days off. Sleeping in, a slow start, then deciding later is how you get your energy back. Most weeks, you'll begin rested, which is exactly what those days are for.
insight.step: Next day off, try one small new thing in the afternoon, once the rest is done.

options.label: Chores and errands that didn't fit the week

insight.reveal: Your days off are where the week's leftovers go. Shopping, washing and fixing things all wait for you there. By evening you feel accomplished, and maybe still a little tired when the week begins again.
insight.research: Across four countries, people who paid to save time, such as getting help with chores, tended to be more satisfied with life.
insight.step: Next day off, start with one hour that's purely for you, before the first errand.

options.label: People: family, friends, visits

insight.reveal: Your free days belong to the people you love. Visits, meals and long chats fill them up, and that's how you recharge. Just keep an eye out for days that are all giving and no resting.
insight.research: In data from about 271,000 people in nearly 100 countries, those who valued their friendships reported better health and happiness.
insight.step: This week, keep a few hours of one day off for yourself alone, and see how it feels.

options.label: Mostly other people's plans

insight.reveal: You go along with others' plans, often happily, sometimes less so. 'Whatever you like' comes more easily to you than saying what you'd actually enjoy. Your wishes are worth putting on the table too.
insight.step: Next day off, suggest one thing you'd genuinely love to do, and see who says yes.

questions.prompt: What actually leaves you feeling rested?

options.label: A long, proper sleep

insight.reveal: Your body knows exactly what it needs, and it's sleep. A good night fixes more for you than any weekend plan. It shows in your patience first: one short night and the world gets a little more annoying.
insight.research: An expert panel recommends 7 to 9 hours of sleep a night for adults and 8 to 10 hours for teenagers.
insight.step: This week, go to bed half an hour earlier one night and notice the next day's mood.

options.label: Good company and a long meal

insight.reveal: People fill your tank. A long meal with laughter rests you better than a lie-in ever could. After a good evening out, you come home tired in body and wide awake in spirit.
insight.research: In every world region, people who share more meals with others tend to report higher wellbeing.
insight.step: This week, plan one long, slow meal with someone you enjoy, with nowhere to be afterwards.

options.label: A whole day completely alone

insight.reveal: Quiet, empty days are how you refill. A day with no one to answer to is when you feel most like yourself. People who love you may not always get it, but you're kinder and more patient after that quiet.
insight.step: This month, book yourself a full day alone, and tell the people close to you that it's coming.

options.label: Honestly, I rarely feel rested

insight.reveal: You've been tired for so long that it feels normal. Rest may be happening in the gaps, but it isn't reaching you. That isn't a personal failing; it can mean you need a different kind of rest, not just more of it.
insight.research: Across 140 countries in 2025, 71% of adults said they felt well rested the day before, so nearly 3 in 10 did not.
insight.step: This week, try one kind of rest you never usually choose: a nap, a walk, a day alone or an evening out.

questions.prompt: On a day off, do you check messages about work or other duties?

options.label: No. Off means off

insight.reveal: A day off, for you, is a real day off. You've drawn a clear line and you keep to it, so you come back sharper. People who work with you likely respect that line more than you think.
insight.research: Mentally switching off from work in free time went with less exhaustion, better wellbeing and better sleep, across 91 samples and 38,000 people.
insight.step: This week, help someone else switch off by not messaging them on their day off.

options.label: Once, just to be safe

insight.reveal: One quick look, and then you can relax. Checking once settles your mind so the rest of the day can be yours. It's how you handle most worries: face them briefly, then put them down.
insight.step: Next day off, choose the exact time you'll check, and don't look before then.

options.label: Often, telling myself it's quick

insight.reveal: Part of you never quite clocks off. Each quick check feels harmless, yet together they keep a corner of your mind at work all day. A single unchecked afternoon may leave you more rested than you'd expect.
insight.research: When students kept phone alerts on for a week, they reported more trouble focusing and more restlessness than in a week with alerts off.
insight.step: Next day off, turn off notifications for one afternoon and see how your evening feels.

options.label: Yes, I like feeling needed

insight.reveal: Being needed is one of the ways you feel you belong. A message asking for you can feel more like warmth than work. That's a lovely quality, and you're worth just as much on the days nobody needs anything from you.
insight.step: Next day off, spend an hour with someone who needs nothing from you, just company.

questions.prompt: Your message shows as read, but no reply comes. What do you do?

options.label: Assume they're busy and get on with my day

insight.reveal: You give people the benefit of the doubt, and it saves you hours. Friends find you easy to text, because a slow reply never turns into a sulk with you. When you write 'no rush', you genuinely mean it.
insight.step: Today, answer one message you've read and left, so someone else gets the same ease you give.

options.label: Check when they were last online

insight.reveal: You notice the smallest signals. Checking a last-seen time is rarely nosiness; it's your way of settling a question that's already tugging at you. In person, you likely read a room fast and catch a mood shift before anyone names it.
insight.research: Adults differ in attachment anxiety (worry about rejection) and attachment avoidance (discomfort with closeness), and both shape how relationships feel.
insight.step: Next time you check, put the phone face down for ten minutes and see if the question still feels as urgent.

options.label: Reread what I sent, looking for the problem

insight.reveal: You look for the mistake in yourself before you blame anyone else. It's a generous habit with a cost. You might draft a message three times before sending and still reread it after, hunting for a problem the other person almost never sees.
insight.research: Going over and over a worry in your head without acting on it tends to deepen low mood and make problems harder to solve.
insight.step: Tonight, if you catch yourself rereading a sent message, close the chat and write down two other reasons they might be quiet.

options.label: Go a little cooler with them next time

insight.reveal: You protect your heart by matching the distance you're given. It's a sensible defence, and it's easy to miss in yourself. Watch for it in small ways: replying a little later on purpose, or keeping a message short when you'd like to say more.
insight.step: This week, send one warm message to someone you've gone cool on, and let them surprise you.

questions.prompt: A big group chat (family, neighbours, old classmates) has hundreds of unread messages. You…

options.label: Mark it all as read and carry on

insight.reveal: You don't let other people's noise set your pace. The important news still reaches you, usually because someone tells you in person. Busy places probably don't rattle you much either; a crowded bus stop can still be somewhere to read.
insight.step: This week, pick one group you actually love and catch up on it properly, start to finish, once.

options.label: Scroll up looking for my name

insight.reveal: You find what's yours without drowning in the rest. That's a real skill. You tend to answer the single question meant for you, a day late but exactly right, and you rarely miss the deadline that matters.
insight.research: When students kept phone alerts on for a week, they reported more trouble focusing and more restlessness than in a week with alerts off.
insight.step: Today, mute one busy group for a week and see whether you miss anything you'd have wanted.

options.label: Read every message so I don't miss anything

insight.reveal: Being in the loop matters to you more than you let on. You know who's travelling, who's unwell and whose child just finished school, and people come to you for the news. The cost is time, and sometimes the feeling of being everyone's archive.
insight.step: Tonight, skim the group once, close it, and trust that anything big will find its way to you.

options.label: Think about leaving, but stay so nobody's hurt

insight.reveal: Nobody gets left behind on your watch, not even in a group chat. That kindness shows up everywhere: staying at gatherings longer than you planned, saying yes to one more favour. Keeping everyone comfortable may be tiring you more than you let on.
insight.research: Across four studies, helping because you chose to boosted the well-being of both people, while helping under pressure did not bring the same benefits.
insight.step: This week, mute one group instead of leaving it. Nobody is told, and you get some quiet back.

questions.prompt: It's late and you're still scrolling. What's really keeping you there?

options.label: Just one more funny video

insight.reveal: You know how to find a laugh at the end of a long day. That makes you good company, and the funny thing usually gets forwarded the next morning. The catch is that 'one more' never knows where to stop, so your evenings run later than you meant.
insight.research: Children and teens who used a phone or tablet at bedtime were about twice as likely to sleep too little; just having one in the bedroom was linked to worse sleep.
insight.step: Tonight, send the funniest video to a friend, then let that be the last one.

options.label: I'm waiting to feel tired enough to stop

insight.reveal: Your mind needs a soft landing before it lets go of the day. Maybe you keep the radio or TV on for company, or read the same line twice when you're worn out. The screen feels like a way down, though it often keeps your head a step ahead of your body.
insight.research: In a survey of 423 young adults, frequent binge-watchers slept worse and felt more tired, linked to a busier mind at bedtime.
insight.step: Tonight, swap the last ten minutes of scrolling for something slow on paper: a book, a list, a page of notes.

options.label: It's the only time that feels like mine

insight.reveal: Your days go to everyone; the night is when you're yours. Staying up for it usually means you've spent the day being dependable, quick to help and slow to sit down. The scrolling isn't really the point; the freedom is.
insight.research: Many people go to bed later than they meant to for no outside reason; this 'bedtime procrastination' was linked to too little sleep and next-day tiredness.
insight.step: This week, find twenty minutes of daylight that belong only to you, and guard them like a meeting.

options.label: If I put it down, my thoughts will start

insight.reveal: Your phone keeps your thoughts company so you don't have to. It's a clever trick, and a common one. Busy minds often go looking for noise at night and wake more tired for it, and the worries you're dodging often look smaller on paper than in the dark.
insight.research: Most people in 11 studies did not enjoy 6 to 15 minutes alone with just their thoughts, and many gave themselves a mild shock instead.
insight.step: Tonight, before you pick up the phone, write down the three things on your mind, then decide if you still need the scroll.

questions.prompt: A friend calls you instead of sending a text. Your first feeling?

options.label: Glad, I pick up straight away

insight.reveal: A voice means more to you than a typed message. You can sort out in two minutes what a group chat would take two days to settle, and friends feel closer to you after a call than they'd ever guess.
insight.research: People expected a phone call with an old friend to feel more awkward than a text or email, but calls built a stronger bond and weren't more awkward.
insight.step: Today, call one person you'd normally text, even if it's only for two minutes.

options.label: Let it ring, then text 'what's up?'

insight.reveal: Conversations go best for you when you've had a moment to think. Texting lets you choose your words, and what you write is often warmer than what you'd say on the spot. Once you know what a call is about, you're great on it.
insight.research: Calls with friends tended to feel no more awkward than texting, even though people expected them to, and they built a stronger bond.
insight.step: This week, pick up one call without knowing what it's about, and notice how it actually goes.

options.label: Worried that something's wrong

insight.reveal: You care so much that a surprise call sounds like an alarm. When something really is wrong, you show up fast. Most calls turn out to be ordinary, yet your body braces for the worst each time, which is a lot to carry around.
insight.research: People felt most stressed when they couldn't tell whether a bad outcome was coming, more than when it was very likely: not knowing can feel worse than knowing.
insight.step: Next time a call makes your chest tighten, take one slow breath before answering, and let the call tell you the news.

options.label: Dread; I need a minute before I can talk

insight.reveal: Talking on the spot asks a lot of you. Maybe you rehearse a call to a shop before dialling, and feel a little relief when nobody answers. It isn't rudeness; you give conversations your whole self, so you need a moment to gather it.
insight.step: Today, text one friend 'can I call you at six?' A call you've planned often feels lighter than one that surprises you.

questions.prompt: You post something and it gets fewer likes than you expected. You…

options.label: Barely notice; I don't check much

insight.reveal: You post for yourself, and the numbers come second. You share what you actually enjoyed, a meal, a view, a song, rather than what will do well. Funnily enough, that's exactly why friends find your posts so easy to like.
insight.step: This week, post something only because it made you smile, then put the phone away for the evening.

options.label: Check back a few times that day

insight.reveal: You want to know that what you share lands with someone. It isn't vanity; it's the same instinct that makes you watch a friend's face while you tell a story. Offline, you may ask 'was that all right?' a little more often than you need to.
insight.step: Next time you post, wait until evening to look, and notice how your day feels without checking.

options.label: Delete it

insight.reveal: A quiet post can feel to you like a crowd turning away. You may edit yourself in person too, holding back a joke until you're sure it'll land. Yet the version of you that you hide is often the one people would like most.
insight.research: People tend to feel far more noticed than they are: students in an embarrassing T-shirt thought half the room saw it, but only about a quarter did.
insight.step: Next time you want to delete a post, leave it up for a day first and see how you feel tomorrow.

options.label: Wonder if people are tired of me

insight.reveal: You take silence personally because people really matter to you. Likes rise and fall for reasons nobody controls: the hour, the app, a busy week. Your mind still goes to 'is it me?', which usually means you notice when a friend goes quiet, too.
insight.research: People tend to underestimate how much a friend will appreciate a quick message or call out of the blue.
insight.step: Today, send a private message to one person who'd be glad to hear from you. One real reply beats a hundred likes.

questions.prompt: A news alert lights up your screen. What do you do?

options.label: Swipe it away without reading

insight.reveal: You decide when the world gets your attention. That may be why you stay calm when the headlines are loud: you haven't spent the whole week soaking in them. The big news still reaches you, just from a person rather than a ping.
insight.research: Across 48 countries, 40% of people sometimes or often avoid the news, up from 29% in 2017, and most have never had news alerts or have turned them off.
insight.step: This week, choose one time of day for news and switch off the alerts you never open.

options.label: Open it and read the whole story

insight.reveal: A headline is never enough for you; you want the whole story. At lunch, you're the one explaining it to everyone, including the part they missed. Curiosity is your strength, and it can turn one alert into an hour before you notice.
insight.step: Next time you open an alert, give it five minutes, then finish with one question: what actually changed for me?

options.label: Send it to someone to talk it over

insight.reveal: News feels real to you once you've talked it through. There's one person you always message first, and by now they expect it. Sharing helps you make sense of things, and it's also your way of checking that your people are all right.
insight.step: Today, when you share a story, add one line about how you are, not just what happened.

options.label: Keep checking for updates all day

insight.reveal: You stay alert because part of you feels you ought to know. Relatives call you first when something happens, because you'll have the latest. The updates rarely change what you can do, yet each one asks your body to brace again, which can leave you drained by evening.
insight.research: Students reported more trouble focusing and more restlessness in a week with phone alerts on than in a week with them off.
insight.step: Today, after you check once, write down what you'd actually do differently. If nothing, make the next check wait an hour.

questions.prompt: After scrolling through other people's holidays, weddings and wins, you feel…

options.label: Happy for them, mostly

insight.reveal: Other people's good news genuinely warms you. You're first with the congratulations, and you mean every word. Friendships tend to last around someone like you, partly because nobody has to shrink their joy when you're in the room.
insight.research: When someone shares good news, an interested, enthusiastic reply is linked to more trust and closeness, while a flat or distracted one is linked to less.
insight.step: Today, send one person a real message about their news, not just a like.

options.label: Inspired to plan something of my own

insight.reveal: You treat other lives as a menu of ideas, not a scoreboard. Places, recipes and projects become plans for you, and now and then you actually try one. The trick is choosing what you want, not just what looked good in someone else's photo.
insight.research: A friendly kind of envy, wanting what someone has without wishing them harm, pushed people to work harder, but only when they believed they could improve.
insight.step: This week, pick one idea you've saved and take a first small step: a search, a call or a date in the calendar.

options.label: Behind, as if everyone's ahead of me

insight.reveal: You measure yourself more harshly than you'd ever measure a friend. Feeds put everyone's best day beside your ordinary Tuesday, so the contest is never fair. Often what you're working hard on simply doesn't photograph well.
insight.research: People tend to underestimate how often others feel bad and overestimate how often they feel good; those who did this most felt lonelier and less satisfied.
insight.step: Tonight, write down one thing you did this week that nobody posted about, and that you're proud of.

options.label: Lonely, even after seeing everyone

insight.reveal: Seeing everyone at once can leave you further from all of them. That's a sign you want closeness, not more pictures. You light up in a one-to-one conversation, and a single real exchange will do more for you than an hour of scrolling.
insight.research: Students who cut three social apps to 10 minutes each a day for three weeks felt less lonely and less low than students who carried on as usual.
insight.step: Today, pick one face from your feed and send them a message that starts a real conversation.

questions.prompt: Your phone dies and you can't charge it for hours. You feel…

options.label: Free, honestly

insight.reveal: You're at home in the actual room, not the one on your screen. A dead phone feels like a small holiday, and you notice more when it happens: faces, signs, the weather. Friends may find you hard to reach but easy to be with.
insight.step: This week, leave your phone in another room for one hour on purpose and see what you notice.

options.label: Fine, as long as someone knows where I am

insight.reveal: You think ahead for the people who'd worry about you. That's care with a practical side. 'I'll message when I'm home' is a promise you actually keep, and you still know a few important numbers by heart.
insight.step: Today, write two important phone numbers on paper and keep them in your bag or wallet.

options.label: Restless; my hand keeps reaching for it

insight.reveal: Your hand learned a habit your mind never quite agreed to. The reach fills the small gaps: the queue, the lift, the pause in a chat. Strangely, the first hour without it is usually the hardest, and by the third you may feel lighter than you have in weeks.
insight.research: In a small study, young adults used their phones about 85 times a day, more than twice as often as they guessed (37).
insight.step: Next time your hand reaches for a phone that isn't there, look up instead and find one thing you'd have missed.

options.label: Anxious about what I might be missing

insight.reveal: Being reachable feels like part of how you love people. A dead phone can feel like leaving someone waiting at the door. Others rely on you to answer, and that weight is heavy even on a good day, though most things can wait a few hours more easily than you'd think.
insight.research: Without their phone, 72% of US teens at least sometimes feel peaceful, but 44% feel anxious.
insight.step: This week, tell the two people who'd worry most that you'll sometimes be offline, so they can share that load with you.

questions.prompt: How many messages are waiting for your reply right now?

options.label: None; I answer them as they come

insight.reveal: Loose ends bother you, and your messages show it. That makes you easy to plan with, at work and at home. The one risk is that other people's questions get your best minutes before your own plans do.
insight.step: Tomorrow morning, give your first half hour to your own task before you open a single message.

options.label: Lots; I read them and forget to reply

insight.reveal: You live in the moment, and your messages catch up later. Warm in person and patchy in text is a common mix, and friends who know you don't take it personally. A forgotten reply usually means you read it while doing three other things.
insight.step: Today, find the oldest unanswered message and send a short reply, even just 'only seeing this properly now, sorry'.

options.label: A few I'm saving for a longer reply

insight.reveal: A proper reply matters more to you than a fast one. You may keep certain messages marked unread, waiting for a calm moment that rarely comes. The people you write to treasure those long replies, even when they arrive days later.
insight.research: People tend to underestimate how much someone will appreciate a quick message, especially one that arrives as a surprise.
insight.step: This week, answer one saved message with three honest lines instead of waiting for the perfect long reply.

options.label: Some I'm avoiding because the reply feels heavy

insight.reveal: Some replies weigh more than the rest, and you feel every one. The message you're avoiding often holds something without a neat answer yet: a no, an apology, a decision. The longer it waits, the heavier it gets, though the person on the other end is rarely as upset as you picture.
insight.research: People put tasks off most when the task feels unpleasant and they doubt they will manage it.
insight.step: Today, open the heaviest message and write a first line, even if you don't send it yet.

questions.prompt: Your phone shows your weekly screen time. Your first reaction?

options.label: Swipe it away without looking

insight.reveal: You'd rather live your days than count them. You judge a week by how it felt, not by the numbers, and that keeps you light. Every now and then, though, the number could tell you something your feelings are too busy to notice.
insight.research: In data from 355,358 teenagers, screen use explained at most 0.4% of the differences in their wellbeing: a real but very small link.
insight.step: This week, look at the number once, with no plan to change it, and just see whether it surprises you.

options.label: About what I expected

insight.reveal: Your number matched your guess, so you watch your habits closely. You could probably name the app that eats your evenings without looking, and your own week rarely surprises you. Knowing yourself like that makes change easier, whenever you want some.
insight.research: People are poor judges of their own screen time: across 106 comparisons, what they reported rarely matched what their devices actually logged.
insight.step: Today, check which single app took the most time, and decide whether it earned it.

options.label: Shocked, and I promise myself to cut down

insight.reveal: You hold yourself to high standards, and that number stung. You make honest promises, then find the phone back in your hand by evening. That isn't weakness; a vague promise is simply no match for a habit that's always within reach.
insight.research: Across 94 studies, making a specific when-then plan ("When X happens, I will do Y") had a medium-to-large effect on reaching goals.
insight.step: Today, swap 'less phone' for one when-then plan: 'When I sit down to eat, my phone stays in my bag.'

options.label: A bit sad about what those hours could have been

insight.reveal: You care about your time because you care about your life. That small sadness points at what you'd rather be doing: a book, a walk, a friend. Once you name the thing you actually miss, you're the kind of person who makes real room for it.
insight.step: Tonight, name one thing you'd love more of, and give it the first half hour you'd usually give your phone.

questions.prompt: You're stuck in traffic and nothing has moved for ten minutes. You…

options.label: Put on music or a podcast and wait

insight.reveal: Traffic doesn't steal your day, because you won't let it. You're the calm one in the car, the bus or the taxi, with something good to listen to. Stuck time becomes found time for you, which is why you tend to arrive in a good mood.
insight.step: This week, save one podcast or playlist just for slow traffic, so a jam becomes something you almost look forward to.

options.label: Check the map for a faster way

insight.reveal: Sitting still bothers you more than a longer road does. You know three routes to every place and always have a plan B. That same energy makes you handy in a crisis, though now and then the shortcut takes longer than the wait would have.
insight.step: Next jam, stay on the usual road once and compare. It might tell you something about your need to act.

options.label: Get tense and keep checking the time

insight.reveal: Being on time matters to you because people are counting on you. Each glance at the clock is you carrying them along. You leave early for important things, so a jam feels like letting someone down even when it's nobody's fault.
insight.step: Next time, once it's safe to, send one 'running late' message, then stop watching the clock until you arrive.

options.label: Sigh, mutter or lean on the horn

insight.reveal: Stuck time lands in your whole body. You're probably a doer who minds waiting far more than hard work. The muttering feels like letting off steam, yet it usually leaves you more wound up by the time you finally arrive.
insight.research: People who vented anger while dwelling on the person who annoyed them became angrier and more aggressive than people who did nothing.
insight.step: Next jam, try one slow breath out each time you want to hit the horn, and notice how you feel when you arrive.

questions.prompt: You're going to be fifteen minutes late. What do you do?

options.label: Message them before they notice

insight.reveal: The person waiting is never far from your mind. You apologise quickly and sincerely, and you're forgiven just as quickly. Friends trust your plans because even when you're late, they're never left guessing.
insight.step: Next time you run late, give them something to do with the wait, like 'order without me' or 'grab us a seat'.

options.label: Hurry and hope to make it up on the way

insight.reveal: You're an optimist about time, and sometimes time wins. You believe one more task fits before you leave, and it nearly does. You're brilliant at the last-minute dash, though the rush can follow you in through the door.
insight.research: People tend to underestimate how long tasks take: students' everyday tasks took nearly twice as long as they predicted.
insight.step: Next time you're getting ready, leave the moment you think 'just one more thing', and do that thing when you're back.

options.label: Turn up late; everyone's a bit late anyway

insight.reveal: You see time as flexible, and in plenty of places it is. You rarely mind waiting yourself, and you'd never let a schedule cut short a good conversation. Just know that your clock isn't always theirs, and the person waiting may be counting the minutes.
insight.research: People tend to overestimate how many others share their own choices and opinions (the false consensus effect).
insight.step: This week, for one plan that matters to someone else, arrive five minutes early and notice how they greet you.

options.label: Feel awful about it the whole way there

insight.reveal: Other people's time is precious to you, so lateness stings. Being late feels like breaking a small promise. You're early most days, which is why the rare late one hurts so much, and the person waiting is likely far less upset than you are.
insight.research: Across 65 samples with nearly 18,000 people, those better able to forgive themselves after doing wrong tended to have better well-being.
insight.step: Next time you're late, send one apology and let it be. One sorry is enough; a second only takes something from you.

questions.prompt: On your usual daily journey, how do you spend the time?

options.label: Look out of the window and let my mind drift
