insight.research: In 5,276 US adults over 50 followed for 4 years, those who felt their neighbourhood was close-knit and trusting were less likely to have a heart attack.
insight.step: This week, introduce two neighbours to each other who you think would get along.

options.label: A few nearby

insight.reveal: You know the ones who matter to your daily life. A small, solid set of neighbours is your go-to when the power cuts out or a parcel arrives, and that handful can turn into real friends over time.
insight.research: When new students were given random seats, those placed next to each other tended to be closer friends a year later: being near someone makes friendship more likely.
insight.step: Next time you pass a neighbour you only nod to, ask their name, and use it the time after.

options.label: I know faces, not names

insight.reveal: You recognise everyone, but you've never quite crossed the bridge. After years of nodding, asking a name can feel too late, yet the neighbour often feels exactly the same and would be relieved if you asked.
insight.research: In 12 experiments, conversations with strangers felt less awkward and more enjoyable than people expected, and they underestimated how interested the other person would be.
insight.step: Say "I don't think we've ever properly met" to one familiar face this week, and swap names.

options.label: I've lived here a while and know almost no one

insight.reveal: Your home is private, and the street stays outside it. Your community probably lives elsewhere, at work, in faith, with friends or online, but one neighbour you could knock on in an emergency can make home feel surprisingly different.
insight.research: In a 2025 US survey, only 26% knew all or most of their neighbours, yet 59% had one they'd feel comfortable asking to keep a spare key.
insight.step: Greet one neighbour today and say your name. That's all; it's a start.

questions.prompt: Someone in your neighbourhood has died, and neighbours are gathering to help. You…

options.label: Go and help with whatever's needed

insight.reveal: You show up with your hands when words aren't enough. You're likely the one carrying chairs, cooking or making calls, and grieving families often remember those practical helpers more vividly than any speech.
insight.research: Following 233 grieving adults for two years, longing for the person who died was the strongest painful feeling, peaking around four months after the loss.
insight.step: This week, check in on the family again, after the crowds have gone home.

options.label: Send a contribution and my condolences

insight.reveal: You honour a loss in a steady, respectful way. Giving like this makes you someone the community counts on, and families tend to notice who remembered them, even when they can't thank everyone in person.
insight.step: Next time, add one handwritten line: a memory or a kind word about the person who died.

options.label: Want to go, but don't know what to say

insight.reveal: You care, and you're afraid of saying the wrong thing. Hesitating like this often comes from being sensitive to other people's pain, and grieving families tend to remember who came and sat with them more than the exact words.
insight.step: Next time, just go and say "I'm so sorry." Those few words are enough.

options.label: Stay home; it brings back my own losses

insight.reveal: Someone else's loss can stir up your own, so you stay close to home. Staying back isn't coldness; it usually means you've loved and lost deeply and know your limits, and a quiet gesture from a distance still counts.
insight.research: People who did a small ritual after a loss felt less grief and upset, mainly because it gave them a sense of control, even if they didn't believe in rituals.
insight.step: This week, light a candle, say a prayer or write a few words for your own loved one, in your own way.

questions.prompt: A neighbour's family is planning a big wedding and asks the street to pitch in. You…

options.label: Join in, I love a celebration

insight.reveal: You're happiest when the whole street shares the joy. Parties run on your energy, and you may end up on the organising team for the next event before you've even noticed you volunteered.
insight.research: Tasting chocolate at the same moment as another person made good chocolate taste better and bitter chocolate worse: sharing an experience tends to make it feel stronger.
insight.step: Offer to help with one fun part of the preparations this week: the music, the food or the decorations.

options.label: Help with one clear task

insight.reveal: You like to help in a way you can finish and do well. Choosing one clear job makes you the quiet engine of community events: when you say you'll bring the chairs, the chairs arrive, and organisers learn fast who they can rely on.
insight.step: Next time you're asked to help, name the exact task and time you can give.

options.label: Send something, but stay out of the fuss

insight.reveal: You're generous, and you'd rather give from a quiet distance. Celebrations get your support in your own way, and you might be surprised how much a short appearance, even half an hour, means to the family.
insight.step: At the next local celebration, go for just thirty minutes, then feel free to leave.

options.label: Feel pressure to give more than I can

insight.reveal: You want to give well, and your budget can't always keep up. That pressure brings a quiet shame it doesn't deserve: families tend to remember who came and helped, and help you can give gladly usually does more good for both of you than help squeezed out by pressure.
insight.research: Across four studies, helping because you chose to boosted the well-being of both helper and helped, while helping under pressure did not bring the same benefits.
insight.step: Decide today what you can give comfortably, before anyone asks, and stick to it with a smile.

questions.prompt: At your local shop or market stall, how much do you chat?

options.label: Just a quick greeting

insight.reveal: You keep it friendly and simple, then get on with your day. That efficiency runs through much of your life, and you might be surprised how well the shopkeeper knows you: the polite regular who always says thank you.
insight.research: On days when people had more chats with casual acquaintances, not just close friends, they tended to feel happier and a stronger sense of belonging.
insight.step: Next time you're there, ask the shopkeeper one small question, like how business is going.

options.label: We catch up on news

insight.reveal: You treat the local shop as part of your social world. What's happening nearby reaches you early, and the shopkeeper may well save a bit of news, or the last loaf, just for you.
insight.step: Pass on one bit of good local news you heard at the shop today.

options.label: I hear all the local gossip there

insight.reveal: You're plugged into the street's quiet news network. Hearing everything makes you a keeper of local stories, and how you choose to pass them on can shape the way people on your street see each other.
insight.step: Next time you hear gossip, pass on only what would help someone, and let the rest stop with you.

options.label: Sometimes it's the only real chat of my day

insight.reveal: That small chat carries real weight in your day. Quiet stretches between conversations can feel long, and adding a few more small, regular contacts, a neighbour, a call, a class, tends to warm up the whole week.
insight.research: People tended to feel happier and a stronger sense of belonging on days when they had more chats with casual acquaintances.
insight.step: Add one more small, regular chat to your days this week: a call, a walk with someone, a class.

questions.prompt: There's a local meeting about your area this evening. Do you go?

options.label: Yes, I like knowing what's going on

insight.reveal: You want a say in the place you live. The broken light or the new plan catches your eye early, and over time neighbours may start bringing their concerns to you without being asked.
insight.step: At the next meeting, share one small idea, even if it's just about a light or a bin.

options.label: Only if it affects my home

insight.reveal: You save your energy for what touches your life directly. That practical streak means you show up when it counts, and your voice may carry extra weight because people know you only speak when it matters.
insight.step: Ask a neighbour this week what's been decided lately, so nothing catches you off guard.

options.label: No, meetings feel like a waste of an evening

insight.reveal: You'd rather spend the evening on your own life than on long talks. Your help likely comes in other ways, and now and then you can find decisions made without you that you'd have liked a say in.
insight.research: At US town meetings about new housing, the people who spoke up were more often older, male, long-time homeowners, and far more opposed to new homes than residents overall.
insight.step: This month, ask someone what was decided at a meeting, just once, and see if anything matters to you.

options.label: Go, but never speak up

insight.reveal: You care enough to come, and you keep your thoughts to yourself. Your ideas are usually well thought through, and meetings tend to hear from the same few voices, so when you do speak, people often lean in.
insight.research: At US town meetings on new housing, those who spoke up were more often older, male, long-time homeowners, far more opposed to new homes than residents overall.
insight.step: At the next meeting, ask one question. A question is often easier than an opinion.

questions.prompt: A new family moves in next door. What do you do?

options.label: Wave and say hello when I see them

insight.reveal: You're friendly without making a fuss of it. Letting things grow at their own pace suits you, and a casual hello now often leads, months later, to a neighbour you can truly count on.
insight.research: It takes time to make a friend: on average about 50 hours together to become casual friends, and over 200 hours to become close friends.
insight.step: This week, add one line to your hello, like "Let me know if you need anything."

options.label: Knock and introduce myself

insight.reveal: You open the door to newcomers, sometimes literally. New arrivals feel at home quickly around you, and you may become their first stop for every local question, from the best bread to the nearest clinic.
insight.step: Next time someone new arrives, bring a small welcome: a snack, or a list of useful numbers.

options.label: Wait for them to come to me

insight.reveal: You'd rather be found than go looking. Reserve like yours usually melts once someone makes the first move, and you might be surprised to learn the newcomers were waiting too, unsure whether to knock.
insight.research: Commuters asked to talk to a stranger had a nicer ride than those who sat alone, though most expected the opposite, assuming others wouldn't want to talk.
insight.step: Take the first step this week: one wave, one hello, and let them do the rest.

options.label: Watch quietly to see what they're like

insight.reveal: You like to know who people are before you let them close. Your instincts are probably good and you rarely get burned, though the watching can last so long that newcomers decide you're not interested.
insight.step: Next time you see them, say hello first, even while you're still making up your mind.

questions.prompt: Rubbish keeps piling up in one spot on your street. What do you do?

options.label: Pick some up when I pass

insight.reveal: You fix small things without waiting for permission. The office kitchen, the bus seat, the shared yard: every place ends up a little better for your passing, and a tidier spot tends to stay tidier, because people litter less where it's already clean.
insight.research: In field experiments, people dropped litter more in places already littered (41%) than in clean ones (11%).
insight.step: This week, pick up three pieces of litter on your street, and notice if anyone joins you.

options.label: Report it to whoever's in charge

insight.reveal: Problems, in your view, belong with the people who can solve them. You know which office or number handles what, and neighbours may already be asking you how to get things done around here.
insight.step: Today, save the contact for whoever handles rubbish or repairs in your area.

options.label: Get a few neighbours together to clear it

insight.reveal: You turn a shared problem into a shared afternoon. A single clean-up often leaves a street with something better than tidiness: neighbours who now know each other, helpers who feel good about pitching in, and a thank-you or two with your name on it.
insight.research: A review of 40 papers found volunteers tended to report better well-being and life satisfaction, though the few experiments didn't show clear health gains.
insight.step: Ask one neighbour today if they'd help with a short clean-up, and pick a date together.

options.label: Get annoyed each time, but leave it

insight.reveal: It bothers you every time, and you still walk past. When a problem belongs to everyone, it feels like it belongs to no one. That small daily irritation tends to fade fast once you do one tiny thing about it.
insight.step: Tomorrow, do one tiny thing about it, pick up one piece or send one message, and see how you feel.

questions.prompt: Someone invites you to join a local group, like a savings circle, sports club or choir. You…

options.label: Go once and see

insight.reveal: You're curious enough to try and free enough to leave. A few groups may get a visit before one sticks, and when it does, you'll bring fresh energy from everywhere you've been.
insight.step: This month, go to one local gathering you've never tried, just once.

options.label: Join happily, I like belonging to something

insight.reveal: Belonging to a group feels like home to you. You remember birthdays, chase contributions and keep the chat alive, and all that care builds you a wide safety net for when life gets hard.
insight.research: In over 5,000 adults followed for years, belonging to more groups went with less low mood later.
insight.step: Invite one person who seems a bit alone to come along to your group this week.

options.label: Say maybe, then never go

insight.reveal: Your maybe is a kind way of saying not yet. The idea of the group appeals more than the first awkward visit, and that's normal: the first meeting is the hardest one, and after it, faces start becoming names.
insight.step: This week, go to one meeting of a group you said maybe to, with a friend if it helps.

options.label: Decline; groups make me feel on show

insight.reveal: Groups put you on a stage you never asked for. Fewer eyes are on you than it feels, but one-on-one is still where you shine, and groups built around doing something together, cooking, walking, fixing, suit you best, because nobody has to perform.
insight.research: Students made to wear an embarrassing T-shirt guessed that about half the room noticed it; only about a quarter did. People overestimate how much others notice them.
insight.step: This month, look for one small group where people do an activity side by side, not just talk.
